Two running examples
  • Two qubits, N = 4. Here sin α = 1/2, so α = 30°, and a single Grover iteration lands exactly on the marked item. Every matrix is 4 × 4 or smaller, so each claim in the chapter can be checked by hand.
  • Four qubits, N = 16. This is the paper's own example in Section IV. Here α = arcsin(1/4) ≈ 0.2527 rad ≈ 14.5°, the best count is r0 = 3, and three iterations overshoot the target by about 0.2 rad, leaving a noiseless success probability of 0.9613. Three of the four animations run on this register.
1 · SEARCHING WITHOUT STRUCTURE

What problem does Grover's algorithm solve, and how is it set up?

Suppose a function f on n-bit strings returns 1 on exactly one string w and 0 everywhere else, and the only way to learn anything about f is to evaluate it. A classical computer has no choice but to try strings one by one, so on average it needs about N/2 evaluations to find w. Grover's algorithm needs about (π/4)√N. For a million items that is roughly 785 queries instead of 500,000, and the paper notes that no quantum algorithm can do better. The point of the paper is to ask how much of this square-root advantage survives when the hardware is noisy.

The quantum computer holds a register of n qubits. Its state is a unit vector in an N-dimensional complex vector space, written in the basis of the N bit strings: |ψ⟩ = Σx cx|x⟩ with Σ|cx|2 = 1. Measuring the register returns the string x with probability |cx|2. Inner products ⟨φ|ψ⟩ = Σx conj(bx)cx work as for ordinary vectors, and an outer product |φ⟩⟨φ| is the matrix that projects onto |φ⟩. Gates are unitary matrices, which preserve lengths and angles.

The algorithm starts in |0⟩⊗n, the all-zeros string (Eq. 1), and a layer of Hadamard gates turns this into the equal superposition

Eq. 2

Measuring |s⟩ right away would give w with probability 1/N, no better than a random guess. The rest of the algorithm is a sequence of r identical Grover iterations, each of which queries f once and moves probability toward w.

Definition · the search plane

Let |w⟩ be the marked basis state and |w⊥⟩ = (N − 1)−1/2 Σx≠w |x⟩ the normalized superposition of all unmarked states. The Grover plane is the two-dimensional subspace spanned by these two orthonormal vectors. In it,

Eq. 3

In words: the starting state is a unit vector lying almost along the "unmarked" axis, tilted toward the "marked" axis by a small angle α. The whole noiseless algorithm happens inside this plane.

For the two-qubit example, |w⟩ = |00⟩ and |w⊥⟩ = (|01⟩ + |10⟩ + |11⟩)/√3. The overlap ⟨w|s⟩ is 1/2, so sin α = 1/2 and α = 30°. For four qubits, sin α = 1/4 and α ≈ 0.2527 rad. For large N the angle is small, α ≈ 1/√N.

In short: the register's state is a unit vector; the equal superposition |s⟩ sits at the small angle α = arcsin(1/√N) from the unmarked direction, inside a plane that contains the answer.

2 · TWO REFLECTIONS MAKE A ROTATION

How does each iteration move the state toward the answer?

The oracle is how the algorithm asks f a question. Instead of writing f(x) into a separate bit, it writes the answer into a sign: Uf|x⟩ = (−1)f(x)|x⟩ (Eq. 5). Only the marked state changes, and because the basis projectors sum to the identity, the oracle has a compact form.

Eq. 7

This is a reflection. It leaves every vector orthogonal to |w⟩ alone and reverses the component along |w⟩. In the Grover plane it flips the state across the |w⊥⟩ axis, sending an angle θ to −θ.

The second ingredient is the diffusion operator V = H⊗nU0H⊗n, where U0 = 2|0⟩⟨0| − I reflects about the all-zeros state (Eqs. 9 and 10). Since the Hadamard layer sends |0⟩⊗n to |s⟩, conjugating by it turns a reflection about |0⟩ into a reflection about |s⟩.

Eq. 11

In terms of amplitudes, V replaces each cx by 2m − cx, where m is the mean amplitude, so it is often described as inversion about the mean. After the oracle has made the marked amplitude negative, it sits far below the mean, and inverting about the mean lifts it far above.

derivationWhy is 2|s⟩⟨s| − I the same as inversion about the mean?

For any state Σcx|x⟩, the inner product ⟨s|ψ⟩ is Σcx/√N = √N m, where m is the mean amplitude. So 2|s⟩⟨s|ψ⟩ = 2√N m · (1/√N)Σ|x⟩ = Σ 2m|x⟩. Subtracting |ψ⟩ leaves Σ(2m − cx)|x⟩. Each amplitude is reflected through the value m.

∎

Fact · one iteration is a rotation by 2α

The Grover iteration G = VUf maps the plane to itself and rotates it by the angle 2α toward |w⟩. After r iterations,

Eqs. 14 and 15

proofWhy does a reflection followed by another reflection give a rotation by twice the angle between their axes?

The paper's argument is geometric. Start at angle θ from |w⊥⟩. The oracle reflects across the |w⊥⟩ axis, to −θ. The diffusion step reflects across the line through |s⟩, which sits at angle α; reflecting an angle φ across a line at angle α gives 2α − φ. So −θ goes to 2α + θ. Each iteration adds 2α, and starting from θ = α gives (2r + 1)α after r rounds.

In the basis {|w⊥⟩, |w⟩} the paper writes V explicitly as cos 2α on the diagonal and sin 2α off it (Eq. 12). In the density-matrix language of the paper, one iteration takes ρ2 = |s⟩⟨s| to a matrix with sin23α on |w⟩⟨w|, cos23α on |w⊥⟩⟨w⊥|, and (sin 6α)/2 on the off-diagonal entries (Eq. 13), which is |ψ1⟩⟨ψ1| at angle 3α.

∎

The success probability peaks when (2r + 1)α is closest to π/2. For large N, with α ≈ 1/√N, this gives the familiar count

Eq. 16

Both running examples make this concrete. For N = 4, one iteration takes the angle from 30° to 90°, exactly onto |w⟩, and the success probability is sin290° = 1. In amplitudes: the four amplitudes start at 1/2 each, the oracle makes the marked one −1/2, the mean becomes 1/4, and inversion about the mean sends −1/2 to 1 and each 1/2 to 0. For N = 16 the angle after r = 1, 2, 3 is 3α, 5α, 7α, with success probabilities 0.4727, 0.9084 and 0.9613. Since 7α ≈ 1.769 exceeds π/2 by about 0.198 rad, the third iteration slightly overshoots, which the paper notes will matter in Section 9. A fourth iteration would carry the state further past the target, down to 0.5817.

The animation runs the full 16-dimensional state vector through four iterations. The left panel shows the 16 amplitudes; the right panel shows the same state as an arrow in the Grover plane. Watch the oracle flip the arrow below the axis and the diffusion step swing it back above, each round ending 2α higher than the last.

Animation · Grover on 16 items
marked amplitudeunmarked amplitudesmean, |s⟩ direction

The animation multiplies the 16-entry vector by Uf and V directly; the angle shown is computed from the amplitudes, not assumed. Its numbers agree with Eq. 15 to every digit shown.

In short: the oracle reflects across the unmarked axis, the diffusion step reflects across |s⟩, and together they rotate the state by 2α, so about (π/4)√N iterations reach the answer.

3 · DENSITY MATRICES AND NOISE

How do we describe a state that has been hit by random errors?

A state vector describes a register we know perfectly. Once errors strike at random, the register is in state |ψ1⟩ with some probability and |ψ2⟩ with another, and the right description is a weighted average of projectors. This is the density matrix, and the paper uses it from its first equation on.

Definition · density matrix

If the register is in state |ψi⟩ with probability qi, its density matrix is ρ = Σi qi|ψi⟩⟨ψi|. The probability of measuring x is the diagonal entry ⟨x|ρ|x⟩, and a gate U acts as ρ ↦ UρU†.

In words: a matrix whose diagonal holds the measurement probabilities (the populations) and whose off-diagonal entries (the coherences) record how much the components can still interfere.

For a pure state such as |s⟩ every coherence is as large as it can be. At the other extreme sits the maximally mixed state I/N, whose diagonal is uniform and whose coherences are all zero: it is the state of a register about which nothing is known, and measuring it gives a uniformly random string. Interference, the engine of Grover's algorithm, lives in the off-diagonal entries. Noise eats them.

On one qubit, any error between two gates can be expanded in the Pauli operators X (the bit flip, swapping |0⟩ and |1⟩), Z (the phase flip, negating |1⟩) and Y = iXZ (both at once). The general Pauli channel applies each with some probability.

Eq. 17

Three cases are standard. The bit-flip channel has (px, py, pz) = (p, 0, 0), the phase-flip channel (0, 0, p), and the depolarizing channel (p/3, p/3, p/3), which is the same as replacing the qubit by I/2 with probability 4p/3. The paper always compares channels at the same total error probability p, so that differences come from the kind of error and not its frequency.

A one-qubit example shows how differently X and Z treat the same state. Take |+⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2, whose density matrix has all four entries equal to 1/2. A bit flip maps |+⟩ to itself, so the bit-flip channel leaves this state alone. A phase flip maps it to |−⟩ = (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2, so the phase-flip channel keeps the diagonal at 1/2 but multiplies the off-diagonal entries by 1 − 2p. Which error hurts depends on which state it hits. This simple observation, scaled up to n qubits, is the heart of Section 6.

The paper places a noise channel on every qubit after every gate layer: once after the initial Hadamard layer and, inside each iteration, after the oracle, after the first Hadamard layer of the diffusion step, and after U0. A circuit with r iterations therefore has 3r + 1 noise layers and n(3r + 1) chances for an error. This models both gate errors and idle decoherence.

In short: a density matrix stores populations on its diagonal and interference in its coherences; a Pauli channel applies X, Y or Z at random, and the paper puts one on every qubit after every gate layer, 3r + 1 layers in all.

4 · AN EXACTLY SOLVABLE CASE

What happens if the whole register is depolarized at once?

Independent channels on n qubits push the state out of the Grover plane, and no exact solution for all N is available. So the paper first solves a cleaner reference model, in which each noise layer acts on the register as a whole.

Definition · global depolarizing channel

Eq. 18

In words: during each gate layer, with probability pg the register forgets everything and becomes uniformly random; otherwise nothing happens.

The key property is that the identity matrix does not care which gate acts on it: UIU† = I for every unitary U. So

Eq. 19

The channel commutes with every gate, and that makes everything solvable. All 3r + 1 channels can be slid to the end of the circuit. Each multiplies whatever coherent part remains by 1 − pg and moves the lost weight into I/N.

Fact · Eq. 29 and Eq. 30

After r noisy iterations the state is the noiseless Grover state with a geometrically decaying weight, plus a uniform remainder, and the success probability is

Eq. 30

derivationHow do the four channels of one iteration collapse into one factor?

The paper traces one iteration slice by slice (Eqs. 20 to 28). After the initial Hadamard layer and the first channel, the state is (1 − pg)|s⟩⟨s| + (pg/N)I. The oracle acts on the first term and leaves the second alone, by Eq. 19. The next channel gives (1 − pg)2Uf|s⟩⟨s|Uf + [1 − (1 − pg)2]I/N, because a channel applied to aρ + (1 − a)I/N gives (1 − pg)aρ + [1 − (1 − pg)a]I/N: the uniform part stays uniform and the weights still sum to one. Repeating through the Hadamard layer, U0 and the last Hadamard layer gives

Eq. 28

That is four factors: the one after the initial Hadamard layer and the three inside the iteration. Every later iteration contributes three more, for 3r + 1 in total (Eq. 29). The |w⟩ population of |ψr⟩⟨ψr| is sin2[(2r + 1)α], and that of I/N is 1/N, which gives Eq. 30.

∎

Equation 30 is a damped oscillation in r. The oscillation is the ordinary Grover rotation with the same period; the damping factor (1 − pg)3r+1 is the probability that the register has survived every channel. Noise does not slow the rotation. It drains the rotating part.

The two-qubit example can be done by hand. With r = 1 and pg = 0.1, the weight is 0.94 = 0.6561, the noiseless success probability is 1, and the floor contributes (1 − 0.6561)/4 ≈ 0.0860, so P1 ≈ 0.7421 (our arithmetic). For four qubits with pg = 0.02, Eq. 30 gives 0.4408, 0.7969 and 0.7969 at r = 1, 2, 3, against 0.4727, 0.9084 and 0.9613 without noise: at this noise level two iterations are already as good as three.

The animation below simulates the full 16 × 16 density matrix of the four-qubit register, applying the global channel after every gate layer exactly as in the paper's circuit, and plots the success probability after each iteration. The simulation does not use Eq. 30; it confirms it.

Animation · damped Grover oscillation
noisy Pr (density-matrix simulation)noiselessweight (1 − pg)3r+1

For every setting the simulated values agree with Eq. 30 to at least four decimal places (our check). The oscillation keeps its period; only its height shrinks, toward the floor at 1/16.

In short: a global depolarizing channel commutes with every gate, so the noisy state is the noiseless one with weight (1 − pg)3r+1 plus a uniform remainder, which gives the exact damped oscillation of Eq. 30.

5 · WHEN TO STOP, AND WHAT IT COSTS

How does noise change the best number of iterations and the cost of the search?

Once the success probability is known exactly, the practical questions are how high it can get, when to stop, and how many oracle queries a search costs on average. The answers depend on N and pg mainly through the product pg√N, which measures the noise accumulated over a full-length circuit.

For weak noise, stopping at the noiseless optimum costs about 3r0 ≈ (3π/4)√N layers' worth of survival probability.

Eq. 31

A database four times larger needs twice as many iterations, so for the same loss it tolerates only half the noise per gate layer.

The best stopping point moves earlier, because each extra iteration gains a little rotation but costs three more channels. Setting dPr/dr = 0 in Eq. 30, with λ = 1 − pg, gives a balance between the two (Eq. 32): the gain 2α sin[2(2r + 1)α] on the left and the loss 3 ln(1/λ){sin2[(2r + 1)α] − 1/N} on the right. Solving near the noiseless optimum gives the shift.

Eq. 33

derivationWhere does 3pg(N − 1)/8 come from?

The paper writes (2r + 1)α = π/2 − ε with ε small and uses ln(1/λ) ≈ pg and α2 ≈ 1/N. The details below are our filling-in of that step. The left side of Eq. 32 becomes 2α sin(π − 2ε) ≈ 4αε. The right side becomes 3pg(cos2ε − 1/N) ≈ 3pg(N − 1)/N. Setting them equal, ε ≈ 3pg(N − 1)/(4αN). Since ε = 2α(r0 − r) when r0 is the exact noiseless optimum, r0 − r* ≈ 3pg(N − 1)/(8α2N) ≈ 3pg(N − 1)/8.

∎

The shift grows like pgN, faster than r0 itself, so once pg√N is of order one it is no longer a small correction. When pg√N ≫ 1 (with pg still small), the coherent part dies long before the rotation gets anywhere, sin[(2r + 1)α] ≈ (2r + 1)α, and maximizing λ3r+1(2r + 1)2 gives

Eq. 34

derivationWhy does the best count stop depending on N?

This calculation is ours, filling in the paper's one-line statement. Write λ3r+1 ≈ e−pg(3r+1) and set the derivative of −pg(3r + 1) + 2 ln(2r + 1) to zero: 3pg = 4/(2r + 1), so 2r + 1 = 4/(3pg), which is Eq. 34's r*. At that point 3r + 1 = (3/2)(2r + 1) − 1/2 ≈ 2/pg, so the weight is about e−2, and the success probability is e−2(2r + 1)2α2 ≈ e−2 · 16/(9pg2) · 1/N. Nothing about N enters r*: the register simply cannot survive more than about 2/pg layers.

∎

The cost of a search is the next question. A run with r iterations makes r queries and succeeds with probability Pr. Repeating until a check confirms the answer takes 1/Pr runs on average, so the expected number of queries is

Eq. 35

Its noiseless value Q0 is slightly below r0, because stopping a bit before the peak and repeating occasionally is cheaper than always running to the peak. For weak noise Q*/Q0 ≈ exp(3πpg√N/4), so the overhead depends only on pg√N. For strong noise, minimizing Eq. 35 directly gives

Eq. 36

derivationWhere does the constant 3e/4 come from?

Our filling-in. In the strong-noise regime, Pr ≈ e−3pgr(2r)2/N for large r, so Q(r) ≈ N e3pgr/(4r). The function e3pgr/r is smallest where 3pg = 1/r, that is r = 1/(3pg), and there Q ≈ N · e · 3pg/4. Minimizing Q directly picks a count about half of the r* that maximizes P, because a cheap run that succeeds less often can still win on average.

∎

Fact · the speedup has a horizon

Under global depolarizing noise the query cost follows the √N law while pg√N is small, and becomes linear in N, about 2pgN, once pg√N is large. The bend in the paper's Fig. 4 sits where pg√N reaches about one half, so the largest useful register is about nmax ≈ 2 log2(1/pg).

The linear regime is not a failure of the analysis but a known limit: the paper notes that lower bounds by Vrana, Reeb, Reitzner and Wolf and by Rosmanis show that any search against an oracle that depolarizes with fixed probability needs of order pN queries. Eq. 36 says Grover's algorithm, stopped at the right time and repeated, attains that bound with a small constant, keeping only a factor of about 4pg over a classical scan of half the database.

As a check on all of this, we evaluated Eq. 30 numerically at n = 16 and n = 20 (our computation). At n = 16 and pg = 0.0005, so pg√N = 0.128, the best count is 188, where Eq. 33 predicts 188.3. At n = 20 and pg = 0.01, so pg√N ≈ 10, the best count is 65 against 66.2 from Eq. 34, and the least expected cost is about 21,070 queries against 21,380 from Eq. 36. On the four-qubit register the regimes are too close together for the formulas to apply, and the noiseless cost there is lowest at r = 1, about 2.1 queries, which is a small-N effect.

In short: noise pulls the best stopping point earlier by about 3pgN/8 and lowers the peak to about e−3πpg√N/4; once pg√N ≫ 1 the cost becomes about 2pgN, linear like classical search.

6 · LOCAL NOISE: WHAT ONE ERROR DOES

Why are some errors more harmful than others, and when?

Real errors strike individual qubits, not the whole register. Such errors do not commute with the gates, and they push the state out of the Grover plane. The paper's key observation is that the Grover operator treats everything outside the plane in the simplest possible way.

Fact · amplitude outside the plane is frozen

Eq. 37

In words: on the orthogonal complement of the search plane, an ideal Grover iteration only flips the sign. It never amplifies such amplitude and never brings it back into the plane.

proofWhy is G just −1 off the plane?

Let |χ⟩ be orthogonal to both |w⟩ and |w⊥⟩. Since |s⟩ lies in their span, |χ⟩ is also orthogonal to |s⟩. Then Uf|χ⟩ = |χ⟩ − 2|w⟩⟨w|χ⟩ = |χ⟩, and V|χ⟩ = 2|s⟩⟨s|χ⟩ − |χ⟩ = −|χ⟩. So G|χ⟩ = VUf|χ⟩ = −|χ⟩.

∎

Since only the in-plane part of the state can ever reach |w⟩, the effect of a single Pauli error is decided by its in-plane part. Taking w = 0⋯0 without loss of generality and writing Π for the projector onto the plane, the paper computes, for a Pauli on any qubit k,

Eq. 38

checkDo these formulas hold for two qubits?

Our check, with N = 4, w = 00 and an error on the first qubit. The phase flip Z1 leaves |00⟩ alone and sends |w⊥⟩ = (|01⟩ + |10⟩ + |11⟩)/√3 to (|01⟩ − |10⟩ − |11⟩)/√3, whose overlap with |w⊥⟩ is (1 − 1 − 1)/3 = −1/3 = −1/(N − 1). The bit flip X1 sends |00⟩ to |10⟩, whose overlap with |w⊥⟩ is 1/√3 = 1/√(N − 1), and sends |w⊥⟩ to (|11⟩ + |00⟩ + |01⟩)/√3, with overlap 2/3 = (N − 2)/(N − 1) with |w⊥⟩ and 1/√3 with |w⟩. All four entries match Eq. 38.

∎

For a large database, drop the terms of order 1/√N and the picture becomes stark. A phase flip keeps the marked component, since Zk|w⟩ = ±|w⟩, but scrambles the signs of the unmarked component and throws it almost entirely out of the plane. A bit flip does the opposite: flipping one bit of an unmarked string almost always gives another unmarked string, so the unmarked component stays, while Xk|w⟩ is an unmarked basis state and leaves. A Y error throws out both. Either way the coherence between |w⊥⟩ and |w⟩ is gone.

Now combine this with the rotation. Suppose one error strikes when the in-plane state is at angle θ, and the remaining iterations would have carried it to π/2. After a phase flip only sin θ|w⟩ is left, at angle π/2, and the remaining rotation carries it on to π − θ. After a bit flip only cos θ|w⊥⟩ is left, at angle 0, carried to π/2 − θ. The success probabilities are

Eqs. 39 and 40

and P(Y) ≈ 1/N. The two basic errors are dangerous at opposite times. A phase flip is worst early, when almost all the amplitude is unmarked: one phase flip right after the initial Hadamard layer leaves a success probability of order 1/N. A bit flip is worst late, when the amplitude has gathered on |w⟩, and a bit flip at the very start costs nothing at all, because Xk|s⟩ = |s⟩. A Y error is fatal at any time.

Fact · average cost of one error

Averaging over a full search, with θ sweeping uniformly from 0 to π/2, a phase flip or a bit flip costs a fraction

Eq. 41

of the success probability, and a Y error costs cY = 1. The paper notes that 5/8 agrees with Azuma's earlier perturbative result for phase errors.

derivationWhy is the average of sin⁴θ equal to 3/8?

Our filling-in. Using sin2θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2, sin4θ = (1 − 2cos 2θ + cos22θ)/4 = 3/8 − (cos 2θ)/2 + (cos 4θ)/8. Over 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2 the cosines average to zero, leaving 3/8. The same holds for cos4θ, which is why cX = cZ.

∎

The animation tests these predictions on an eight-qubit register, N = 256, where r0 = 12. For each error time j from 0 to 12 it runs the full 256-entry state vector, inserts a single Pauli error on one qubit just before the oracle of iteration j + 1 (when the state sits at θ = (2j + 1)α), finishes the remaining iterations, and records the final success probability. Choose Z, X or Y.

Animation · one error, 256 items
exact simulationprediction, Eqs. 39 and 40

Two things in the simulation (ours) are worth noting. The weight left in the plane right after the error is exactly the weight left in the plane at the end, to every printed digit, which is Eq. 37 at work. And the exact curves follow sin4θ and cos4θ closely at N = 256, with the remaining gap coming from the 1/√N terms dropped from Eq. 38. On the four-qubit register the gap is large: a bit flip at the very start costs nothing, as the paper says, while cos4α predicts 0.879. Averaged over the 13 error times, the exact loss is 0.60 for both X and Z, near the continuous average 5/8.

One more twist concerns where the error sits. Since HXH = Z and HZH = X, an error between the two Hadamard layers of the diffusion step acts on the register like the conjugate error outside them. Of the three noise layers per iteration, one sees an error as it is and two see it conjugated. Physical bit-flip noise therefore produces one bit-flip-like and two phase-flip-like events per iteration, and phase-flip noise the reverse.

In short: G = −1 off the plane, so whatever an error knocks out is lost; a phase flip keeps only the marked part (P ≈ sin4θ, worst early), a bit flip keeps only the unmarked part (P ≈ cos4θ, worst late), and each costs 5/8 of the success probability on average.

7 · THE GROVER PLANE AS A NOISY QUBIT

What happens when many errors accumulate?

One error at a time is instructive, but a real circuit sees errors everywhere. Because frozen amplitude stays out, it can be discarded, and the search is fully described by the 2 × 2 block of the density matrix that lives in the plane.

Definition · in-plane state

Eq. 42

In words: B is the success probability, A is the unmarked weight still available for amplification, and C is the coherence that the rotation converts from one into the other. Unlike a true density matrix, A + B can fall below 1, because weight leaks out of the plane.

Two approximations close the description: frozen amplitude can return only if a later error undoes an earlier one on the same qubit, which the paper estimates at a fraction of order 1/n of two-error events and neglects, and the 1/√N terms of Eq. 38 are dropped. Within these, each noise layer simply multiplies A, B and C by survival probabilities. The unmarked weight A survives a layer if no qubit gets a Z or Y, probability (1 − pz − py)n. The marked weight B survives if no qubit gets an X or Y, probability (1 − px − py)n. The coherence C survives only if no qubit gets any error, probability (1 − p)n. A layer seen through the Hadamard conjugation swaps px and pz.

Fact · decay rates per iteration

Eq. 43

derivationHow do three layers add up to these rates?

For small p, (1 − q)n ≈ 1 − nq, so the per-layer loss rates are n(pz + py) for A, n(px + py) for B and np for C. One layer per iteration sees the channel as it is; the other two see px and pz exchanged. Adding, A loses n(pz + py) + 2n(px + py) = n(pz + 2px + 3py), B loses n(px + 2pz + 3py) by the same count, and C loses 3np, because the exchange does not change p.

∎

For a large database α is small, so the iterations can be treated as continuous time t counted in iterations, with the rotation advancing the angle at the rate ω = 2α. A pure state at angle θ has A = cos2θ, B = sin2θ, C = sin θ cos θ, and differentiating with dθ/dt = ω gives Ȧ = −2ωC, Ḃ = 2ωC and Ċ = ω(A − B). Adding the decay terms gives the paper's Grover-plane equations.

Eq. 44

The initial condition is A = cos2α, B = sin2α, C = sin α cos α. These are the Bloch equations of a two-level system driven at a constant rate, familiar from nuclear magnetic resonance, with separate decay rates for the two populations and the coherence. The Grover plane behaves like a qubit that the algorithm rotates while noise drains it at the rates γA, γB and dephases it at γC. The global channel is the special case γA = γB = γC = 3pg, for which Eq. 44 reproduces Eq. 30 in the continuum limit.

ChannelγAγBγC
global depolarizing3pg3pg3pg
bit flip2npnp3np
phase flipnp2np3np
depolarizing2np2np3np
amplitude damping(n/4)γ(n/2 + h)γ(3n/4 + h/2)γ

Table 1

Local noise differs from the global channel in one respect: it destroys coherence faster than it drains weight, since γC exceeds both population rates, because an error on one qubit removes one component of the state from the plane but not the other. Amplitude damping, the relaxation of |1⟩ to |0⟩, is not a Pauli channel, but the paper handles it the same way to first order. Because it singles out |0⟩, its rates depend on h, the number of ones in the marked item's label, and the marked weight always decays faster than the unmarked weight; the worst case is a label of all ones.

In short: keeping only the in-plane 2 × 2 block turns the noisy search into a rotated, leaking, dephasing qubit, Eq. 44, with rates read off by counting which errors remove which component.

8 · SOLUTIONS AND THE NOISE BUDGET

How much local noise can a search of a given size tolerate?

Equation 44 is a linear system with constant coefficients, so its solution is a sum of exponentials. The structure shows up in the total weight S = A + B and the difference D = A − B. With γ̄ = (γA + γB)/2, δ = (γA − γB)/2 and κ = (γC − γ̄)/2, the paper rewrites Eq. 44 as

Eq. 45

derivationHow does Eq. 44 turn into Eq. 45?

Our check. The identity γAA + γBB = γ̄(A + B) + δ(A − B) holds by expanding the right side. Adding the first two lines of Eq. 44 cancels the 2ωC terms and gives Ṡ = −γ̄S − δD. Subtracting them gives Ḋ = −4ωC − (γAA − γBB), and γAA − γBB = γ̄D + δS. The last line is unchanged, with γC = γ̄ + 2κ by definition of κ.

∎

The weight S decays at the mean rate γ̄. The pair (D, C) is a damped oscillator that carries the Grover oscillation and decays at the rate γ̄ + κ, faster than the weight by the extra dephasing κ. The asymmetry δ couples the two. When the populations decay equally, δ = 0, everything separates and, writing γ for the common rate and assuming κ ≪ 2ω,

Eq. 46

The first term is half the weight left in the plane; the second is the Grover oscillation, decaying faster by e−κr and picking up a small phase lag. At κ = 0 it reduces to the continuum form of Eq. 30, since (1 − cos 2x)/2 = sin2x. This applies directly to depolarizing noise, with γ = 2np and κ = np/2. For bit-flip, phase-flip and amplitude-damping noise, δ ≠ 0 and the exponents come from a cubic (Eq. 47); the paper reports that the resulting corrections at the optimum are a few percent for bit and phase flips, with bit-flip noise slightly less damaging than phase-flip noise, and can reach several percent for amplitude damping.

At the noiseless optimum the cosine in Eq. 46 equals −1, and to first order in the rates

Eq. 48

derivationWhy does the effective rate come out as γ̄ + κ/2, and what is it for each channel?

The step is ours. For small κr0, (1 + e−κr0)/2 ≈ 1 − κr0/2 ≈ e−κr0/2, and r0 ≈ π√N/4. For depolarizing noise, γ̄ = 2np and κ = (3np − 2np)/2 = np/2, so γ̄ + κ/2 = 9np/4 = 3 · (3/4)np. For bit flips, γ̄ = 3np/2 and κ = (3np − 3np/2)/2 = 3np/4, so γ̄ + κ/2 = 15np/8 = 3 · (5/8)np, and phase flips give the same. These match the paper's statement after Eq. 48.

∎

Fact · local noise is global noise times n

To first order, local noise of strength p per qubit acts like a global channel with pg = cnp, where c = 5/8 for bit or phase flips and c = 3/4 for depolarizing noise. These constants are exactly the average single-error costs of Section 6. The noise budget per qubit and gate layer is

Eq. 49

The √N comes from the depth of the circuit and the extra n from the number of qubits that can each go wrong, so each added qubit costs a factor of about √2 from the longer circuit and a further (n + 1)/n from the extra qubit. For local depolarizing noise Eq. 49 has the form of the threshold 1/(√N log2N) found by Cohn and co-workers, since log2N = n; the paper's contribution is the constant, its explanation through single errors, and the extension to the other channels. The paper's Fig. 6 shows all channels falling parallel to 1/(n√N) beyond about six qubits, with depolarizing noise the least tolerable of the Pauli channels, bit and phase flips nearly equivalent, and amplitude damping tolerated at a several times higher rate.

To put numbers on Eq. 49 (our arithmetic, for local depolarizing noise with c = 3/4): a 10-qubit search, N = 1024, needs p below about 1/(0.75 · 10 · 32) ≈ 0.0042 per qubit and layer. A 20-qubit search, N ≈ 106, needs p below about 6.5 × 10−5.

In short: the in-plane equations give Pr0 ≈ exp[−(γ̄ + κ/2)π√N/4], so local noise acts like a global channel of rate cnp, and the tolerable error per qubit falls as 1/(c n√N).

9 · COHERENT ROTATION ERRORS

What if every gate is precise in kind but slightly off in angle?

A second kind of error does not randomize the state at all. A miscalibrated oracle or diffusion step rotates the state by slightly the wrong amount, and such errors can have the same sign every time, so they add up. The paper models this as a worst case: the angle after each oracle may be off by at most δ, and the angle after each diffusion step by a further amount of at most Δ, with signs unspecified. The state then lies somewhere in an interval of angles.

Tracking the interval is bookkeeping. The center advances by 2α per iteration as before. Each oracle widens it by δ on each side and each diffusion step by Δ, so after the first iteration the angle lies in [3α − δ − Δ, 3α + δ + Δ] (Eq. 51), and in general

Eqs. 56 and 57

so the width of the interval is

Eq. 58

The uncertainty grows linearly in depth, and at r ≈ π√N/4 it is of order √N(δ + Δ), the same combination of noise and size as before. The probability of measuring an unmarked item at angle φ is cos2φ (Eq. 59), so the two extreme histories, every error under-rotating or every error over-rotating, give

Eqs. 60 and 61

The paper adds two cautions. Since cos2φ is not monotonic, an interval that straddles π/2 reaches error zero even if neither end does, so the labels min and max refer to the ends, not the extremes. And when r0 overshoots, a little under-rotation helps. At the noiseless optimum both ends give the same worst case,

Eq. 62

derivationWhy does the error at r0 become sin2[r0(δ + Δ)]?

Our one-line filling-in. If (2r0 + 1)α = π/2 exactly, then cos2(π/2 ∓ x) = sin2x with x = r0(δ + Δ), the same at both ends. For small x, sin2x ≈ x2, and r0 ≈ π√N/4 gives the last form.

∎

The worst-case loss is quadratic in √N(δ + Δ), milder than the exponential damping of depolarizing noise, but with the same scaling: the angle error per iteration must shrink as 1/√N. The paper notes that this matches Long and co-workers' result for systematic phase errors, and that errors with random signs spread only as √r, so the tolerable error then falls only as N−1/4, matching Shenvi, Brown and Whaley.

The animation reproduces the paper's Fig. 9: the four-qubit register with δ + Δ = 0.06 rad per iteration, for r = 0 to 10. On the left the interval of possible angles is drawn in the plane; on the right each bar is the exact range of cos2φ over that interval, with the noiseless error as a dot.

Animation · the error band, 16 items
range of error probabilitynoiseless errorpossible angles

The computed values match the paper's description of Fig. 9: at the first minimum, r = 3, the error stays below about 0.14 (0.136 in our computation), while at the second minimum, r = 9, it can lie anywhere from 0 to about 0.35 (0.346). For Fig. 8 the paper reports that the under-rotated end at r0 = 3 reaches zero error at δ + Δ ≈ 0.066 rad; solving 7α − 3(δ + Δ) = π/2 gives 0.0660 (our arithmetic). Depolarizing noise shrinks the signal with depth; coherent noise makes it uncertain with depth. Both say: stop at the first optimum.

In short: bounded angle errors widen the set of possible angles by 2(δ + Δ) per iteration, so the error band at r0 has width about [(π/4)√N(δ + Δ)]2, and the tolerable angle error falls as 1/√N.

In short: exact results for global depolarizing noise, a frozen-complement argument for single local errors, Bloch-type equations and a 1/(c n√N) budget for many local errors, and a linearly widening band for coherent errors.

11 · ASSESSMENT

What is shown, and what isn't

What is shown exactly: the global depolarizing model is solved without approximation, and Eq. 30 is a true identity for the stated circuit (our 16 × 16 density-matrix simulation reproduces it to every digit we printed). The off-plane identity Eq. 37 and the in-plane Pauli matrices of Eq. 38 are exact for every N. The interval bookkeeping for bounded coherent errors, Eqs. 50 to 61, is exact under the stated worst-case model. The asymptotic formulas Eqs. 31, 33, 34 and 36 follow from Eq. 30 by standard expansions in clearly stated regimes, and our numerical checks at n = 16 and n = 20 agree with them.

What rests on approximations: everything about many local errors. The Grover-plane equations neglect amplitude returning to the plane (argued to be a fraction of order 1/n of two-error events), drop the 1/√N terms of Eq. 38, treat iterations as continuous time, and use first-order survival probabilities. So Eqs. 44 to 49 are leading-order statements for large N and small p, and the paper says as much. The single-error formulas Eqs. 39 and 40 are likewise large-N approximations; at N = 16 our simulation shows sizable deviations, though at N = 256 they are close. For bit-flip, phase-flip and amplitude-damping noise the paper describes the corrections from the population asymmetry δ as "a few percent" and "several percent" without tabulating them, and the amplitude-damping rates rest on a first-order argument given in prose. The noise budget in Fig. 6 comes from integrating Eq. 44, not from a simulation of the full n-qubit density matrix, so it inherits these approximations.

The model choices also matter. Noise follows every gate layer with the same strength, errors on different qubits and layers are independent, and the coherent-error analysis is worst case: it says how far the state can wander, not how far it typically does. Correlated and time-dependent noise are left to future work, as is error correction or mitigation. Much of the content is a unified, closed-form rederivation of scalings found before (Cohn et al., Long et al., Shenvi et al., Azuma); the new parts are the frozen-complement picture, the rates of Table 1 and the explicit constants. The paper is a two-author preprint posted on November 12, 2026, not yet refereed, and its acknowledgments state that an AI assistant was used to revise the text, check derivations and develop and extend analytical results.

A connection, oursThe same rotation picture powers amplitude amplification, the subroutine behind quantum speedups for Monte Carlo estimation (including option pricing proposals) and for some optimization heuristics. Any of these inherits the budget of this paper: the total noise over a √N-deep amplification circuit must stay of order one, which is one reason such speedups are usually discussed for error-corrected machines rather than today's devices.

In short: the global-noise and coherent-error results are exact under their models; the local-noise budget is a careful leading-order estimate that recovers known thresholds and adds explicit constants.

The Frustration Index of Fully Frustrated Hypercubes

Lujia Wang · posted Nov 11, 2026 · math.CO · arXiv 2611.14906

Overview

Color the edges of an n-dimensional cube red and blue so that every square face has an odd number of red edges, and ask how few red edges you can get away with: this paper finds the exact answer in infinitely many dimensions, pins it down to within a vanishing error in all of them, and settles dimension nine at 772. The question is three things at once. It is a puzzle about square-free subgraphs that Erdős asked about, it is the ground-state energy of a spin model that physicists have simulated since 1979, and it is an eigenvalue problem for a signed version of the cube's adjacency matrix, the same matrix that Hao Huang used to prove the Sensitivity Conjecture in 2019. The main idea is to solve the problem first on a tiny cube whose edges carry weights, where the answer is easy to see, and then to unfold that weighted cube into an ordinary one of higher dimension without losing anything. A parity argument shows that the unfolded answer cannot be beaten.

By the end you'll be able to explain
  • what a signed graph is, what switching does, and why the minimum number of red edges Fn is the same for every fully frustrated coloring of the n-cube;
  • why the same number is the ground-state energy of a fully frustrated Ising model, the kind of energy function a quantum annealer minimizes;
  • how the signed adjacency matrix An satisfies An2 = nI, and how that turns the counting problem into the formula Fn = (n − μn)2n−2 of Eq. 1.4;
  • how a parity argument on signed degrees gives the lower bound of Eq. 1.1, and exactly when it is met;
  • what a weighted cube is, and how the four-way and pair refinements of Lemma 2.1 unfold it into an ordinary cube while copying every local field;
  • why a weight vector can be unfolded precisely when its entries are integers whose squares sum to n and whose gcd is a power of two (Theorem 2.2);
  • how these pieces give Fr²+1 = (r² − r + 1)2r²−1 for every r, the bound Fn = (n − √n + O(n−1/2))2n−2, and F9 = 772.
notationSymbols used throughout
Qn
the n-dimensional cube: vertices are the 2n bit strings x = (x0, …, xn−1), edges join strings that differ in one bit; it has n2n−1 edges
ei, x ⊕ ei
the i-th coordinate vector, and the neighbor of x obtained by flipping bit i
|x|
the Hamming weight, the number of ones in x; its parity splits the vertices into two classes of equal size
signing
a choice of sign +1 (blue) or −1 (red) for every edge
Fn
the frustration index of the fully frustrated n-cube: the fewest red edges in a coloring where every square has an odd number of red edges
Γi, An
the signed adjacency operator in direction i, and the signed adjacency matrix An = Γ0 + ⋯ + Γn−1
Pd
the parity operator, multiplying a function by (−1)|x|
f
a Boolean function, here meaning a function from vertices to {−1, 1}; it describes a switching
h(x)
the local field: the signed degree of x after switching, h(x) = f(x)(Anf)(x)
⟨f, g⟩
the normalized inner product 2−dΣx f(x)g(x), an average over vertices; ⟨B⟩f = ⟨f, Bf⟩
μn
the largest mean local field, maxf ⟨An⟩f
w, Γw
a weight vector (w0, …, wd−1) and the weighted operator Γw = Σ wiΓi; ‖w‖22 = Σ wi2
