Running examples
  • The path P3. Three sites in a row, 1 – 2 – 3, with sites 1 and 3 each joined to the sink. Every site has degree 2, so a stable site holds 0 or 1 grain, and there are only eight stable configurations, written as strings η(1)η(2)η(3) from 000 to 111. Most claims in the chapter are checked on it, and the second animation searches all 864 of its policies by brute force.
  • The star with two leaves. A center z joined to the sink and to two leaves, each leaf joined only to z. It shows how a site with a high price can be irrelevant because it can never hold a grain.
1 · GRAINS, TOPPLINGS, AVALANCHES

What is the system being controlled?

The Abelian sandpile was introduced by Bak, Tang and Wiesenfeld in 1987 and given its mathematical form by Dhar in 1990. It was designed as the simplest system that organizes itself into a critical state, a state in which a single small push can set off a cascade of any size, without anyone tuning a parameter to get there. Physicists call this self-organized criticality, and the paper lists earthquakes, forest fires, fluctuations in financial markets and evolution among the phenomena it has been associated with. The paper's question is practical: if cascades are costly, can removing a little material at the right places, at a price, make them smaller on average?

The setting is a finite graph with an extra vertex s called the sink. Each ordinary vertex, or site, holds a pile of indistinguishable grains. The height η(x) is the number of grains at site x, and the degree deg(x) is the number of edges at x, including edges to the sink.

Definition · stability and toppling

A site x is stable in η if η(x) < deg(x), and a configuration is stable if every site is. A site is critical if η(x) = deg(x) − 1. An unstable site topples: it loses deg(x) grains and sends one along each of its edges. Grains sent to the sink disappear.

In words: a site can hold at most one grain fewer than it has neighbors. When it gets one more, it tips over and gives one grain to every neighbor, and the edge of the graph is where grains fall off.

Time runs in steps. At each step a site x is chosen uniformly at random and one grain is added there; this is the operator αx. If some site becomes unstable it topples, which may make neighbors unstable, and so on until everything is stable again. The paper calls this relaxation and writes η° for the stable result. The total number of topplings in one relaxation is the avalanche size, the quantity everyone wants to keep small.

Toppling is linear algebra. Let Δ be the graph Laplacian restricted to the ordinary sites, the matrix with Δxx = deg(x) and Δxy = −bxy for x ≠ y, where bxy counts the edges between x and y. Treating η as a row vector, toppling x subtracts row x of Δ:

The diagonal entry removes deg(x) grains from x, and the off-diagonal entries add one grain to each neighbor. Grains sent to the sink simply do not appear, because the sink has no row or column. On P3, where every site has degree 2,

Fact · the Abelian property (Dhar)

Starting from a stable η and adding a grain at x, the number of times each site y topples, ny(η, x), does not depend on the order in which unstable sites are toppled. So the stable result (αxη)° and the avalanche size n(η, x) = Σy ny(η, x) are well defined, and (αxη)° = αxη − Σz nz(η, x)Δz,·.

The name "Abelian" refers to this order-independence: adding grains and relaxing commute, just as numbers in an Abelian group can be added in any order. It is what makes the model solvable, and the paper uses it in nearly every proof.

Here is an avalanche on P3, worked by hand and then animated below. Start from 111, every site critical, and add a grain at site 2. Site 2 now has 2 grains and topples, giving one each to sites 1 and 3, which now have 2 each. Site 1 topples, sending one grain into the sink and one back to site 2. Site 3 does the same. Site 2 has 2 again and topples a second time, leaving 101. The toppling counts are n = (1, 2, 1), so the avalanche size is 4, and the Abelian property's formula checks out: (1, 1, 1) + (0, 1, 0) − (1, 2, 1)Δ = (1, 2, 1) − (0, 2, 0) = (1, 0, 1).

Animation · one avalanche on P₃
grainunstable sitesink

Because the new grain lands at a random site, the size of the next avalanche from η is a random variable, written N(η), with P(N(η) = k) equal to the fraction of sites x with n(η, x) = k. From 111 on P3, adding at site 1 or site 3 gives an avalanche of size 3 and adding at site 2 gives size 4, so E[N(111)] = (3 + 4 + 3)/3 = 10/3. The last frame of the animation computes E[N(η)] for all eight stable configurations.

In short: grains land at random sites; a site with deg(x) grains topples and sends one grain along each edge; toppling x subtracts row x of the Laplacian Δ; the order of topplings does not matter, and the avalanche size is the total number of topplings.

2 · THE UNCONTROLLED PILE IN THE LONG RUN

How large is an avalanche on average if nobody intervenes?

Before asking whether intervention helps, one needs the baseline. Adding a grain at a random site and relaxing defines a Markov chain on the stable configurations: the next configuration depends only on the current one and the random site. Its transition probabilities are Eq. 2,

Eq. 2

A short reminder about Markov chains, since everything below depends on it. A set of states is closed if the chain can never leave it, and a recurrent class is a closed set in which every state can reach every other. A stationary distribution μ is a probability distribution that one step of the chain leaves unchanged. Long-run averages of anything the chain does are averages against a stationary distribution on the recurrent class the chain ends up in.

The paper uses Dhar's result that the sandpile chain has exactly one recurrent class and that its stationary distribution is uniform on that class. On P3 the recurrent class is {011, 101, 110, 111}, the configurations with at most one empty site. The paper quotes this description for every path from Redig's lecture notes; on P3 it can be checked by hand: from each of these four configurations, all three possible additions lead back into the set, and from any stable configuration, adding grains at empty sites reaches 111. The animation's last frame averages E[N] over these four configurations and gets (4/3 + 2/3 + 4/3 + 10/3)/4 = 5/3.

A standard fact the paper uses implicitly

This remark is ours. The number of recurrent configurations of a sandpile always equals det Δ, which by Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem is the number of spanning trees of the graph with the sink included. For P3, det Δ = 4, matching the four recurrent configurations above. The paper's discussion section mentions these spanning trees as a possible route to understanding topple-freeness.

The paper's formula for the average avalanche size goes through the inverse of the Laplacian. Since every site has a path to the sink, Δ is invertible, and its inverse G = Δ−1 is called the Green's function. Define, as Eq. 9,

Eq. 9

In words, φ = G1, the vector that solves Δφ = 1. That equation, written out at a site u, says deg(u)φ(u) − Σv buvφ(v) = 1, and it is the property every proof below leans on. The function also has a probabilistic meaning. Run a random walk in continuous time that jumps along each edge at rate 1, so it leaves x after an exponential time with mean 1/deg(x) and then moves to a uniformly random neighbor. Then Eq. 10 says

Eq. 10

the expected time for that walk to reach the sink from x.

our derivationWhy does the expected hitting time satisfy Δφ = 1?

The paper cites Durrett's textbook for Eq. 10; the one-step argument below is the standard one, written out by us. Let T(x) be the expected time to reach the sink from x, with T(s) = 0. From x, the walk waits on average 1/deg(x), then moves to a neighbor v with probability bxv/deg(x) (or to the sink with probability bxs/deg(x)). So

Multiplying by deg(x) gives deg(x)T(x) − Σv bxvT(v) = 1, which is (ΔT)(x) = 1. Since Δ is invertible, T = Δ−11 = φ.

On P3, by symmetry T(1) = T(3). The equations read T(1) = 1/2 + T(2)/2 (half the time the walk falls into the sink) and T(2) = 1/2 + T(1). Substituting, T(1) = 3/4 + T(1)/2, so T(1) = 3/2 and T(2) = 2.

∎

For a path of L sites the paper uses the known Green's function, Eq. 44, G(x, y) = x(L + 1 − y)/(L + 1) for x ≤ y, and sums it to get Eq. 45,

Eq. 45

a downward parabola, largest in the middle. On P3 the prices are φ = (3/2, 2, 3/2), matching the hitting times just computed. Now the main formula for the baseline.

Fact · Theorem 3.1, gain of never intervening

Without intervention, the long-run average avalanche size is the same from every starting configuration and equals the average price,

Eq. 11

Moreover the bias, defined in Section 3, is h(η) = Σx (η(x) − deg(x) + 1)φ(x) + C (Eq. 12).

On P3, Eq. 11 gives (3/2 + 2 + 3/2)/3 = 5/3, the same number as the direct average over the recurrent class. For a general path, Corollary 4.1 evaluates it as (L + 1)(L + 2)/12, which is 5/3 at L = 3.

proof ideaWhy should the average avalanche equal the average of φ?

The heart of the paper's proof is one identity. Weight each grain at site y by φ(y) and add up: H(η) = Σy η(y)φ(y). Adding a grain at x and relaxing changes η by 1x − Σz nzΔz,·, so

because Σy Δzyφ(y) = (Δφ)(z) = 1. Each new grain adds φ(x) to the total price, and each toppling removes exactly 1. This is the line in the proof of Theorem 3.1 that turns into Eq. 12.

The rest is the following reading, which is ours. Summing over T steps, the total number of topplings equals Σt φ(xt) minus the change in H. Since H is bounded on stable configurations, dividing by T and letting T grow leaves the average of φ(x) over uniformly random sites. So φ(x) really is the price of a grain at x: the number of topplings it will eventually cause, on average. The paper notes (Remark 3.2) that Eq. 11 also follows from Dhar's formula for expected toppling numbers.

∎

The animation below runs the uncontrolled pile on P3 and keeps this ledger step by step: the price added, the topplings, and the running total. Its last frame runs 20 000 steps and compares the average avalanche size with 5/3.

Animation · the price ledger
grainlanding siterunning average

In short: the uncontrolled pile settles into a uniform distribution on its recurrent configurations; φ = Δ−11 is the expected time for a random walk to reach the sink, it is also the average number of topplings a grain will cause, and the average avalanche is the average of φ (Eq. 11), 5/3 on P3.

3 · A CONTROLLER AND ITS COSTS

How do you make "is intervening worth it?" into a precise optimization problem?

Removing grains always makes the next avalanche smaller or equal, but it costs something, and a grain removed now changes every future step. Comparing strategies fairly needs a framework that adds up costs over an unending future. That framework is the Markov decision process, or MDP, the mathematical core of optimal control and of reinforcement learning.

Definition · the sandpile MDP

The states are the stable configurations Ω. Before each grain is added, the controller picks an action a from A(η) = V+(η) ∪ {0}: a site that currently holds a grain, or 0 for no intervention. Action a gives the post-decision configuration ηa, equal to η with one grain removed at a (or unchanged if a = 0); then a grain lands at a uniformly random site and the pile relaxes. The cost of the step is Eq. 3,

Eq. 3

In words: you pay β whenever you remove a grain, and you pay one unit for every toppling in the avalanche that follows.

A stationary deterministic policy π = d∞ chooses its action by a fixed rule d(η) that looks only at the current configuration. The paper restricts to these, citing Puterman's textbook: because there are finitely many states and actions, some stationary deterministic policy is optimal among all policies, including randomized ones and ones that remember the past. On P3 the number of such policies is the product of the number of available actions over the eight states, 1 · 23 · 33 · 4 = 864.

The yardstick is the long-run average cost per grain added, called the gain, Eq. 4:

Eq. 4

The gain may depend on the starting configuration, because a controlled chain can have several recurrent classes. The paper writes it as Eq. 5, a weighted average of the stationary average costs of the recurrent classes Ri, weighted by the probability δi(η) of ending up in each:

Eq. 5

On P3, consider three policies. Never intervening has gain 5/3 for every β, as computed above. The policy that always removes the leftmost grain soon reaches configurations with exactly one grain, which it removes before every addition, so no site ever reaches 2 grains, nothing topples, and the gain is β. The policy that removes the grain at site 2 whenever there is one is the interesting middle case; Section 6 shows its gain is 1/3 + 2β/3.

The gain says nothing about where you start, and the bias, Eq. 6, fills that gap. It is the total amount by which costs exceed the average, accumulated forever:

Eq. 6

In words, h(η) − h(η′) is how much more it will cost in total to start from η instead of η′. Gain and bias are tied together by the policy evaluation equations, Eqs. 7a and 7b, in which Pd is the transition matrix and cd the cost vector of the policy:

Eqs. 7a and 7b

The second equation reads, state by state: today's cost, minus the average, plus the expected change in bias over one step, is zero. It is a bookkeeping identity, and it determines the bias up to adding a constant on each recurrent class.

our sketchWhy does the bias satisfy Eq. 7b?

This sketch is ours and assumes a single recurrent class, so that g is a constant. Split the sum in Eq. 6 into its first term and the rest. The first term is cd(η) − g. The rest is the same sum started one step later, from the random next state η2, whose expectation is Ση′ Pd(η, η′)h(η′). So h(η) = cd(η) − g + (Pdh)(η), which rearranges to Eq. 7b. Eq. 7a holds because a constant vector is unchanged by a transition matrix. The paper cites Puterman, Theorem 8.2.6, for the general multichain case.

∎

Finally, optimality. A policy π* is average-cost optimal if gπ*(η) ≤ gπ(η) for every state η and every policy π. The paper states the optimality equations, Eqs. 8a and 8b, which say that a pair (g, h) is optimal when no single deviation from the policy, followed by business as usual, can lower "cost now plus expected bias next." In this paper the gains turn out to be constant, so Eq. 8a is automatic, and the working condition is Eq. 8b:

Eq. 8b (with g constant)

In short: the controller removes at most one grain per step at price β and also pays for every toppling; policies are compared by their gain, the long-run average cost per grain (Eq. 4); the bias measures the head start or handicap of a starting configuration, and Eq. 8b checks that no one-step deviation helps.

4 · WHEN IS DOING NOTHING OPTIMAL?

How expensive must intervention be before it is never worth it?

The simplest policy deserves the first question. Removing a grain at site a costs β now. Section 2 says what it saves: the grain would have caused φ(a) topplings on average. The comparison should be β against φ(a), and the bias formula Eq. 12 makes this precise, since h(η) − h(ηa) = φ(a): removing a grain at a lowers the total future cost by exactly its price.

Fact · Theorem 3.3

Never intervening is optimal if and only if

Eq. 13

In words: doing nothing is best exactly when the removal fee is at least the largest price of a grain at any site that can hold one. Sites of degree 1 never hold a grain in a stable configuration, so they are left out.

proofWhy is Eq. 13 sufficient?

The gain of never intervening is the constant of Eq. 11, so the optimality equation 8a holds and every action is allowed in 8b. Because removing grain a and then doing nothing is the same as doing nothing from ηa, c(η, a) = β1{a ≠ 0} + c(ηa, 0), and the transition from η under a equals the transition from ηa under 0. Using Eq. 7b for the never-intervene policy at ηa, the quantity inside the minimum of Eq. 8b for action a equals β1{a ≠ 0} + h(ηa) − h(η). So action 0 attains the minimum exactly when β ≥ h(η) − h(ηa) for all feasible a. By Eq. 12, h(η) − h(ηa) = φ(a), and a site a can hold a grain in some stable configuration precisely when deg(a) ≥ 2. This is Eq. 15, equivalent to Eq. 13.

∎

proofWhy is it necessary? If β is a bit below φ(a), why must some policy do strictly better?

The paper writes the cost of any action in terms of the never-intervene bias, Eq. 16:

Eq. 16

Suppose β < φ(a) for a site a with deg(a) ≥ 2, and use the policy πa that removes a grain at a whenever there is one (Eq. 17). Any recurrent class of πa contains a configuration with a grain at a, because a grain landing on an empty a stays there. Average Eq. 16 against the stationary distribution of that class. The bias terms cancel, because the distribution is unchanged by a step, and what remains is gπa = gπ∅ + (β − φ(a)) · (stationary probability that a holds a grain). The last factor is positive and β − φ(a) is negative, so πa is strictly better.

∎

On P3 the largest price is φ(2) = 2, so never intervening is optimal exactly when β ≥ 2. For a general path, Corollary 4.1 gives the threshold (L + 1)2/8 for odd L and L(L + 2)/8 for even L, the value of the parabola Eq. 45 at the center.

The star with n leaves shows why the restriction deg(a) ≥ 2 matters. Its center z has degree n + 1, and each leaf has degree 1. The paper computes the Green's function and gets Eq. 58: φ(z) = n + 1 and φ = n + 2 at every leaf. The leaves have the highest price, since a grain there must first reach the center, but a leaf can never hold a grain: one grain makes it topple. So the threshold is β ≥ n + 1, the price at the center (Corollary 4.11), and the never-intervene gain is (n + 1 + n(n + 2))/(n + 1) = n + 2 − 1/(n + 1), Eq. 59. For two leaves, the threshold is 3 and the gain is 11/3.

On the complete graph with every site also joined to the sink, Eq. 57 shows that φ = 1 at every site, so the threshold is β ≥ 1 (Corollary 4.7). Every toppling there sends one grain straight to the sink, so every grain causes on average exactly one toppling.

In short: removing a grain at a saves φ(a) topplings on average; never intervening is optimal exactly when β is at least the largest price at a site that can hold a grain (Eq. 13): 2 on P3, n + 1 on the star, 1 on the complete graph.

5 · LOCAL INTERVENTION POLICIES

If intervention is worth it, where should grains be removed, and what does the pile then look like?

Below the threshold, Theorem 3.3 says some intervention helps, but there are astronomically many policies. The paper focuses on a natural family: pick a set of sites W and remove a grain from W whenever W has one.

Definition 2.1 · local intervention policy

Given W ⊆ V, a policy πW is a local intervention policy with intervention set W if dW(η) is some site in W that holds a grain whenever such a site exists, and dW(η) = 0 otherwise.

In words: keep W as empty as you can, one grain per step. Which occupied site of W to pick is left open, so one W can correspond to several policies. The choice W = ∅ is never intervening, and W = V is "always intervene when there is anything to remove."

The key construction is the contracted graph G̃W, obtained by merging all of W into the sink. An edge from a site outside W to a site in W becomes an edge to the sink, and edges inside W ∪ {s} are discarded. The intuition is that a site kept empty acts almost like a sink: grains that wander into it are soon taken away. Let R̃W be the recurrent class of the ordinary sandpile on G̃W, and let φW be its prices. For P3 with W = {2}, the contracted graph is two separate sites, 1 and 3, each joined to the sink by two edges (its original sink edge and its edge to site 2). Each has degree 2 and holds 0 or 1 grains, every configuration of the pair is recurrent, and φW(1) = φW(3) = 1/2, which is Eq. 45 with L = 1.

Fact · Theorem 3.4

For any local intervention policy πW, the restriction to V \ W of every recurrent configuration of the controlled chain is a recurrent configuration of the uncontrolled sandpile on G̃W.

proof ideaWhy does the outside of W behave like a sandpile on the contracted graph?

One step of πW, seen only on V \ W, adds the new grain (if it lands outside W) and also adds whatever grains the sites of W send out when they topple, γu grains at each u. By the Abelian property this is the same as adding all those grains on G̃W and relaxing there. The recurrent class of a sandpile is closed under adding grains and relaxing, so once the restriction is in R̃W it stays there. Conversely, if it is outside R̃W, a suitable finite sequence of additions outside W brings it in with positive probability, and it can never come back. So it was not recurrent.

∎

The inclusion can be strict. The paper's counterexample has two sites, x joined to y and y joined to the sink. Site x has degree 1 and is always empty, so πx never acts, and the only recurrent configuration is (0, 1). On the contracted graph, y has two edges to the sink and both 0 and 1 are recurrent. So only {1} of {0, 1} is seen. The trouble is that x topples every time a grain lands on it, sending grains to y that the contracted model does not see.

That suggests the condition that makes the reduction exact: the sites of W should never topple.

Definition 3.6 · topple-free

A set W is topple-free under a policy π if, under every stationary distribution of the chain induced by π, the probability that some site of W topples during a step is zero.

In words: once the controlled pile has settled into its long-run behavior, grains reach W only to be removed, never to set off topplings there.

Fact · Theorems 3.7 and 3.8

If W is topple-free under πW, then every recurrent class R of the controlled chain restricts onto all of R̃W (Eq. 19). If moreover W = {x} is a single site, then every stationary distribution of πx, viewed on V \ {x}, is the uniform distribution on R̃x.

Theorem 3.5 handles a single site without the topple-free assumption: there, the restricted distribution gives equal weight to the orbits of the operator Bx that adds the grains a toppling of x would send to its neighbors and relaxes, which are the cosets of a cyclic subgroup of the sandpile group. When x never topples, Bx is never applied, and the restricted distribution is fully uniform.

On P3 with W = {2}: before each grain lands, site 2 is emptied, so after the grain lands it has at most one grain and cannot topple. The set {2} is topple-free. The paper's Theorem 4.2 with L = 3 and k = 1 says the recurrent class is every configuration except 000, seven in all. The second animation computes the stationary distribution: 1/4 on 010, 1/6 on each of 011, 101 and 110, and 1/12 on each of 001, 100 and 111. Grouping by the pair (η(1), η(3)) gives 1/4 + 0, 1/12 + 1/6, 1/12 + 1/6 and 1/6 + 1/12, each 1/4, which is the uniformity of Theorem 3.8.

In short: a local policy keeps a set W as empty as it can; outside W the controlled pile is an ordinary sandpile on the graph with W merged into the sink (Theorem 3.4), exactly so when W never topples (Theorems 3.7 and 3.8), which is easy to check on P3 with W = {2}.

6 · THE COST OF A TOPPLE-FREE POLICY

What does a local intervention policy cost in the long run?

A policy's cost has two parts, avalanches and interventions, and topple-freeness makes both computable. The avalanche part comes straight from the contracted graph. The intervention part comes from a conservation law: grains can leave W only by being removed, so in the long run the removal rate equals the rate at which grains enter W.

The rate at which grains enter W is where random walks come in. If the grains are labeled and each toppling sends the deg(x) grains at x in a uniformly random arrangement, every grain performs a simple random walk, taking one step per toppling it takes part in. A grain added at x outside W therefore reaches W before falling into the sink with probability

the probability that a random walk from x hits W before the sink. The walks of different grains are correlated, but each grain's contribution to the long-run cost is additive, so the correlations do not matter. The paper credits this coupled random-walk picture to Dhar's 2006 review.

Fact · Theorem 3.9

If W is topple-free under πW, then for every starting configuration

Eq. 20

where g̃W is the never-intervene gain on the contracted graph. The bias on each recurrent class is the contracted graph's bias plus β times Σx∈W η(x) + Σx∉W pW(x)η(x), up to a constant (Eq. 21).

In words: avalanches happen only when the grain lands outside W, and then they are avalanches of the contracted pile; interventions happen at the rate grains arrive in W, which is directly with probability |W|/|V| plus the chance a grain landing elsewhere wanders in.

proofHow does the conservation argument give the intervention rate?

Let IT be the number of interventions in the first T steps, JT the number of grains that enter W, and Zt the number of grains in W at time t. Since W is topple-free, grains leave W only by removal, one per intervention, so ZT+1 − Z1 = JT − IT. Each Zt lies between 0 and Σx∈W(deg(x) − 1), so IT/T and JT/T have the same limit. A new grain lands in W with probability |W|/|V|, and otherwise enters W with probability pW(x), which gives Eq. 28 for the intervention rate.

For the avalanche part, couple the controlled chain with a lazy uncontrolled chain on G̃W that does nothing whenever the grain lands in W, which happens with probability |W|/|V|. Because W never topples, the two chains agree outside W and have identical avalanches, which gives Eq. 24, (|V| − |W|)/|V| times g̃W.

The bias is then verified directly through Eq. 7b. The key fact is that pW is harmonic off W: pW(y) is the average of its values at the neighbors of y, with value 1 on W and 0 at the sink. So the weight function qW (1 on W, pW elsewhere) has (ΔqW)(u) = 0 for u ∉ W, and topplings outside W do not change Σ η(x)qW(x). This gives Eqs. 31 to 34 and confirms Eq. 29.

∎

On P3 with W = {2}, a random walk from site 1 steps to site 2 or to the sink with equal chances, so pW(1) = pW(3) = 1/2. The contracted graph is two copies of a one-site path, whose gain is (1 + 1)(1 + 2)/12 = 1/2. Eq. 20 gives

The second animation confirms both pieces from the stationary distribution: the expected avalanche cost averages to 1/3, and the stationary probability that site 2 holds a grain, which is the intervention rate, is 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/12 = 2/3.

On the star, W = {z} is topple-free: after the center is emptied it has at most n − 1 grains, and each step adds exactly one grain to it (directly, or through a leaf that topples once), so it never reaches n + 1. Every leaf walks to the center with probability 1, so pz = 1, and on the contracted graph each addition at a leaf causes exactly one toppling, so g̃z = 1. Eq. 20 gives Eq. 61, g = n/(n + 1) + β, which is 2/3 + β with two leaves. Since leaves never hold grains, this policy is the same as always intervening.

In short: for a topple-free set W, the long-run cost is the contracted pile's avalanche cost, scaled by the chance the grain lands outside W, plus β times the rate at which grains reach W, computed from hitting probabilities pW(x) (Eq. 20); on P3 with W = {2} it is 1/3 + 2β/3.

7 · CERTIFYING OPTIMALITY

Knowing what a local policy costs, how do you prove that nothing else is cheaper?

Comparing a policy with every alternative one by one is hopeless; P3 already has 864 policies, and the count grows exponentially. The paper instead extends the price idea of Section 2: give each grain a price that already includes the expected intervention fees it will cost, and check that no single deviation can beat the prices.

The price of a grain at x, when following πW, is

A grain in W will be removed at cost β. A grain outside W will cause φW(x) topplings on average in the contracted pile and will reach W, and be removed, with probability pW(x). The total price of a configuration is HW(η) = Σy η(y)qW(y), Eq. 35, which agrees with the bias of πW up to a constant on each recurrent class.

Fact · Theorem 3.10

Let W be topple-free under πW, and define

where FW(u) = bus + Σv∉W buv(1 − pW(v)). If the lower bound is at most the upper bound, then πW is optimal for every β in between.

In words: β must be high enough that removing grains outside W is not worth it, and low enough that letting a site of W fill up and topple is not worth it.

Each bound has a plain meaning; the reading below is ours, the algebra is in the proof. Removing a grain at a outside W costs β and saves its price φW(a) + pW(a)β, so it does not pay when β(1 − pW(a)) ≥ φW(a): that is the lower bound. The upper bound asks whether letting a site u ∈ W topple could be cheaper than removing its grains. A toppling costs 1, plus φW(v) further topplings for each grain sent to an outside neighbor v. What it saves is the removal fee β for every grain that then leaves the system without coming back to W: on average FW(u) of them, counting the bus grains sent straight into the sink and, for each outside neighbor v, the chance 1 − pW(v) of reaching the sink before W. A toppling at u is never a bargain when FW(u)β ≤ 1 + Σ buvφW(v).

proofHow do the two inequalities turn into optimality against every policy?

The paper first shows that on recurrent configurations of πW, cdW(η) = gπW + HW(η) − (PdWHW)(η), Eq. 41. This uses (ΔφW)(u) = 1 and (ΔpW)(u) = 0 off W, so (ΔqW)(u) = 1 there: each toppling outside W lowers the total price by exactly 1, as in Section 2.

For an arbitrary policy and action a, the same computation gives Eq. 42:

Eq. 42

The last two terms are what a deviation can gain or lose. The term β1{a ≠ 0} − qW(a) is 0 for actions in W or no action, and β(1 − pW(a)) − φW(a) for a ∉ W, which is nonnegative when β ≥ the lower bound. A direct computation gives 1 − (ΔqW)(u) = 1 + Σ buvφW(v) − βFW(u) for u ∈ W, nonnegative when β ≤ the upper bound. Dropping both terms and averaging over the landing site gives cd(η) ≥ gπW + HW(η) − (PdHW)(η), Eq. 43, for every policy. Summing over T steps telescopes the HW terms; since HW is bounded, dividing by T gives gπ(η) ≥ gπW for every π and every η.

∎

The proof is a potential-function argument of the kind used throughout optimization: find a function whose one-step change bounds the cost from below for every possible move, then telescope. Here the potential is the total price of the grains on the pile.

On P3 with W = {2}: the lower bound is φW(1)/(1 − pW(1)) = (1/2)/(1/2) = 1. For the upper bound, site 2 has no sink edge and two outside neighbors with pW = 1/2, so FW(2) = 2 · 1/2 = 1, and the numerator is 1 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 2. So π{2} is optimal for β ∈ [1, 2]. With W = V, there are no outside sites and the lower bound is 0, while FV(u) = bus, which is 1 at sites 1 and 3 and 0 at site 2, giving the upper bound 1. So always intervening is optimal for β ∈ [0, 1]. With W = ∅, the lower bound is the largest φ, which is 2, and there is no upper bound. The three intervals fit together exactly.

On the star with W = {z}, the lower bound is 0 because no outside site can hold a grain, and the upper bound is (1 + n · 1)/1 = n + 1, using bzs = 1, pz = 1 and φz = 1 at the leaves (Corollary 4.14). On the complete graph with W = V, FV(u) = bus = 1, so always intervening is optimal for β ≤ 1 (Corollary 4.8). In both cases the interval meets the never-intervene threshold of Section 4, so the two simplest policies already cover every β (Corollaries 4.9 and 4.15).

In short: give each grain a price that includes the intervention fees it will cost; πW is optimal when removing outside grains does not pay (lower bound) and letting W topple does not pay (upper bound); on P3, W = V, {2} and ∅ are optimal on [0, 1], [1, 2] and [2, ∞).

8 · THE PATH, SOLVED COMPLETELY

On a line of L sites, which policy is optimal for each β?

The tools are now in place, and the line is where they give a complete answer. The pattern seen on P3 holds in general: the optimal sets are central intervals that grow as β falls, because φ is a parabola peaked in the middle.

For k = 0, 1, …, ⌊L/2⌋, let Wk = {k + 1, …, L − k}, the sites at distance more than k from both ends, and let πk be a local policy with intervention set Wk. Then W0 is everything and W⌊L/2⌋ is empty when L is even.

Fact · Theorem 4.2, the recurrent classes

For 1 ≤ k ≤ ⌊(L − 1)/2⌋, πk has a unique recurrent class Rk: the 0/1 configurations with at most one empty site in each outer strip of k sites and at most one grain in the central strip, except the single configuration η̄k−1 (Eq. 48), which has its k − 1 outermost sites on each side full and everything else empty.

For P3 and k = 1 every condition is automatic, and the only excluded configuration is η̄0 = 000, giving the seven configurations of Section 5. The excluded configuration cannot be reached because producing an empty site next to the central strip always pushes a grain into the strip (Case VII of the proof). For k = 0, Proposition 4.3 shows the single-grain configurations always form a recurrent class, that an always-intervene policy such as "remove the leftmost grain" has no other, and that always-intervene policies with extra recurrent classes are never optimal. The paper gives one, which prefers the boundary sites, with a second class of two-grain configurations.

Every Wk is topple-free: in a recurrent configuration the central strip holds at most one grain, and that grain is removed before the next one lands. A random walk started inside an outer strip of length k, i sites away from the central strip, reaches the central strip before the sink with probability 1 − i/(k + 1), the gambler's ruin probability (Eq. 55). The contracted graph is two separate paths of length k. Theorem 3.9 then gives Eq. 53:

Eq. 53

our checkHow do Eqs. 20, 46 and 55 combine into Eq. 53?

This arithmetic is ours, following the paper's proof. Here |V| = L and |Wk| = L − 2k. The contracted graph is two paths of length k, and a grain landing outside Wk lands on each with probability 1/2, so its never-intervene gain is (k + 1)(k + 2)/12 by Eq. 46. The avalanche term of Eq. 20 is (2k/L) · (k + 1)(k + 2)/12 = k(k + 1)(k + 2)/(6L). For the intervention term, each strip contributes Σi=1k (1 − i/(k + 1)) = k − k/2 = k/2, so the two strips give k, and (|Wk| + k)/L = (L − k)/L.

∎

Fact · Theorem 4.5, the complete answer

Let K = ⌊(L − 1)/2⌋, βk = k(k + 1)/2 for k = 0, …, K, and βK+1 = (L + 1)2/8 for odd L, L(L + 2)/8 for even L. Then, for each k = 0, …, K,

In words: start with β large and lower it. At first, doing nothing is best. At βK+1 it becomes worth clearing the center; at each triangular number βk = k(k + 1)/2 the cleared interval grows by one site at each end; below 1 it is best to remove a grain every step.

proofWhere do the triangular numbers come from, and why is each interval exact?

Sufficiency is Theorem 3.10. The contracted graph is two paths of length k, so φWk at the site i sites away from the central strip is i(k + 1 − i)/2, and with Eq. 55,

attained at i = 1, the site next to the central strip. For the upper bound, only the two endpoints of Wk have F > 0; each has F = 1/(k + 1) and numerator 1 + k/2 = (k + 2)/2, giving βk+1 = (k + 1)(k + 2)/2. When WK is the single center site of an odd path, F = 2/(K + 1) and the numerator is K + 1, giving (L + 1)2/8.

Necessity is a comparison of the gains in Eq. 53: gπk − gπk−1 = (βk − β)/L, and gπK − gπ∅ = (L − K)(β − βK+1)/L. Outside its interval each policy is strictly beaten by a neighbor in the chain.

∎

For L = 3 the thresholds are β0 = 0, β1 = 1 and β2 = 2, and the three gains are β, 1/3 + 2β/3 and 5/3, crossing exactly at 1 and 2. The animation below checks this from scratch. For each policy it builds the 8 × 8 transition matrix, computes the long-run distribution numerically, and reads off the gain. For the chosen β it then does the same for all 864 policies and reports the smallest gain from every starting configuration.

stationary probabilitysite 2 is clearedoptimal gain

The thresholds for a longer path, evaluated by us from Theorem 4.5: for L = 7, K = 3, and the optimal policy is always intervening for β ≤ 1, clearing sites 2 to 6 for 1 ≤ β ≤ 3, sites 3 to 5 for 3 ≤ β ≤ 6, the center site 4 for 6 ≤ β ≤ 8, and nothing for β ≥ 8. The last threshold, 8 = φ(4) = 4 · 4/2, is the largest grain price, as Theorem 3.3 requires.

A reading of the result

This paragraph is ours. The rule has the shape of an optimal stopping or hedging rule in finance: pay a fixed fee to remove risk exactly where the expected future damage of keeping it exceeds the fee. On a path the expected damage of a grain grows toward the middle, like the parabola x(L + 1 − x)/2, so the zone where removal pays is a central interval, and it widens as the fee falls. The paper itself mentions financial markets and systemic risk only as motivation.

In short: on a line the optimal intervention sets are central intervals Wk, the cost of πk is Eq. 53, and πk is optimal exactly for β between the triangular numbers k(k + 1)/2 and (k + 1)(k + 2)/2, with never intervening optimal above the largest price.

9 · OTHER GRAPHS AND THE LIMITS OF THE METHOD

How far does the topple-free method reach beyond the line?

Everything from Section 6 on assumes topple-freeness, so the question for any other graph is whether natural intervention sets have it.

The complete graph. With n sites, each joined to all others and to the sink, Δ = (n + 1)I − J and G = (I + J)/(n + 1), so φ = 1 everywhere (Eq. 57). Always intervening has gain β, since in the long run the mass cannot grow and every toppling would lose a grain to the sink, so nothing topples. Together with Section 4, always intervening is optimal for β ≤ 1 and never intervening for β ≥ 1 (Corollary 4.9). Single-site sets behave differently: the authors checked by exhaustive search that every single site is topple-free when n ≤ 6, and Lemma 4.10 proves that for n ≥ 7 no single site is, by exhibiting a sequence of additions after which the policy cannot keep up and the site reaches height 2n − 7 ≥ n.

The star. Never intervening is optimal for β ≥ n + 1 and always intervening for β ≤ n + 1 (Corollary 4.15), with gains n + 2 − 1/(n + 1) and n/(n + 1) + β, as computed in Sections 4 and 6.

The two-dimensional grid. On an L × L grid with boundary edges to the sink, the Green's function has a sine series, Eq. 56. The never-intervene threshold is φ at the center (or the four central sites when L is even), Corollary 4.6, proved by writing the walk's two coordinates as independent one-dimensional walks and integrating the product of their survival probabilities. Beyond that, the paper reports that a numerical investigation found intervention sets on the grid that are not topple-free, so Theorems 3.9 and 3.10 do not apply in general and the optimal policies on the grid are not determined.

In short: on the complete graph and the star, the two simplest policies cover every β with the switch at the largest price; topple-freeness can fail (single sites of the complete graph with n ≥ 7, intervention sets on the grid), and there the method stops.

ASSESSMENT

What is shown, and what is claimed

Proved in the paper. Theorems 3.1, 3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 3.7, 3.8, 3.9 and 3.10 hold on every finite graph and come with complete proofs; the characterizations on the path (Theorem 4.5), the complete graph (Corollary 4.9) and the star (Corollary 4.15) are if-and-only-if statements, also fully proved. The optimality claims are against every stationary deterministic policy, and through the cited MDP theory against every policy. Our brute-force check on P3 agrees with Theorem 4.5 at every β we tried.

How the proofs are built. The gain formula of Theorem 3.9 is first motivated by a coupled random-walk picture of the grains, credited to earlier work and described rather than proved in detail. The paper does not rely on that picture alone: the bias formula is checked directly against the policy evaluation equation, and the proof of Theorem 3.10 re-derives the gain from harmonic-function identities, so the final results do not depend on the heuristic.

Limits of the method. Theorem 3.10 is only a sufficient condition and needs topple-freeness, which must be checked graph by graph. The paper shows it can fail (single sites of the complete graph with n ≥ 7) and reports, from a numerical investigation without details, that it fails for intervention sets on the two-dimensional grid. The optimal policies on the grid, the case closest to the physics motivation, are therefore open. The restriction to local intervention policies is a modeling choice; on the three graph classes solved, the paper proves these are optimal, but nothing is claimed elsewhere.

Modeling choices. The cost is linear in the number of topplings and the criterion is the long-run average. The authors point out that a discounted criterion, which weighs the near future more, or costs that punish large avalanches more than proportionally, could give different optimal policies, and that controlling where grains land is a different mechanism altogether. The link to earthquakes or fires is qualitative, as the paper says itself.

Open. Whether the nested, peaked structure of the line extends to grids and other graphs, with intervention sets growing around the maximizers of φ; a graph-theoretic test for topple-freeness, possibly through spanning trees; and approximate methods, such as reinforcement learning, guided by these exact results when no closed form exists.

M. C. de Jongh, R. J. Boucherie, M. N. M. van Lieshout, Optimal local interventions in the two-dimensional Abelian sandpile model, arXiv:2603.24459 (2026). The predecessor, which studies the effect of one intervention on the very next avalanche rather than the long run, by computing the expected size of an avalanche started from a connected cluster of critical sites.

R. Meester, F. Redig, D. Znamenski, The Abelian sandpile; a mathematical introduction, arXiv:cond-mat/0301481. An introduction to the model for mathematicians. Redig is also the author of the lecture notes the paper cites for the recurrent class of the path.

Built from a full read of arXiv 2611.15549v1. Equation, theorem and lemma numbers match the paper. All three animations run real computations: the toppling sequence and expected avalanche sizes on P3; a seeded random run of the uncontrolled pile with the price ledger and a 20 000-step average; and, for each policy, the transition matrix and its long-run distribution, followed by an exhaustive search over all 864 policies. The hitting-time derivation of φ on P3, the bias sketch, the reading of φ as a price, the spanning-tree remark, the arithmetic behind Eq. 53, the L = 7 thresholds, the finance reading and the P3 tables are ours.

Exact Failure Probabilities for d-Choice Cuckoo Hashing

Chenyang Zhang, Ling Ren · posted Nov 13, 2026 · cs.DS · arXiv 2611.17688

Overview

When each of n items may sit in any one of d random slots of a table, and no two items may share a slot, the chance that no valid seating exists had only been computed exactly for d = 2; this paper computes it exactly for every n, table size M and d, in O(n² log n) time. Cuckoo hashing, the scheme behind this question, is used in key-value stores, network switches, approximate membership filters, page tables and cryptographic protocols, and in all of them a failed table is an expensive event whose probability designers want to know. The paper's route is short and surprising. It writes "this bipartite graph has no perfect matching" as an explicit polynomial in the missing edges, using a coefficient formula due to Gal Beniamini, sums that polynomial over all random outcomes in closed form, and then evaluates the resulting sum of exponentially many terms with a dynamic program that merges terms sharing a boundary. The chapter builds each of those steps on two tables small enough to check by hand.

By the end you'll be able to explain
  • what d-choice cuckoo hashing is, why a failure is exactly the absence of a matching that covers every item, and how Hall's theorem detects it;
  • why every yes/no function of a graph has a unique multilinear polynomial, and what that polynomial looks like for "no perfect matching" on a 2 × 2 grid (Eq. 1);
  • what a totally ordered graph and its representing sequence are, and how Beniamini's theorem gives the coefficients (Theorem 2.2, Eqs. 2 to 4);
  • how summing the polynomial over all outcomes turns into a sum over representing sequences, each term a product of binomial coefficients and powers (Eqs. 5 to 9);
  • why that sum factors block by block, and how a forward dynamic program over boundaries (ℓ, b) evaluates it with O(M4) operations (Eqs. 10 to 15);
  • how the same machinery handles draws with replacement and d separate tables (Eqs. 16 to 20), and what the stated running times are.

Running examples
  • Table A: 3 items, 4 slots, d = 2. Each item picks one of the C(4, 2) = 6 pairs of slots, so there are 63 = 216 equally likely outcomes. It is small enough that the whole failure count, the whole polynomial sum and the whole dynamic program fit in a paragraph each.
  • Table B: 4 items, 5 slots, d = 2. Each item picks one of C(5, 2) = 10 pairs, for 104 = 10 000 outcomes. It is the smallest case where the paper's sum has a negative term and the dynamic program visibly merges two terms into one. Both animations run on it.
1 · HASHING AS A MATCHING PROBLEM

When exactly does a cuckoo hash table fail?

A hash table stores items in an array of slots and uses a hash function to decide which slot an item belongs in, so that looking an item up means computing its hash and checking one place. The trouble is collisions: two items can hash to the same slot. Cuckoo hashing, introduced by Pagh and Rodler in 2004, handles collisions by giving each item a few alternatives. Each item has d candidate slots, chosen by d hash functions, and it must sit in one of them. A lookup therefore checks at most d slots, which is why the scheme is popular wherever worst-case lookup time matters. Insertion is where the name comes from: if all of a new item's candidates are occupied, it evicts one occupant, which moves to one of its own other candidates, possibly evicting someone else, the way a cuckoo chick pushes other eggs out of the nest.

Sometimes no rearrangement works. The paper asks for the exact probability of that event, under the standard idealization that the hash functions behave like truly random choices.

Definition · the one-table model (Section 2.1)

There are n items and M slots, with 1 ≤ d < n < M. Each item i independently draws a candidate set Γ(i), a uniformly random d-element subset of the M slots, so it has Q = C(M, d) possible candidate sets. An outcome ω = (Γ(1), …, Γ(n)) lists all candidate sets, and the Qn outcomes are equally likely. The candidate graph Gω is the bipartite graph with items on one side, slots on the other, and an edge (i, j) for each j ∈ Γ(i). A placement is a matching of Gω that covers every item. The outcome fails if no placement exists, and

where Nbad is the number of failing outcomes.

In words: every item gets d random slots, a matching is a way to seat each item in one of its own slots with no slot used twice, and the table fails when no such seating exists. Because all outcomes are equally likely, the probability is a count divided by Qn, and the whole paper is about computing that count.

A matching is a set of edges no two of which share an endpoint. Insertion with evictions is a search for a matching: an eviction chain that ends at an empty slot is what graph theorists call an augmenting path, and it enlarges the matching by one edge. The question of failure is therefore a question about matchings in a random bipartite graph, and it does not depend on the order in which items arrive or on how the insertion algorithm searches. The tool that decides it is a classical theorem, which the paper does not need to state but which makes every hand count in this chapter possible.

Background · Hall's marriage theorem (not from the paper)

For a set S of items, write Γ(S) for the union of their candidate sets. A matching that covers every item exists if and only if |Γ(S)| ≥ |S| for every set S of items. In words: failure happens exactly when some group of items is crowded into fewer slots than there are items in the group.

our sketchWhy is Hall's condition enough, and not only necessary?

Necessity is the pigeonhole principle: if some S has |Γ(S)| < |S|, the items of S cannot all get different slots. For sufficiency, the standard argument is the one cuckoo insertion carries out. Suppose a matching covers some items and item i is still unplaced. Search outward from i: look at its candidate slots, then at the items sitting in them, then at their candidate slots, and so on. If the search ever reaches an empty slot, shifting every item along the path by one step places i and keeps everyone else placed. If it never does, let S be i together with every item reached. Every slot the search reached is occupied by an item of S other than i, and every candidate of an item in S was reached, so Γ(S) consists of |S| − 1 occupied slots. That violates Hall's condition. So when the condition holds, every unplaced item can be added, one at a time.

∎

Table A shows the condition at work. A single item has 2 slots, and two items have at least 2 slots between them, so no set of one or two items can violate it. Three items violate it only if their union has 2 slots, which happens only when all three picked the same pair. There are 6 pairs, so Nbad = 6 and pfail = 6/216 = 1/36, about 2.8%. Notice that a whole free slot can sit unused while the table fails.

Table B needs a little more care, because two kinds of crowding are possible: three items sharing one pair, or all four items fitting inside three slots. Counting both, without double counting the outcomes that do both, gives Nbad = 910, so pfail = 910/10 000 = 0.091.

our countWhere does 910 come from on Table B?

Sort the outcomes by the number of slots in the union of all four candidate sets. Hall's condition for the full set of four items fails when the union has at most 3 slots. If the union has exactly 2 slots, all four items picked the same pair: 10 outcomes. If the union is a particular 3-slot set T, every item picked one of the 3 pairs inside T, giving 34 = 81 outcomes, of which 3 have a 2-slot union; so 78 outcomes for each of the 10 choices of T. Together, 10 + 780 = 790 outcomes fail this way.

If the union has 4 or more slots, failure needs three items sharing one pair P, with the fourth item's pair disjoint from P (otherwise the union would have at most 3 slots). There are 10 choices of P, 4 choices of the odd item out, and C(3, 2) = 3 pairs disjoint from P: 120 outcomes. Sets of one or two items never violate the condition. Hence Nbad = 790 + 120 = 910.

∎

The animation below runs cuckoo insertion on Table B. Items arrive one at a time and take their lowest free candidate; when both candidates are full, a breadth-first search looks for an eviction chain ending at an empty slot. The first scenario needs a chain of three moves. The second fails, and the search itself hands over the crowded group that Hall's theorem says must exist. The third draws a fresh random outcome.

Animation · cuckoo insertion on Table B
placedeviction chaincrowded group
Fact · what was known before (Section 1)

Earlier work established load thresholds for d-choice cuckoo hashing, the fraction n/M below which tables succeed with high probability as they grow, and proved upper bounds on the failure probability. The exact failure probability was known for d = 2 and, as the paper notes citing Kutzelnigg's thesis and Angel, Chen, Laine and Setty, had remained open for d ≥ 3. The paper computes pfail(n, M, d) exactly for every n, M and d in O(n2 log n) time.

In short: each item draws d random slots; the table fails exactly when the candidate graph has no matching covering every item; by Hall's theorem that means some group of items is crowded into fewer slots than its size; pfail is the number of failing outcomes over Qn, which is 1/36 on Table A and 910/10 000 on Table B.

2 · A POLYNOMIAL THAT DETECTS FAILURE

How can a yes/no property of a graph be summed over all outcomes?

Counting failures by listing outcomes takes Qn steps, which is hopeless beyond toy sizes. Hall's theorem does not help directly either, because it involves all 2n groups of items at once. The paper's idea is algebraic: if the indicator "this graph has no perfect matching" were a polynomial in variables describing the edges, then the sum over outcomes could be moved inside the polynomial, monomial by monomial, and each monomial might be easy to sum.

To use a statement about perfect matchings, the graph must be square, with the same number of vertices on both sides. Section 2.2 handles this by adding z = M − n dummy items that can be placed in any slot. The padded graph Ĝω has M vertices on each side, and it has a perfect matching if and only if Gω has a matching covering every real item: real items take their slots, and the dummies fill the slots left over. On Table A there is one dummy item; on Table B also one.

Definition · missing-edge indicators and BPM* (Eq. 1)

Let G be a bipartite graph with M left and M right vertices. For a left vertex i and right vertex j, set xij = 1 if the edge (i, j) is missing from G and xij = 0 if it is present. Beniamini and Nisan studied the multilinear polynomial BPM*M(x), which equals 1 if G has no perfect matching and 0 otherwise, and showed it has integer coefficients:

Eq. 1

In words: there is one monomial for every set H of possible edges, and xH = 1 exactly when every edge of H is missing from G. Weighting these monomials by the right integers a*H produces exactly the indicator of "no perfect matching".

Why should such a polynomial exist at all? Because the variables only take the values 0 and 1, any function of them can be written as a multilinear polynomial (no variable squared, since x2 = x on {0, 1}), and in exactly one way.

backgroundWhy is the multilinear polynomial of a 0/1 function unique, and what are its coefficients?

This is a standard fact, written out by us. Identify a 0/1 vector with the set S of coordinates equal to 1. A multilinear polynomial ΣH aH xH evaluated at S gives ΣH ⊆ S aH, since xH = 1 exactly when H ⊆ S. So the polynomial represents f precisely when f(S) = ΣH ⊆ S aH for every S. Solving from the smallest sets upward determines each aH uniquely, and inclusion–exclusion (Möbius inversion) gives the closed form

Applied to f = "no perfect matching" with S the set of missing edges, this defines the a*H in Eq. 1. It also shows why the coefficients are integers. What it does not give is a usable formula: the sum has 2|H| terms, each needing a matching test. Beniamini's theorem in the next section is the usable formula.

∎

For M = 2 the polynomial can be found by hand. A 2 × 2 bipartite graph has a perfect matching exactly when the "straight" pair of edges (1, 1), (2, 2) is present or the "crossed" pair (1, 2), (2, 1) is present. So it has none exactly when at least one straight edge is missing and at least one crossed edge is missing. The indicator that at least one of two edges is missing is x + y − xy, so

This derivation is ours. It has 9 nonzero monomials out of 16, with coefficients +1, −1 and +1. The four quadratic terms correspond to a row or a column of the 2 × 2 grid being completely missing, and the monomial x11x22, the missing diagonal, does not appear at all, even though it uses two missing edges.

The choice of missing-edge variables, rather than present-edge variables, is what makes the method feasible. Beniamini and Nisan's abstract states the contrast: in present-edge variables the matching polynomial has full degree and nearly all of its 2M² possible monomials, while in the dual representation used here the number of monomials is only exponential in Θ(M log M). Most graphs H have coefficient zero, and the next section says exactly which ones survive.

In short: padding with z = M − n dummy items turns "every item placed" into "perfect matching"; the no-perfect-matching indicator is a unique multilinear polynomial in the missing-edge indicators xij (Eq. 1); for M = 2 it has 9 monomials, and in general far fewer than all 2M².

3 · TOTALLY ORDERED GRAPHS

Which monomials survive, and with what coefficients?

In the M = 2 example the surviving monomials had a pattern: in each, the rows of missing edges were nested. For x11x12x21, row 1 is missing {1, 2} and row 2 is missing {1}, and {1} ⊆ {1, 2}. For the absent monomial x11x22, row 1 is missing {1} and row 2 is missing {2}, and neither contains the other. Beniamini's theorem says this pattern is the whole story.

Definition 2.1 · totally ordered graphs and representing sequences

For a bipartite graph H, let TH(i) be the neighborhood of its i-th left vertex. H is totally ordered if these neighborhoods are totally ordered by inclusion: for all left vertices i and i′, either TH(i) ⊆ TH(i′) or TH(i′) ⊆ TH(i). List the distinct neighborhoods as T1 ⊊ T2 ⊊ ⋯ ⊊ TL; the left vertices with neighborhood Ti form block i. Let bi = |Ti| and let ki be the number of left vertices in blocks 1 through i, with k0 = 0:

Eq. 2

The pair (k, b) = (ki, bi)i ≤ L is the representing sequence of H.

In words: sort the left vertices by how many edges they have; H is totally ordered when each vertex's neighbors include all neighbors of every vertex below it, like a staircase. Block i then has ki − ki−1 vertices, each joined to the same bi right vertices.

The paper's Figure 1 has M = 7 and representing sequence (2, 0), (4, 3), (7, 5): two left vertices with no neighbors, two with the same three neighbors, and three with the same five neighbors, the three-element set inside the five-element one. In the M = 2 example, the graph of x11x12x21 has neighborhoods {1} and {1, 2}, so L = 2 with (k1, b1) = (1, 1) and (k2, b2) = (2, 2).

Throughout, the paper sets the binomial coefficient C(a, b) to 0 unless a and b are integers with 0 ≤ b ≤ a, and lets empty products and 00 equal 1. This convention silently switches off impossible terms everywhere below.

Fact · Theorem 2.2 (Beniamini)

If H ⊆ KM,M is not totally ordered, then a*H = 0. If H is totally ordered with representing sequence (2), then

Eq. 3

where

Eq. 4

The coefficient depends on H only through its representing sequence, so the paper writes it 𝔞(k, b). In words, Eq. 3 is one factor for the last block and one factor φ for each earlier block, and each factor looks only at the block's own size and degree and at the next block's degree, all measured relative to ki−1, the number of vertices below the block. That local structure is what Section 5 exploits. Graphs that differ only by relabeling vertices on either side have the same coefficient.

Here is Eq. 3 on the M = 2 monomials, a check that is ours. For x11x12 (row 1 fully missing), the neighborhoods are ∅ and {1, 2}, so (k, b) = (1, 0), (2, 2), and a* = C(2 − 1 − 1, 2 − 2) · φ(2, 0, 1) = C(0, 0) · C(1, 1) = 1. For x11x21 (column 1 missing) both rows have neighborhood {1}, one block with (k, b) = (2, 1), and a* = C(2 − 0 − 1, 2 − 1) = 1. For x11x12x21, a* = C(0, 0) · φ(2, 1, 1) = −C(0, 0) · C(0, 0) = −1. For the full graph, a* = C(1, 0) = 1. For the empty graph, a* = C(1, 2) = 0, as it must be, since a graph with no missing edges has a perfect matching. All nine agree with the expansion of Section 2.

Our check

The paper cites Theorem 2.2 from Beniamini's 2022 paper and does not reprove it. As a sanity check we computed every coefficient for M = 3 by the inclusion–exclusion formula, over all 29 = 512 graphs H, and compared with Eqs. 3 and 4: all 512 agree, and 121 of them are nonzero.

In short: only graphs whose left neighborhoods are nested, the totally ordered ones, have nonzero coefficients; such a graph is described by its blocks (k, b) (Eq. 2), and its coefficient is a product of one factor per block (Eqs. 3 and 4).

4 · FROM THE POLYNOMIAL TO A COUNT

What does each monomial contribute when summed over all outcomes?

With the polynomial in hand, counting failures means adding BPM* over all Qn outcomes. Swapping the order of summation, Eq. 5 reads

Eq. 5

where x(ω) are the missing-edge indicators of the padded graph Ĝω. Two observations cut the sum down. First, by Theorem 2.2 only totally ordered H matter. Second, a dummy item is joined to every slot, so if H has an edge at a dummy item, that edge is never missing and xH(ω) = 0 for every outcome. So only totally ordered graphs in which every dummy item is isolated contribute.

Now fix such an H. The monomial xH(ω) is 1 exactly when every edge of H is missing, that is, when every item i avoids the slots TH(i). The paper calls TH(i) the forbidden set of item i. The number of candidate sets that avoid a forbidden set of size b is

Eq. 6

since the d candidates must be chosen among the M − b allowed slots. Items choose independently, so the number of outcomes in which every item avoids its forbidden set is a product,

Eqs. 7 and 8

with H ranging over totally ordered graphs whose dummy items are isolated. Something remarkable has happened: the hard global question, does a matching exist, has become a sum of products of simple counts, each of which only asks how many ways one item can avoid a set of slots.

Many graphs H share a representing sequence and hence a term, so the next step groups them. Dummy items have degree 0, so they lie in the first block, which forces b1 = 0 and k1 ≥ z. Let u1 = k1 − z and ui = ki − ki−1 for i ≥ 2; then ui is the number of real items in block i, and Σi ui = n. Every item in block i has a forbidden set of size bi, so the term of H is 𝔞(k, b) Πi h(bi)ui. Counting the graphs with a given representing sequence takes two choices: which real items go in which block, n!/Πi ui! ways, and which nested slot sets T1 ⊊ ⋯ ⊊ TL to use, Πi C(M − bi, bi+1 − bi) ways, since each set grows the previous one by bi+1 − bi new slots chosen from the M − bi not yet used. Writing 𝒮L(n, M) for the representing sequences with L blocks, b1 = 0 and k1 ≥ z, this gives Eq. 9:

Eq. 9

On Table A (M = 4, n = 3, d = 2, z = 1) only one representing sequence gives a nonzero term: k = (1, 4), b = (0, 2), so the dummy forms block 1 alone and all three real items share a forbidden set of size 2. Its coefficient is 𝔞 = C(4 − 1 − 1, 4 − 2) · φ(2, 0, 1) = 1 · 1 = 1, the item factor is 3!/(0! 3!) = 1, the slot factor is C(4, 2) = 6, and h(2)3 = C(2, 2)3 = 1. So Nbad = 6, as Hall's theorem gave. The reading is direct (ours): choose a pair of slots to forbid, 6 ways, and the three items must all avoid it, leaving each of them only the other pair.

Table B is more instructive. Enumerating all representing sequences with a short program of ours, exactly four give nonzero terms:

(1, 5)(0, 2)(0, 4)111081810
(1, 5)(0, 3)(0, 4)6110160

The total is 810 + 60 + 400 − 360 = 910, the number found with Hall's theorem. The negative term comes from φ with a positive middle argument: in the last row, the second block has φ(3 − 1, 2 − 1, 1) = φ(2, 1, 1) = −1. Individual terms overcount and undercount; only the total means anything, just as in inclusion–exclusion.

our checkHow do these four terms add up to exactly 1 for a single failing outcome?

Each outcome contributes BPM* = 1 or 0 to the total, so its weights across the four rows must add to 1 or 0. Take the outcome where all four items picked the same pair P. In row 1 the forbidden 2-set must avoid P, and the 3 slots outside P contain 3 such sets: weight 3. In row 2 the forbidden 3-set must be exactly the complement of P, with coefficient 6: weight 6. In row 3 any of the 4 items can be the unconstrained one and the others avoid the complement of P: weight 4. In row 4 one of 4 items forbids a 2-set inside the complement of P, which has 3 choices, with sign −1: weight −12. The total is 3 + 6 + 4 − 12 = 1.

Now take three items on P and the fourth on a pair disjoint from P, which fails by Hall. Rows 1 and 2 need all four items inside 3 slots, which is impossible: 0. Row 3 needs the unconstrained item to be the odd one: weight 1. Row 4 needs the odd item to avoid a 2-set inside the complement of P, but its own pair occupies two of those three slots: 0. Total 1 again.

∎

The number of representing sequences grows exponentially with M, so evaluating Eq. 9 term by term is out of the question for realistic tables. That is the problem the next section solves.

In short: summing Eq. 1 over outcomes turns each monomial into a product of counts h(b) = C(M − b, d) of ways to avoid a forbidden set (Eqs. 5 to 8); grouping graphs by representing sequence gives Eq. 9, a signed sum of products whose terms on Table B are 810, 60, 400 and −360.

5 · THE FORWARD RECURRENCE

How can exponentially many terms be added in polynomial time?

The answer is the same trick that counts paths through a grid without listing them. To count monotone paths from one corner to another, one does not enumerate paths; one records, for each grid point, how many paths reach it, and gets each count by adding the counts of its predecessors. That works because a path's future does not care how it arrived. Section 3.2 of the paper shows that each term of Eq. 9 is a product of factors, one per block, and that each factor depends only on where its block starts and ends. Representing sequences then behave like paths, and the dynamic program records, for each boundary, the total weight of all sequences that reach it.

The coefficient 𝔞 already factors block by block, by Eq. 3. The slot factor C(M − bi, bi+1 − bi) and the power h(bi)ui belong to block i by definition. The multinomial coefficient also factors, by choosing the items of each block in turn among those not yet placed:

Eq. 10

For a nonfinal block i < L, think of (ki−1, bi) as its start boundary and (ki, bi+1) as its end boundary. Let ν(ℓ) = max{0, ℓ − z} be the number of real items among the first ℓ left vertices (dummies come first). A nonfinal block from (ℓ, b) to (r, c) carries the multiplier

Eq. 11

In words, the four factors are the block's share of Beniamini's coefficient, the number of ways to grow the forbidden set from b to c slots, the number of ways to pick this block's u real items among the n − ν(ℓ) not yet assigned, and the number of ways those u items can avoid their b forbidden slots. Each summand of Eq. 9 is then

Eq. 12

one multiplier per nonfinal block and one factor for the final block.

Definition · prefixes and the forward state (Section 3.2)

A prefix consists of the first i < L blocks of a representing sequence together with bi+1, so it ends at the boundary (ki, bi+1). Its weight is Πj ≤ i τ(kj−1, bj; kj, bj+1). The forward state F[ℓ, b] is the sum of the weights of all prefixes ending at (ℓ, b).

In words: F[ℓ, b] adds up every way of having placed the first ℓ left vertices in blocks, with the next block about to have a forbidden set of size b.

Since τ depends only on the start and end boundaries, every complete sequence that continues a prefix ending at (ℓ, b) contributes (weight of the prefix) × τ × (later factors), with the same τ and later factors whichever prefix came first. So prefixes with the same boundary can be added together before being extended. Starting from the empty prefix,

Eq. 13

with all other entries zero. By the binomial convention τ(ℓ, b; r, c) vanishes unless z ≤ r and c > r, so only those entries are filled, for z ≤ r < M and r < c ≤ M:

Eq. 14

A final block takes all remaining items, which closes every prefix:

Eq. 15

proofWhy does the recurrence compute exactly the sum in Eq. 9?

This follows the paper. Each summand F[ℓ, b] τ(ℓ, b; r, c) in Eq. 14 extends every prefix ending at (ℓ, b) by one block ending at (r, c), multiplying its weight by τ. By induction on ℓ, F[ℓ, b] is the total weight of prefixes ending at (ℓ, b): the base case is Eq. 13, and every prefix ending at (r, c) arises from exactly one shorter prefix and one block. Eq. 15 multiplies each prefix by the final-block factor of Eq. 12, with the uL = n − ν(ℓ) items that remain. Each complete representing sequence is a prefix followed by its final block in exactly one way, so Eq. 15 reproduces each summand of Eq. 9 exactly once.

∎

Fact · cost of the basic recurrence

There are O(M2) states and O(M2) predecessors per state, so the recurrence uses O(M4) integer operations and O(M2) cells.

On Table B (z = 1) the filled table is F[0, 0] = 1; F[1, 2] = 10, F[1, 3] = 20, F[1, 4] = 15, F[1, 5] = 4; F[2, 3] = 40, F[2, 4] = 240, F[2, 5] = 120; F[3, 4] = 900, F[3, 5] = 1080; F[4, 5] = 2640. These values are from our implementation of Eqs. 11 to 15. The entry F[2, 3] = 40 is where merging happens: it adds F[0, 0] τ(0, 0; 2, 3) = 400 and F[1, 2] τ(1, 2; 2, 3) = 10 · (−36) = −360, the third and fourth rows of the table in Section 4, into one number. In Eq. 15 only three states survive: F[1, 2] gives 10 · C(3, 3) · 34 = 810, F[1, 3] gives 20 · C(3, 2) · 1 = 60, and F[2, 3] gives 40 · C(2, 2) · 1 = 40. All other states die because h(b) = 0 for b ≥ 4 or because C(M − ℓ − 1, M − b) = 0. The total is 910.

In short: every term of Eq. 9 is a product of block multipliers τ that see only the block's two boundaries (Eqs. 10 to 12); summing prefix weights per boundary gives the forward state F[ℓ, b] (Eqs. 13 and 14), and closing every prefix with its final block gives Nbad (Eq. 15) in O(M4) operations.

6 · FASTER EVALUATION AND DRAWS WITH REPLACEMENT

How does O(M4) become O(n2 log n), and what changes if candidates may repeat?

The basic recurrence has two weaknesses: its cost grows with the table size M rather than the number of items n, and the table must be rebuilt for every M. Section 3.3 removes both with three observations, which the paper states in outline.

First, after the initial block of degree 0, the total weight of the remaining blocks depends only on the number of remaining real items p = M − ℓ and the number of available slots v = M − b, where 0 ≤ v < p ≤ n. The paper calls the remaining blocks a suffix and writes V[p, v] for their total weight. This gives O(n2) states that do not depend on M, so one table serves every table size. Second, in the recurrence for V[p, v], the inner sum over the next available-slot count w depends only on v and the next item count q, not on p. Computing these shared sums once splits each transition into two stages and lowers the cost from O(n4) to O(n3). Third, the binomial coefficients in both stages can be rearranged into convolution kernels, so both stages become polynomial multiplications, which the fast Fourier transform performs in O(n log n) time each. The result is O(n2 log n).

Background · why convolutions are fast (not from the paper)

A sum of the form ck = Σj aj bk−j is a convolution: it is exactly how the coefficients of a product of two polynomials are computed. Done directly it costs O(n2) for n coefficients. The fast Fourier transform evaluates both polynomials at the n-th roots of unity in O(n log n) steps, multiplies the values pointwise, and interpolates back, for O(n log n) in total. Binomial coefficients turn into convolution kernels by writing C(a, b) = a!/(b!(a − b)!) and absorbing the factorials into the sequences.

The paper gives this speed-up as a description: it does not write out the suffix recurrence or the convolution kernels, and points to its public implementation, so this chapter does not reconstruct them.

Section 3.4 treats a common variant: each item makes d independent uniform draws from the M slots, so a candidate tuple can repeat a slot. Then Q = Md, and a forbidden set of size b is avoided by h(b) = (M − b)d tuples. Apart from these two counts, the algorithms are unchanged. On Table A with replacement there are 163 = 4096 outcomes, and our implementation of Eq. 15 with h(b) = (4 − b)2 gives Nbad = 448, which a brute-force check of all 4096 outcomes confirms; pfail = 448/4096 = 7/64, about 11%, roughly four times the 1/36 without replacement, because an item that draws the same slot twice has only one place to go.

In short: tracking remaining items and slots (p, v) instead of (ℓ, b) makes the state space O(n2) and independent of M; shared inner sums and FFT convolutions bring the cost to O(n2 log n); draws with replacement only change Q and h(b).

7 · d SEPARATE TABLES

What changes when each choice comes from its own table?

The paper's second model splits the slots into d tables and gives each item one random slot in each. Section 4 extends the method to it.

Definition · the separate-table model (Section 4.1)

There are d disjoint tables of positive lengths m1, …, md. Each item chooses one slot uniformly from each table, independently across tables and items, and must occupy one of these slots. Write m = (m1, …, md), M = Σj mj and Q = Πj mj. There are Qn equally likely outcomes, Nbad(n; m) of which admit no placement, with d < n < M.

In words: same matching problem, but the d candidates of every item are forced to come one from each table.

The one-table recurrence tracked only the total size b of the forbidden set, which was enough because h(b) depended only on b. Now it is not enough. The paper's example: with two tables of length 4, forbidden counts (3, 1) and (2, 2) both total four, but leave 1 · 3 = 3 and 2 · 2 = 4 choices per item. So the state must record the forbidden count b = (b1, …, bd) in each table, with |b| = Σj bj. An item with forbidden counts b has

Eq. 16

candidate choices, and a forbidden set with counts b grows to one with counts c in

Eq. 17

ways. The block multiplier changes in exactly these two places; the coefficient factor and the item-choice factor are unchanged:

Eq. 18

with u = r − max{ℓ, z} and z = M − n as before. Starting from Fd[0, 0] = 1, for z ≤ r < M and 0 ≤ c ≤ m with |c| > r,

Eq. 19

Eq. 20

and pfail = Nbad(n; m)/Qn.

A small example, ours: 3 items and two tables of length 2, so M = 4 as in Table A. Each item picks one slot from each table, Q = 4 and there are 64 outcomes. By Hall's theorem, failure needs three items crowded into two slots, and since each item already uses one slot per table, all three must have picked the same pair: 4 outcomes, so pfail = 4/64 = 1/16. That is more than the 1/36 of Table A with the same four slots, because forcing one choice per table leaves each item only 4 possible candidate sets instead of 6. Our implementation of Eqs. 18 to 20 returns 4, and agrees with brute force on every other small case we tried.

Fact · cost for separate tables (Section 4.3)

If bj = mj for some table, then hm(b) = 0 and the state can be dropped, so only states with bj < mj for every j are kept. In terms of remaining items p = M − ℓ and available slots v = m − b, the retained states satisfy 1 ≤ p ≤ n, v ≥ 1 and |v| < p, at most C(p − 1, d) vectors for each p, so there are at most

states. With precomputed binomials and powers each transition costs O(1), giving O(n2d+2) operations and O(nd+1) cells per vector m. The suffix formulation of Section 3.3 also applies and builds a table depending only on n and d in O(nd+2) operations, after which each table-length vector is evaluated in O(nd+1).

detailWhy is the sum of C(p − 1, d) equal to C(n, d + 1)?

This is the hockey-stick identity, explained by us. Count the (d + 1)-element subsets of {1, …, n} by their largest element p: the other d elements come from {1, …, p − 1}, in C(p − 1, d) ways. Summing over p gives all C(n, d + 1) subsets.

∎

The exponent grows with d because the state must remember a vector of d counts. The paper names as future work an algorithm for separate tables that is polynomial in both n and d.

In short: with separate tables the state records how many slots are forbidden in each table (Eqs. 16 and 17); the multiplier and recurrence keep their shape (Eqs. 18 to 20); the cost is O(nd+2) for fixed d, polynomial in n but not in d.

What the paper establishes

The paper is a methods paper: its results are exact algorithms and their running times, and it contains no tables of numerical failure probabilities or timing experiments. Its claims are collected here.

ASSESSMENT

What is shown, and what is claimed

Proved in the paper. Given Beniamini's coefficient formula (Theorem 2.2), the derivation from Eq. 5 to Eq. 15 is complete and elementary: dummy padding, the vanishing of monomials touching dummies, independence of items (Eq. 7), the count of graphs per representing sequence, the blockwise factorization (Eqs. 10 to 12) and the inductive correctness of the recurrence. The separate-table version (Eqs. 16 to 20) follows the same steps, and its state count is proved. Our brute-force comparisons on small cases, for one table, with replacement and with separate tables, all agree with the formulas.

Imported. Theorem 2.2, which carries all the combinatorial depth, is quoted from Beniamini's 2022 paper and not reproved. Its correctness is the foundation of everything else; we confirmed it exhaustively for M ≤ 3.

Described rather than derived. The O(n2 log n) bound of Section 3.3 and the O(nd+2) bound for separate tables rest on suffix recurrences and convolution rearrangements that the text describes in a paragraph each, without explicit formulas or a proof; the authors point to their public implementation. The counts are of arithmetic operations. Since Nbad and Qn are integers with roughly n log Q digits, the bit cost of exact arithmetic adds a further factor that the stated bounds do not include; this remark is ours, and the paper does not discuss numerical precision.

Scope. The model assumes fully random hash functions, as is standard, and asks only whether a placement exists, not how long an insertion algorithm takes to find it. Variants with a stash, buckets holding several items, or other insertion rules are not treated. There are no numerical results in the paper, so practical speed and the sizes reachable are not reported.

Open. An algorithm for separate tables that is polynomial in both n and d.

FURTHER READING

Further reading

C. Zhang, L. Ren, Exact failure probabilities for d-choice cuckoo hashing, arXiv:2611.17688 (2026). The paper itself; equation and theorem numbers in this chapter follow its HTML version.

G. Beniamini, N. Nisan, Bipartite perfect matching as a real polynomial, arXiv:2001.07642. Introduces the polynomial view of matching and shows that the dual, missing-edge representation has only exp(Θ(n log n)) monomials, against nearly all 2n² in the usual one.

G. Beniamini, The approximate degree of bipartite perfect matching, arXiv:2004.14318. The source of Theorem 2.2: it fully characterizes the dual polynomial's coefficients on the way to its main result about approximate degree.

Built from a full read of arXiv 2611.17688v1. Equation, theorem and section numbers match the paper. Both animations run real computations: cuckoo insertion with breadth-first eviction search on Table B, including the crowded group extracted from a failed search; and the forward recurrence of Eqs. 11 to 15 with its final sum, followed by a Hall's-condition test of every outcome. Hall's theorem and its sketch, the hand counts for Tables A and B, the M = 2 polynomial and its coefficient checks, the M = 3 exhaustive check, the per-outcome weights, the replacement and separate-table examples, the convolution and hockey-stick remarks, the bit-cost remark and the numerical table are ours.
