Portfolio-Size Constraints on Default Correlation: Exact Coherence Tests and Sharp Asymptotic Bounds

M. Palaisti · submitted Nov 11, 2026 · q-fin.RM · arXiv 2611.18759

Overview

A credit model can say that 2% of 100 loans default within one year and 2.5% within two, and still describe something no real portfolio could ever do: in the paper's example, its two-year forecast makes "at least one default" about 24 percentage points less likely than its one-year forecast, although a loan that has defaulted stays defaulted. This paper finds exactly when such contradictions happen in the standard one-factor Gaussian model of credit risk. For a pool of n borrowers, checking all n tail probabilities reduces to checking two events, "nobody defaults" and "everybody defaults". Those two checks give an exact interval of allowed correlations for the next horizon, the interval shrinks as the pool grows, and its width goes to zero at the remarkably slow rate 1/√(log n). The chapter builds this from scratch: stochastic order, quantile couplings, binomial mixtures, a sign-change argument, the Gaussian factor model and an extreme-value estimate, all on a three-borrower pool small enough to check by hand.

By the end you'll be able to explain
  • why a default that cannot be undone forces every tail probability of the default count to grow with the horizon, and why a rising mean is not enough (Eqs. 2 and 3, Example 3.3);
  • how a single uniform random number and a random shuffle build a default process from any stochastically ordered list of count laws (Proposition 3.2);
  • what a binomial mixture is, and how a shared economic factor inflates the variance of the default count (Eqs. 5 and 6);
  • why, when two mixing distributions cross at most once, the "no defaults" and "all defaults" probabilities decide all n tail comparisons (Theorem 4.1, Eqs. 7 to 11);
  • how the one-factor Gaussian model is built and why its correlation parameter has an exact feasible interval at the next horizon, computed from two scalar equations (Eqs. 12 to 17);
  • how an inconsistent correlation curve is repaired by projection, with the paper's 100-loan example (Eq. 18, Tables 1 and 4);
  • why only a constant correlation survives every pool size, and why the interval narrows like C/√(log n) (Corollary 7.2, Lemma 7.3, Theorem 7.4, Eqs. 23 to 31).

The second and third animations recompute the paper's tables in your browser.
1 · DEFAULTS DO NOT HEAL

What must be true of default counts at two horizons?

Banks and investors forecast portfolio losses at several horizons at once: one year, two years, five years. Each forecast is a probability distribution for the number of borrowers who will have defaulted by that date, all made today with today's information. The paper's starting point is that these distributions cannot be chosen freely, because default is a one-way door. A borrower who has defaulted by year one has also defaulted by year two, even if the loan is later cured or repaid, since the record being counted is the history of first defaults.

Definition · absorbing default indicators (Section 2.1)

Let τi be the first default time of borrower i and Di(t) = 1{τi ≤ t} its cumulative default indicator. Then Di(s) ≤ Di(t) whenever s < t, which is what absorbing means. For a homogeneous pool, p(t) = P(τi ≤ t) is the same for every borrower and the default count is

In words: each borrower carries a switch that can flip from 0 to 1 once and never back, and K(t) counts the switches that have flipped by time t.

Since every switch only flips up, the count K(t) can only go up along any realized history. So if the event "at least k defaults by time s" happens, then "at least k defaults by time t" happens too, for every later t. Taking probabilities, every tail P(K(t) ≥ k) must be nondecreasing in t. This is a named relationship between two distributions.

Definition · first-order stochastic order (Section 3)

For counts K and K′ taking values in {0, …, n}, write K ≤st K′ if

In words: K′ is at least as likely as K to reach any threshold. Equivalently, the distribution function of K′ lies on or below that of K at every point.

Stochastic order is much stronger than an ordering of means. It implies E f(K) ≤ E f(K′) for every increasing function f, the mean being one example, but a larger mean does not imply it. The paper gives the comparison a financial meaning through loss layers. With normalized loss L(t) = K(t)/n, a tranche that absorbs losses between (k − 1)/n and k/n of the pool loses

Eq. 2

detailWhy does a one-default-wide tranche lose exactly 1/n times an indicator?

The argument is ours, though the identity is the paper's. Here x+ = max(x, 0). Because K(t) is an integer, L(t) − (k − 1)/n = (K(t) − k + 1)/n is either at most 0, when K(t) ≤ k − 1, or at least 1/n, when K(t) ≥ k. In the first case the positive part is 0, and in the second the minimum with 1/n is 1/n. So the tranche is either untouched or wiped out, according to whether the k-th default has happened.

∎

Taking expectations, the expected loss of the k-th layer is P(K(t) ≥ k)/n. So stochastic order between horizons says exactly that every single-default-wide layer has an expected loss that grows with maturity. To measure how badly a pair of forecasts fails, the paper uses the largest decline,

Eq. 3

which is zero exactly when the later count dominates the earlier one.

The toy pool shows how a forecast can raise the mean and still fail. At the earlier horizon K0 is Binomial(3, 0.2), so P(K0 = 0) = 0.83 = 0.512 and the tails are

In the split forecast the later count is Binomial(3, 0.01) or Binomial(3, 0.59) with probability 1/2 each. Averaging, P(K1 = 0) = (0.993 + 0.413)/2 = (0.970299 + 0.068921)/2 = 0.519610, and the tails are 0.480390, 0.316920 and 0.102690. The mean rose from 0.6 to 0.9, and the two upper tails rose, but the chance of at least one default fell from 0.488 to 0.480390. So V3 = 0.00761, and no default process has these two horizon laws. The calm forecast, with conditional probabilities 0.1 and 0.5, gives tails 0.573, 0.264 and 0.063, all larger than the earlier ones, so it passes. These toy numbers are ours.

The paper's Example 3.3 shows that the failure can also hide in the middle. Take n = 3 with K0 = 2 surely, and K1 equal to 1 or 3 with probabilities 2/5 and 3/5. Both no-default probabilities are 0, the all-default probability rises from 0 to 3/5, and the mean rises from 2 to 11/5. Yet P(K1 ≥ 2) = 3/5 < 1 = P(K0 ≥ 2). The two extreme events look fine and an interior tail breaks. Section 4 identifies the extra structure under which the extremes are enough.

Fact · absorption orders the tails (Section 2.1)

If defaults are absorbing, every count-tail probability P(K(t) ≥ k), k = 1, …, n, is nondecreasing in the horizon t. A rising expected count does not imply this.

In short: defaults are one-way switches, so the default count can only grow and its distribution must rise in stochastic order from horizon to horizon; each tail probability is the expected loss of a one-default-wide tranche (Eq. 2); Vn measures the worst decline (Eq. 3); the split toy forecast raises the mean yet has V3 = 0.00761.

2 · FROM ORDERED COUNTS TO A DEFAULT PROCESS

Is stochastic order also enough for a real default process to exist?

Section 1 showed that ordering is necessary. The converse question is whether, given count distributions at several horizons that are ordered, one can always build borrowers with absorbing default indicators that have exactly those distributions. The answer is yes, and the construction is short enough to run by hand.

Definition 3.1 · absorbing compatibility

Fix horizons t0 < ⋯ < tm and, at each horizon, an exchangeable law νj on {0, 1}n. The laws are absorbing-compatible if some joint distribution has these marginals and satisfies Di,j+1 ≥ Dij almost surely for every borrower i and every j.

In words: a single random history exists in which each horizon looks exactly as forecast and no borrower ever leaves default.

Exchangeable means that relabeling the borrowers does not change the law. Such a law is determined by its count: given Kj = k, each set of k defaulted names has probability 1/C(n, k). So the question is only about counts.

Background · the quantile trick (not from the paper)

If F is the distribution function of a count and U is uniform on (0, 1), the left quantile F−1(U) = min{k : F(k) ≥ U} has distribution function F, because F−1(U) ≤ k exactly when U ≤ F(k). Feeding the same U into two quantile functions couples the two counts: if F1(k) ≤ F0(k) for every k, which is K0 ≤st K1, then F1−1(U) ≥ F0−1(U) for every U.

Proposition 3.2 · ordering is exactly compatibility

The laws ν0, …, νm are absorbing-compatible if and only if K0 ≤st ⋯ ≤st Km. When this holds, an exchangeable absorbing coupling can be built from one uniform random variable and one independent uniform permutation of the borrowers.

proofHow do one uniform number and one shuffle produce the process?

Necessity: summing Di,j+1 ≥ Dij over i gives Kj+1 ≥ Kj pathwise, hence ordered tails. Sufficiency: let Fj be the count distribution function at horizon j and set Kj = Fj−1(U) for one uniform U, using the left quantile. Stochastic ordering gives K0 ≤ ⋯ ≤ Km for every U. Let R1, …, Rn be the ranks of an independent uniform random permutation and put Dij = 1{Ri ≤ Kj}. Given Kj = k, the defaulted set is the k borrowers with the smallest ranks, which is a uniformly random k-set, so the horizon law is νj. Since Kj grows with j, so does each indicator.

∎

Each borrower's default time is then the first horizon at which its indicator turns on. The paper notes that the coupling is one choice among many: the horizon laws do not pin down how the process moves between horizons.

On the toy pool, the distribution functions at k = 0, 1, 2 are F0 = (0.512, 0.896, 0.992) for the earlier horizon, F1 = (0.427, 0.736, 0.937) for the calm forecast and F1 = (0.519610, 0.683080, 0.897310) for the split one. The calm values all sit below F0, as ordering requires. The split value at k = 0 sits above, by 0.00761. If U lands in the thin band (0.512, 0.519610], the earlier count is 1 and the later count is 0: somebody would have to leave default. The animation draws U, reads both quantiles off the staircases, shuffles three borrowers, and then repeats the construction 20 000 times to compare frequencies with the targets.

Animation · the quantile coupling on the toy pool
earlier horizonlater horizondefaulted

In short: exchangeable horizon laws are compatible with absorbing defaults exactly when their counts are stochastically ordered (Proposition 3.2); the proof feeds one uniform U to every quantile function and defaults the borrowers with the smallest random ranks; for the split toy forecast the band of U that would force a cure has width 0.00761.

3 · A SHARED ECONOMY: BINOMIAL MIXTURES

What kind of count distributions do credit models produce?

Borrowers do not default independently. In a recession many default together, and in a boom few do. The standard way to model this is to let a random environment set a common default probability Q, and to let borrowers default independently given Q. The count is then a binomial with a random success probability.

Definition · binomial mixture (Eq. 5)

For a horizon a ∈ {0, 1},

Eq. 5

and Ha denotes the distribution function of Qa, the mixing distribution.

In words: first nature picks the state of the economy, which fixes a default probability Qa; then each borrower flips its own coin with that probability.

Writing pa = E Qa, the mean and variance of the count are

Eq. 6

our derivationWhere does the extra n(n − 1) Var(Q) come from?

The paper states Eq. 6; this derivation is ours and uses the law of total variance, Var K = E[Var(K | Q)] + Var(E[K | Q]). Given Q the count is binomial, so Var(K | Q) = nQ(1 − Q) and E[K | Q] = nQ. Hence

using E Q2 = p2 + Var Q. Collecting terms gives np(1 − p) + n(n − 1) Var Q.

∎

The first term is the binomial variance of independent borrowers. The second is the contribution of the shared environment, and because it grows like n2 rather than n, it dominates in large pools. On the toy pool, Q0 = 0.2 is constant, so Var K0 = 3(0.2)(0.8) = 0.48. The calm forecast has Var Q1 = 0.22 = 0.04 and Var K1 = 0.63 + 6(0.04) = 0.87; the split forecast has Var Q1 = 0.292 = 0.0841 and Var K1 = 0.63 + 0.5046 = 1.1346. Both later forecasts have mean 0.9. The split one spreads its probability toward both extremes, which raised P(K1 = 0) above its earlier value in Section 1.

Fact · common uncertainty fattens both ends (Section 4)

Different mixing laws with the same mean can change the probability of both mild and severe default outcomes. Greater spread in Q raises the probability of zero defaults as well as of many defaults, and that is how a rise in correlation can make a later forecast less likely than an earlier one to show any default at all.

In short: a binomial mixture draws a common default probability Q and then independent defaults (Eq. 5); its variance is the binomial variance plus n(n − 1) Var Q (Eq. 6); on the toy pool the split forecast has variance 1.1346 against 0.87 for the calm one at the same mean.

4 · TWO EVENTS DECIDE ALL n

When do "nobody defaults" and "everybody defaults" settle every tail?

Checking stochastic order means comparing n tail probabilities, each an integral against the mixing distribution. Example 3.3 showed that the first and last tails do not suffice in general. The paper's main structural result is that for binomial mixtures they do suffice, under a mild condition on how the mixing distributions compare.

A function has at most one sign change if it has constant sign, or changes once from nonnegative to nonpositive, or once the other way; zeros are allowed.

Theorem 4.1 · the two-event criterion

Assume H0 − H1 has at most one sign change on (0, 1). Then K0 ≤st K1 if and only if

Eq. 7

In words: E(1 − Q)n is the probability that nobody defaults and E Qn the probability that everybody does. When the mixing distributions cross at most once, the later forecast dominates exactly when it makes "nobody" no more likely and "everybody" no less likely.

The proof turns each tail difference into an integral of H0 − H1 against a positive weight. With g = H0 − H1 and wk(q) = qk−1(1 − q)n−k,

Eq. 8

detailWhy is the tail difference an integral of g against wk?

The paper's reason is that the derivative of the binomial tail in q is n C(n − 1, k − 1) wk(q) and the boundary terms vanish. Filling in the steps is ours. Let Bk(q) = P(Bin(n, q) ≥ k). Think of n uniform numbers on (0, 1); the count of those below q is Bin(n, q), and it is at least k exactly when the k-th smallest is below q. So Bk is the distribution function of the k-th smallest of n uniforms, whose density is the chance that one specific number lands at q (n choices), k − 1 others land below (C(n − 1, k − 1) choices, probability qk−1) and the rest above (probability (1 − q)n−k). That is B′k(q) = n C(n − 1, k − 1) wk(q).

Now P(Ka ≥ k) = ∫ Bk dHa, and integrating by parts on [0, 1],

since Bk(1) = Ha(1) = 1 and Bk(0) = 0 for k ≥ 1. Subtracting the a = 0 version from the a = 1 version leaves ∫ B′k (H0 − H1) dq, which is Eq. 8.

∎

Conditions (7) say T1 ≥ 0 and Tn ≥ 0. The weights wk slide from the left end of (0, 1) toward the right as k grows: w1 = (1 − q)n−1 lives near 0 and wn = qn−1 near 1. If g is positive on the left and negative on the right, then Tn, which weighs the right most heavily, is the hardest to keep nonnegative, and if Tn survives, every intermediate Tk does too. If g is negative on the left and positive on the right, T1 is the hardest. That is the whole idea; the ratio inequalities below make it exact.

proofHow does a single crossing transfer the sign from T1 or Tn to every Tk?

Necessity is the thresholds k = 1 and k = n. For sufficiency, if g ≥ 0 every integral in Eq. 8 is nonnegative. If g ≤ 0, then T1 ≥ 0 and w1 > 0 force g = 0 almost everywhere, and every Tk = 0. Suppose g is nonnegative below a crossing point q* and nonpositive above it. The ratio wn/wk = [q/(1 − q)]n−k is nondecreasing, so for all q

Eq. 9

Below q*, g ≥ 0 and the ratio is at most its value at q*; above, g ≤ 0 and the ratio is at least that value; both give the inequality. Integrating, the left side is a positive multiple of Tn ≥ 0, so ∫ wk g ≥ 0. If instead g is nonpositive below q* and nonnegative above, the nondecreasing ratio wk/w1 = [q/(1 − q)]k−1 gives

Eq. 10

and T1 ≥ 0 finishes the argument. Crossings at a boundary reduce to constant sign.

∎

The toy pool runs through every step. In the calm forecast, H1 jumps by 1/2 at 0.1 and at 0.5, and H0 jumps by 1 at 0.2. So g = H0 − H1 is −1/2 on [0.1, 0.2), +1/2 on [0.2, 0.5), and 0 elsewhere: one sign change, from negative to positive, at q* = 0.2. The criterion says T1 ≥ 0 is the binding check, and indeed Eq. 8 gives T1 = 0.085, T2 = 0.160 and T3 = 0.055, exactly the differences of the tails listed in Section 1 (our computation). The split forecast has the same shape of g, with jumps at 0.01 and 0.59, and its binding check fails: T1 = −0.00761. Example 3.3 escapes the theorem because a count that equals 2 surely is not a binomial mixture with 0 < Q < 1.

In practice the single-crossing condition is easy to verify, because credit models build Q by pushing one random factor through a fixed increasing function.

Corollary 4.2 · location-scale mixtures cross once

Let Z have a continuous strictly increasing distribution function F, let G be a continuous strictly increasing bijection from ℝ onto (0, 1), and let Qa = G(μa + σaZ) with σa > 0. Then the equivalence of Theorem 4.1 holds.

proofWhy does a common factor and link guarantee one crossing?

Ha(q) = F((G−1(q) − μa)/σa). Since F is strictly increasing, H0(q) − H1(q) has the sign of

Eq. 11

an affine function of the increasing quantity G−1(q), which changes sign at most once.

∎

This covers probit-normal mixing (G = Φ, Z normal) and logit-normal mixing, and also non-normal factors with full support, provided both horizons use the same factor distribution and link.

In short: each tail change Tk is the mixing-distribution difference integrated against a weight that slides from 0 to 1 as k grows (Eq. 8); if that difference changes sign once, the end weight on the far side is the hardest test, so the no-default and all-default comparisons decide all n tails (Theorem 4.1, Eq. 7); one-factor location-scale models always cross once (Eq. 11).

5 · THE ONE-FACTOR GAUSSIAN MODEL

How does the industry-standard model fit this picture?

The model used in practice, going back to Li's Gaussian copula and Vasicek's large-pool analysis, gives each borrower a hidden "health" score that mixes a common economic factor with an individual shock. A borrower defaults by the horizon when its score falls below a threshold chosen to match its default probability.

Definition · the homogeneous one-factor Gaussian model (Eq. 4)

Let V, ε1, …, εn be independent standard normals and

Eq. 4

In words: each latent score Xi is standard normal, any two scores have correlation ρ through the shared V, and Φ turns the score into a uniform number Ui. A borrower is in default by time t when its Ui is below p(t), which happens with probability exactly p(t).

If ρ is the same at every horizon, reusing the same Ui makes every indicator nondecreasing whenever p(t) is, so the model is automatically consistent. The paper's question is what happens when a modeler fits a separate correlation at each maturity, which is common practice. Then the horizon laws are still binomial mixtures, but the coupling between horizons has to be found, and Section 2 says the test is stochastic order.

Conditioning on the common factor gives the mixing variable. With Z standard normal and c(p) = Φ−1(p),

Eq. 12

our derivationWhy is this the default probability given the economy, and why is its mean p?

A borrower defaults when Φ(Xi) ≤ p, that is, Xi ≤ c(p). Given V, this reads √(1 − ρ) εi ≤ c(p) − √ρ V, which has probability Φ((c(p) − √ρ V)/√(1 − ρ)). Writing Z = −V, which is also standard normal, gives Eq. 12; the paper notes the sign of Z is immaterial. Given V the borrowers are independent, so the count is Bin(n, Q). For the mean, E Q = P(√(1 − ρ) ε − √ρ Z ≤ c(p)), and √(1 − ρ) ε − √ρ Z is standard normal because its variance is (1 − ρ) + ρ = 1, so the probability is Φ(c(p)) = p, as the paper states.

∎

In probit form, Q = Φ(μ + σZ) with location and scale

Eq. 14

so Corollary 4.2 applies with F = G = Φ. For the paper's pool, c(0.02) = −2.0537, and at ρ = 0.15 the location is μ = −2.2276 and the scale σ = 0.4201 (our arithmetic). Raising ρ raises σ, so Q spreads out: bad economies get worse and good ones better.

The parameter ρ is the correlation of the hidden scores, not of the default indicators. The latter is

Eq. 13

where Φ2(·, ·; ρ) is the bivariate normal distribution function with correlation ρ. So a constant latent ρ can coexist with a changing default correlation as p grows. As an illustration (our computation), Φ2(c, c; ρ) is the probability that two given borrowers both default, which is E Q2; at p = 0.02 and ρ = 0.15 it is 0.000877, and the default correlation is only 0.0243. At p = 0.03 and the same ρ it is 0.0308. Small default correlations are typical, which is why the latent parameter is the one modelers fit.

The two events of Theorem 4.1 get names:

Eq. 15

An is the probability that all n borrowers default and Sn the probability that all survive; at ρ = 0 they reduce to pn and (1 − p)n. The identity Sn(p, ρ) = An(1 − p, ρ) holds because 1 − Φ(x) = Φ(−x) and c(1 − p) = −c(p), together with the symmetry of Z.

Lemma 5.1 · both extremes rise with correlation

For n ≥ 2, An(p, ρ) and Sn(p, ρ) are continuous and strictly increasing in ρ ∈ [0, 1). At fixed ρ, An strictly increases and Sn strictly decreases in p.

proof sketchWhy does more correlation make both extremes more likely?

The monotonicity in p is immediate from Eq. 12. For ρ, An is the probability that all coordinates of an equicorrelated normal vector lie below c(p). A classical identity of Plackett (1954) says the derivative of such an orthant probability with respect to one off-diagonal correlation is the bivariate normal density at the two thresholds, times the conditional probability that the remaining coordinates stay below theirs. Both factors are positive, and along the equicorrelation path the derivative is a sum of such terms over pairs. Continuity at ρ = 0 is dominated convergence. The same applies to Sn at 1 − p.

∎

Two closed forms let one test any implementation, and the paper uses them for exactly that. At p = ρ = 1/2, c = 0 and σ = 1, so Q = Φ(Z) is uniform on (0, 1) and An = ∫01 qn dq = 1/(n + 1). At n = 2 and p = 1/2, A2 = 1/4 + arcsin(ρ)/(2π), the classical orthant formula for two correlated normals. The code behind the animations below reproduces both to about 15 digits.

In short: each borrower's hidden score mixes a common factor with a private shock (Eq. 4); given the factor, the default probability is a probit-normal Q with location c/√(1 − ρ) and scale √(ρ/(1 − ρ)) (Eqs. 12 and 14); An and Sn are the all-default and no-default probabilities (Eq. 15), and both rise with ρ (Lemma 5.1).

6 · THE EXACT INTERVAL OF CORRELATIONS

Which later correlations are consistent with the earlier forecast?

Fix the earlier pair (p0, ρ0) and the later default probability p1 ≥ p0, and ask which later correlations r are compatible. By Corollary 4.2 and Theorem 4.1 the answer is the set of r with An(p1, r) ≥ An(p0, ρ0) and Sn(p1, r) ≤ Sn(p0, ρ0). Lemma 5.1 says both left sides increase in r. So the first inequality holds for all r from some point on, the second for all r up to some point, and the feasible set is an interval.

Theorem 5.2 · the exact interval

Fix a cap ρ̄ < 1 with 0 < ρ0 < ρ̄, and let In(p0, ρ0; p1) be the set of r ∈ [0, ρ̄] for which the two Gaussian horizon laws are absorbing-compatible. For n ≥ 2, In = [ℓn, un] with

Eq. 16

Eq. 17

The interval contains ρ0; it is {ρ0} if p1 = p0 and contains a neighborhood of ρ0 if p1 > p0. For a finite sequence of horizons, compatibility holds exactly when each adjacent pair satisfies its interval.

In words: the lowest allowed correlation keeps "everybody defaults" from becoming less likely, and the highest keeps "nobody defaults" from becoming more likely. Each endpoint solves one equation in one unknown.

proofWhy is ρ0 always inside, and why do adjacent checks suffice for many horizons?

For positive r, Corollary 4.2 reduces compatibility to the two inequalities, and Lemma 5.1 gives the roots and the interval between them. The choice r = ρ0 satisfies both because An increases and Sn decreases in p and p1 ≥ p0. When p1 = p0, strict monotonicity in r forces r = ρ0; when p1 > p0, both inequalities are strict at ρ0 and continuity gives a neighborhood. At r = 0, Q1 = p1 surely, and H0 − H1 is nonnegative below p1 and nonpositive above, so Theorem 4.1 covers that endpoint. Finally, stochastic order is transitive and Proposition 3.2 builds one absorbing coupling across the whole grid.

∎

Only one of the two equations matters in each direction of change. If p1 ≥ p0 and ρ1 ≥ ρ0, compatibility is equivalent to Sn(p1, ρ1) ≤ Sn(p0, ρ0), because the all-default inequality holds automatically; if ρ1 ≤ ρ0, it is equivalent to An(p1, ρ1) ≥ An(p0, ρ0) (Corollary 5.3).

Computing the endpoints needs An accurately when it is astronomically small; at n = 100 and p = 0.02 it is about 10−27. The paper writes it as a one-dimensional integral over x = μ + σZ and works with logarithms:

Eq. 33

The exponent h(x) is strictly concave, its peak x* solves nφ(x*)/Φ(x*) = (x* − μ)/σ2 (Eq. 35), and the integral is taken over x* ± 13σ after subtracting h(x*) (Eq. 34). The roots are found by bracketing, which Lemma 5.1 makes safe. The animation does exactly this in your browser: it plots log10 An(p1, r) and log10 Sn(p1, r) against r for the paper's pool, draws the earlier values as horizontal targets, and bisects for each crossing. The results match Table 2 to all six printed digits.

Animation · bisecting for ℓn and un
later curveearlier targetbracketfeasible

The upper endpoint is far from ρ0 for small pools and the lower one close to it. That asymmetry has a reason: "everybody defaults" is a very rare event, and raising p from 0.02 to 0.03 multiplies its probability by a large factor, so a small drop in correlation is enough to undo the gain. "Nobody defaults" is a common event, and the same change in p moves it only modestly.

Larger pools can only be harder to satisfy.

Proposition 5.4 · the intervals are nested

For every n ≥ 2, In+1(p0, ρ0; p1) ⊆ In(p0, ρ0; p1). Consequently, for fixed parameters, the pool sizes that are compatible form an initial segment {1, 2, …, N}, possibly all integers.

proofWhy can a larger pool never be easier?

Delete one borrower from an absorbing coupling for n + 1 borrowers. What is left is still absorbing, and each horizon law is still the Gaussian binomial mixture with the same (p, ρ) and n borrowers, since the remaining borrowers share the same factor. So any correlation feasible for n + 1 is feasible for n.

∎

For the paper's pool our code gives [0, 0.942] at n = 2, [0.064, 0.809] at n = 3 and [0.099, 0.656] at n = 5, before reaching the paper's [0.118262, 0.495604] at n = 10 and [0.135019, 0.253694] at n = 100. Its n = 50 and n = 500 values, [0.1327, 0.2934] and [0.1380, 0.2081], match the paper's Table 3.

In short: the feasible later correlations form an exact interval [ℓn, un] containing ρ0, with ℓn solving An(p1, r) = An(p0, ρ0) and un solving Sn(p1, r) = Sn(p0, ρ0) (Eqs. 16 and 17); they are computed in log form by one-dimensional quadrature (Eqs. 33 to 35); the intervals shrink as the pool grows (Proposition 5.4).

7 · REPAIRING AN INCONSISTENT CURVE

What should a modeler do with a correlation that falls outside the interval?

Correlations fitted separately at each maturity will sometimes break the interval. The paper's remedy keeps every default probability and moves each offending correlation to the nearest feasible value, one horizon at a time.

Definition · sequential repair (Eq. 18)

Given nondecreasing p0, …, pm and raw correlations ρ̂0, …, ρ̂m in [0, ρ̄], set ρ*0 = ρ̂0. Given ρ*j−1, compute the interval [ℓj, uj] for the step from (pj−1, ρ*j−1) to pj, and put

Eq. 18

In words: clip each raw correlation into the interval allowed by the previous repaired one.

Proposition 5.5 · the repair is valid and minimal step by step

The repaired sequence is absorbing-compatible and keeps every pj. Given the preceding repaired pair, ρ*j is the unique minimizer of |r − ρ̂j|a over the feasible interval, for every a > 0.

proofWhy is the interval never empty, and why is clipping optimal?

Each interval contains the preceding correlation (Theorem 5.2), so it is nonempty and the clip lands in it. Theorem 5.2 and Proposition 3.2 then give compatibility. Every correlation in Eq. 12 keeps the individual probability equal to pj. The closest point of a closed interval to a given number is the clip, whatever power of distance is used.

∎

The paper's main worked example (Section 8.3) is a pool of 100 borrowers going from (p0, ρ0) = (0.02, 0.10) to a raw later pair (0.025, 0.40). Expected defaults rise from 2 to 2.5, but the higher correlation piles probability onto both extremes: P(K = 0) rises from 0.270717 to 0.514092, so the chance of at least one default falls by about 24.34 percentage points. Since ρ rose, Corollary 5.3 says only the no-default equation matters, and solving S100(0.025, r) = 0.270717 gives the closest feasible correlation, 0.153059. The animation computes the whole count distribution for each forecast and plots the change in all of the first 40 tails, so the two-event shortcut can be checked against the full list.

Animation · all tail changes, 100 borrowers
tail rosetail fell

The paper puts the violation in money. With $1 million lost per default, the expected loss of the first $1 million layer is $1 million times P(K ≥ 1), and the raw forecast lowers it by about $243,375 as maturity increases. By direct enumeration the paper also finds that this parameter pair first becomes incompatible at n = 7; our code agrees, with P(K = 0) at 0.873273 earlier and 0.873592 later for n = 7, while n = 6 still passes.

With several horizons the clipping propagates. The paper's Table 4 uses 100 borrowers, default probabilities 0.010, 0.018, 0.026, 0.033, 0.040 and raw correlations 0.12, 0.30, 0.08, 0.25, 0.15 that oscillate. The repaired correlations are 0.120000, 0.291198, 0.269229, 0.254583 and 0.242514, and the repaired no-default probabilities 0.498412, 0.498412, 0.382275, 0.305172, 0.244556 never increase. The cut at horizon 2 only trims 0.30 to 0.291198, but it then forces horizon 3 up from 0.08 to 0.269229, and every later horizon inherits that choice. The paper notes that a joint calibration across the whole grid would optimize these choices together; the sequential projection is greedy.

In short: clip each correlation into the interval allowed by the previous repaired one (Eq. 18); this keeps all default probabilities and is the closest feasible choice step by step (Proposition 5.5); in the 100-loan example the raw correlation 0.40 is cut to 0.153059, which restores all 100 tail inequalities, and the original violation was worth about $243,375 on a $1 million layer.

8 · SMOOTH HORIZON CURVES

What if default probabilities and correlations are given as smooth functions of time?

Term structures are often specified as curves rather than at a few dates. Section 6 of the paper turns the two-event test into a pair of differential inequalities: they limit how fast the correlation may move, given how fast the default probability rises.

Let μ(t) and σ(t) > 0 be continuously differentiable on a compact interval, with σ bounded away from zero, Qt = Φ(μ(t) + σ(t)Z) and Kt | Qt ∼ Bin(n, Qt). Define

Eq. 19

Here mk is the average of the factor Z under a reweighting that favors the economies in which exactly the k-th default is about to happen.

Proposition 6.1 · differential two-event test

All tails P(Kt ≥ k) are nondecreasing in t if and only if, at every t,

Eq. 20

Moreover m1(t) < ⋯ < mn(t) for n ≥ 2.

proofWhy do only the first and last tails matter in the smooth case too?

Differentiating under the integral, which Gaussian integrability justifies, and using the binomial tail derivative from Section 4,

Eq. 21

The chain rule gives dQt/dt = φ(μ + σZ)(μ̇ + σ̇Z), which is where both Jk and mk come from. Going from k to k + 1 multiplies the reweighting density by Qt/(1 − Qt), an increasing function of Z, and tilting toward larger Z raises the mean of Z: for an increasing tilt h, the change in mean is Cov(Z, h(Z))/E h(Z) > 0. So mk strictly increases in k. An affine function of mk is nonnegative at every k exactly when it is nonnegative at the two ends.

∎

In credit language, with c(t) = Φ−1(p(t)) and Eq. 14, the pair becomes

Eq. 22

A correlation that does not move, ρ̇ = 0, leaves only ċ ≥ 0, which is the familiar requirement that default probabilities never fall. Any movement in ρ must be paid for by enough growth in c.

In short: for smooth curves, each tail's rate of change is a positive factor times μ̇ + σ̇ mk (Eq. 21); the tilted factor means mk increase with k, so the first and last conditions imply all the rest (Eq. 20); in credit terms, the speed of a correlation change is limited by the speed of the default curve (Eq. 22).

9 · LARGE POOLS AND THE √(LOG n) LAW

How fast does the freedom to change correlation disappear as the pool grows?

The intervals shrink with n, and Section 7 of the paper answers two questions: what survives at every size, and how fast the endpoints approach ρ0. The first answer uses no Gaussian computation at all.

Proposition 7.1 · compatibility at every size

Let Q0, Q1 have fixed laws on [0, 1] and Ka,n | Qa ∼ Bin(n, Qa). Then K0,n ≤st K1,n for every positive integer n if and only if Q0 ≤st Q1.

proofWhy does the mixing variable itself have to be ordered?

If Q0 ≤st Q1, couple them through common quantiles so Q0 ≤ Q1, and generate both sets of defaults from the same uniforms Ui as 1{Ui ≤ Qa}; the counts are ordered for every n. Conversely, Ka,n/n converges in distribution to Qa, since E[(Ka,n/n − Qa)2] ≤ 1/(4n), and stochastic order survives weak limits. This is the law of large numbers inside each economy: in a huge pool the fraction defaulted is the conditional default probability.

∎

Corollary 7.2 · Gaussian rigidity

For 0 < p0, p1 < 1 and 0 < ρ0, ρ1 < 1, the Gaussian horizon laws are absorbing-compatible at every pool size if and only if ρ1 = ρ0 and p1 ≥ p0.

The reason is Eq. 11: if the scales differ, the affine function of Φ−1(q) takes both signs because Φ−1(q) ranges over all of ℝ, so the mixing variables cross and cannot be ordered. Any change of latent correlation, however small, is therefore incompatible for some finite pool size. The paper describes this as an all-size form of the rigidity Andersen (2006) found in term-structure analysis.

The rate needs one prerequisite from extreme-value theory: the largest of n independent standard normals is close to √(2 log n). A rough reason, ours: P(ε > x) is about e−x²/2, and n times that is of order one when x2/2 ≈ log n. The paper uses sharper tail bounds of exactly this kind.

Uniformly for p and ρ in compact subsets of (0, 1), as n → ∞,

Eq. 23

Everybody defaults when every private shock is below the common hurdle. With Mn = maxi εi and μ, σ from Eq. 14, conditional independence gives

Eq. 24

Turning the expansion around answers a practical question: how large can the pool be before a given correlation change δ becomes impossible?

Corollary 7.5 · the critical pool size

Let N*(δ) be the largest pool size at which (p0, ρ0) and (p1, ρ0 + δ) are compatible. Then N*(δ) is finite for δ ≠ 0 and

Eq. 31

In words: log N*(δ) ∼ C2/δ2, so the critical size grows exponentially in 1/δ2.

proofWhy does nesting turn the boundary rate into a size rate?

Size one is compatible, Proposition 5.4 makes the compatible sizes an initial segment, and Corollary 7.2 makes it finite. Every fixed size is compatible for small enough |δ|, so N*(δ) → ∞. For 0 < η < C, the relevant radius, un − ρ0 or ρ0 − ℓn, is asymptotic to C/√(log n). At sizes near exp[(C − η)2/δ2] and exp[(C + η)2/δ2] the radius is respectively larger and smaller than |δ|, so nesting traps N*(δ) between them. Multiply the logarithms by δ2, let δ → 0, then η → 0.

∎

Because of the slow convergence, the limit can be far from the truth at realistic sizes, and the paper says the exact equations stay relevant for finite pools. To see how far, we computed N* exactly for the paper's pool with the code behind the animations (these numbers are ours). The leading-order law predicts N* ≈ exp(C2/δ2) ≈ 93 000 for δ = ±0.01. The exact answer is about 4 100 for δ = −0.01 and about 5 × 1011 for δ = +0.01. Lowering correlation is caught by the rare all-default event in a pool of a few thousand; raising it is caught by the no-default event only in absurdly large pools.

The last result gives a non-Gaussian, quantitative version of the all-size failure, using Hoeffding's inequality, which bounds the chance that an average of n independent coin flips misses its mean by ε by e−2nε².

Proposition 7.6 · a finite-size certificate

Suppose z ∈ (0, 1), 0 < ε < min(z, 1 − z) and δ = P(Q0 ≥ z + ε) − P(Q1 ≥ z − ε) > 0. Then

Eq. 32

In particular, compatibility fails whenever n > log(2/δ)/(2ε2).

proofHow does concentration certify a broken tail?

Given Q0 ≥ z + ε, the fraction K0,n/n falls below z with probability at most e−2nε², so P(K0,n/n ≥ z) ≥ P(Q0 ≥ z + ε) − e−2nε². Splitting on Q1 ≥ z − ε and using the opposite tail bound gives P(K1,n/n ≥ z) ≤ P(Q1 ≥ z − ε) + e−2nε². Subtract. The threshold count is ⌈nz⌉.

∎

In short: compatibility at every size requires the mixing variables themselves to be ordered (Proposition 7.1), which in the Gaussian model forces a constant correlation (Corollary 7.2); the all-default probability behaves like a power of n set by ρ (Eq. 23), so the interval endpoints approach ρ0 as ρ0 ± C/√(log n) with C = 0.033826 for the paper's pool (Eqs. 27 and 28); the critical size obeys log N* ∼ C2/δ2 (Eq. 31) but convergence is extremely slow; Hoeffding gives an explicit failing size for any mixing law (Eq. 32).

RESULTS

The paper's numbers

All experiments use constructed parameters with a correlation cap of 0.99, and the computations are deterministic (Section 8). The numerical checks: at p = ρ = 1/2 and at n = 2, p = 1/2, nine evaluations of the closed forms have maximum absolute error 1.8 × 10−15; thirty parameter pairs at n = 8, 25 and 60 agree between the two-event test and an independent integration of every tail; tightening tolerances changes log-orthant values by at most 2.8 × 10−14 and boundaries by at most 1.7 × 10−16.

In every row the upper endpoint sits farther from ρ0 than the lower one, and going from 50 to 500 borrowers cuts the width by a factor between about 1.6 and 2.9. ASSESSMENT

What is shown, and what is claimed

Proved in the paper. The equivalence of absorbing compatibility and stochastic order with an explicit coupling (Proposition 3.2); the two-event criterion under single crossing (Theorem 4.1) and its location-scale corollary; the exact Gaussian interval (Theorem 5.2), nesting (Proposition 5.4), the repair property (Proposition 5.5), the differential test (Proposition 6.1), all-size rigidity (Corollary 7.2), the boundary expansion (Theorem 7.4), the critical-size law (Corollary 7.5) and the Hoeffding certificate (Proposition 7.6). The proofs are short and, in the parts we checked step by step, complete. Lemma 5.1 rests on Plackett's identity, which is cited rather than reproved, and Lemma 7.3's tail bounds are stated with constants left implicit.

Shown numerically. The interval values, the 100-loan example, the n = 7 threshold and the five-horizon repair are deterministic computations on constructed parameters, with independent full-tail checks. Our own implementation, written from Eqs. 33 to 35 and Theorem 5.2, reproduces them, which is a useful independent confirmation of the numerics.

Claimed or suggested, not tested. The paper proposes the interval test as a step in a multi-horizon credit pipeline and sketches an empirical application with real default histories, censoring and estimation uncertainty. No real data are used, and whether fitted correlation term structures actually violate the intervals in practice is not examined.

Scope. Borrowers are exchangeable with equal exposures; the paper notes that heterogeneous borrowers and unequal losses need multivariate and loss-distribution conditions it does not supply. All horizons share one information set, so the results say nothing about forecasts updated over time. The Gaussian model fixes a particular tail dependence; the single-crossing theorem applies to other one-factor families only when the same factor and link are used at both horizons. The sequential repair is greedy, and the paper itself points out that a joint calibration across the grid would choose differently.

Our observations. The asymmetry between δ = −0.01 and δ = +0.01 in critical size, about 4 100 against about 5 × 1011, is our computation, as is the toy pool. The asymmetry suggests that in realistic pools it is decreases in correlation, policed by the all-default event, that the test will catch; the paper's Table 3 shows the same pattern at n = 50 and 500.

FURTHER READING

Further reading

M. Palaisti, Portfolio-size constraints on default correlation: exact coherence tests and sharp asymptotic bounds, arXiv:2611.18759 (2026). The paper itself; equation, theorem and table numbers in this chapter follow its HTML version.

The paper's own references are the natural next steps, though we did not open them for this chapter: O. A. Vasicek, "Loan portfolio value" (Risk, 2002), for the large-pool limit of the one-factor model; D. X. Li, "On default correlation: a copula function approach" (Journal of Fixed Income, 2000), for the Gaussian copula; L. Andersen, "Portfolio losses in factor models" (Journal of Credit Risk, 2006), for the term-structure rigidity; and M. Shaked and J. G. Shanthikumar, Stochastic Orders (Springer, 2007), for stochastic order and couplings.

Built from a full read of arXiv 2611.18759v1. Equation, theorem, section and table numbers match the paper. All three animations run real computations: the quantile coupling of Proposition 3.2 on the toy pool, with a 20 000-draw simulation; bisection on the log orthant probabilities of Eqs. 33 to 35 for the interval of Theorem 5.2; and full count distributions for the 100-loan example of Section 8.3, with the repair of Eq. 18. The toy pool and all its numbers, the derivations marked as ours, the default-correlation values, the small-n intervals, the n = 7 check and the exact critical sizes are ours.

QEDist: Practical Exact Distance Certification for Stabilizer Codes

Jong Yeon Lee · posted Nov 16, 2026 · quant-ph · arXiv 2611.21709

Overview

A quantum error-correcting code is only as strong as its lightest undetectable error, and for many of the codes now proposed for real hardware nobody had proved how light that error can be; this paper proves it, exactly, for 88 of 95 surveyed codes, often in seconds on a laptop. The number in question is the distance d. Finding one bad error shows that d is at most its weight, but showing that d is at least some value means ruling out every lighter error, and the number of candidates is astronomically large. QEDist (Quantum Exact Distance) rules them out with a depth-first tree search that grows an error one qubit at a time, guided by the parity checks it violates, and cuts branches with four exact tests: a symmetry reduction, a parity shortcut, a lower bound on how many more qubits any completion still needs, and a rule that throws out partial errors that a stabilizer could shorten. The chapter builds each piece by hand on two small codes and then watches the whole search run on a 50-qubit code.

By the end you'll be able to explain
  • what a parity-check matrix is, how binary arithmetic describes errors, and what the distance of a code means;
  • how a CSS quantum code splits into two binary problems, and why its distance is the minimum in Eq. 1 rather than the classical minimum weight;
  • why an upper bound on distance is one example but a lower bound is a proof about every support up to a cutoff W;
  • how the tree search grows supports through unsatisfied checks, why ordered children with forbidden sets cover every completion exactly once, and how symmetry cuts the starting points (Eq. 3);
  • the parity shortcut, the syndrome-count bound and the disjoint-neighborhood bound (Eq. 4), and how satisfied checks sharpen them into the weighted-check bound (Eqs. 8 to 10);
  • why a partial support that covers more than half of a stabilizer can be discarded (Eq. 5), and why all the rules together never discard a shortest logical (Theorem 1);
  • how lifted-product structure shrinks the search (Eqs. 6 and 7), and what the benchmarks do and do not show.
notationSymbols used throughout
𝔽₂
the two-element field {0, 1} with addition mod 2, so 1 + 1 = 0
n, k
the number of physical qubits and the number of encoded (logical) qubits
HX, HZ
binary check matrices with n columns; their rows are the X-type and Z-type stabilizer generators
H, S
in the Z sector, H = HX (the checks that see Z errors) and S = row HZ (the Z-type stabilizers)
z, supp, wt
a binary vector of length n, its support (the positions holding 1), and its weight |supp z|
ker H
the vectors z with Hz = 0: the undetectable supports
dX, dZ, d
the two sector distances and the code distance d = min(dX, dZ)
L
a logical detector matrix (Eq. 2)
W, Weff
the weight cutoff of an exclusion, and the cutoff after the parity shortcut
T, F
the support selected at a search node, and the forbidden coordinates
s
the syndrome H1T of the selected support; check c is unsatisfied when sc = 1
Nc(T, F)
the available neighborhood of check c (Eq. 3)
b
the remaining budget Weff − |T|
wc, p
the largest column weight of H, and the size of a packing of disjoint neighborhoods
xv, β, cv, D
the 0/1 indicator that qubit v is added, and the constant, coefficients and coefficient cap of a combined inequality (Eq. 10)
g
a stabilizer, used in the shortening rule (Eq. 5)
P
the period of a verified cyclic symmetry
Running examples
  • Code A: the Steane code, 7 qubits. Its checks fit in a 7 × 7 matrix, every set of codewords can be listed by hand, and its distance is 3. We use it to make every definition concrete and to run the search by hand. The specific cyclic presentation below is our choice.
  • Code B: the toric code on a 5 × 5 torus, 50 qubits. Qubits sit on the edges of a square grid whose opposite sides are glued together, and an error is a set of edges you can draw. Its distance is 5. The animation in Section 7 runs the paper's search on it. Neither code appears in the paper; both are standard textbook examples chosen because the paper's rules can be checked on them by eye.
1 · PARITY CHECKS AND DISTANCE

What does it mean for a code to have distance d?

Everything in this paper is linear algebra over the two-element field 𝔽₂, so it is worth starting with a classical code, where the ideas are the same and nothing is quantum yet. A message is stored redundantly as a string of n bits, and noise flips some of them. Record which bits were flipped as a vector z in 𝔽₂n, with a 1 in each flipped position. Adding vectors mod 2 composes flips: flipping a bit twice undoes it, which is the rule 1 + 1 = 0.

A parity check is a question of the form "is the number of flipped bits among these positions odd?". Write the positions as a row of a binary matrix H; then the answers to all checks at once are the vector Hz, computed mod 2. That vector is called the syndrome. An error with syndrome zero passes every check and is undetectable.

Definition · syndrome, weight, distance (background, not from the paper)

For a binary matrix H with n columns, the syndrome of z ∈ 𝔽₂n is Hz, and z is undetectable when Hz = 0, that is, when z lies in the kernel ker H. The support of z is the set of positions where z has a 1, and its weight wt(z) is the size of the support. The distance of the classical code ker H is

In words: the distance is the smallest number of bit flips that every check fails to notice. Any error of smaller weight changes at least one parity and is caught.

The matrix for Code A is a circulant: each row is the previous row shifted one place to the right, wrapping around. Label the positions 0 to 6. Row i checks positions i, i + 2, i + 3 and i + 4, counted mod 7, so

Only three rows are independent (rank 3), because the cyclic shifts repeat information; seven redundant rows are allowed and keep the symmetry visible. Its kernel is the [7, 4] Hamming code: 24 = 16 vectors, namely the zero vector, seven of weight 3, seven of weight 4, and the all-ones vector of weight 7. One of the weight-3 vectors has support {0, 2, 6}. Check row 0, whose support is {0, 2, 3, 4}: it overlaps {0, 2, 6} in two positions, an even number, so it is satisfied, and the same happens for every row. The classical distance is 3.

our checkHow do we know no vector of weight 1 or 2 is in the kernel?

A weight-1 vector with support {j} has syndrome equal to column j of H. Every column has four 1s (each position is checked by four rows), so no column is zero. A weight-2 vector with support {i, j} has syndrome column i + column j, which is zero only if the two columns are equal. Column j of a circulant is column 0 shifted down by j places, and column 0 is (1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0)T, which equals none of its nontrivial cyclic shifts. So all seven columns are distinct and nonzero, and the smallest kernel vectors have weight 3.

∎

In short: errors are binary vectors, checks are rows of H, the syndrome is Hz mod 2, and the classical distance is the smallest weight of a nonzero vector in ker H; for Code A it is 3.

2 · CSS CODES AND THE QUANTUM DISTANCE

What changes when the errors are quantum?

A qubit can suffer two independent kinds of error: a bit flip X and a phase flip Z (their product is the third Pauli error, Y). An X error on a set of qubits is described by a binary support vector, and so is a Z error. The fact that makes quantum codes look like pairs of classical codes is a commutation rule from quantum mechanics: an X-type operator with support a and a Z-type operator with support b commute exactly when a and b overlap in an even number of qubits, and anticommute when the overlap is odd. Measuring an X-type operator therefore detects a Z error precisely when the overlap is odd, which is a parity check.

Definition · CSS code and its Z sector (Section 2.1)

Let HX and HZ be binary matrices with n columns satisfying HXHZT = 0. Their rows generate the X- and Z-type stabilizers, and the code has k = n − rank HX − rank HZ > 0 encoded qubits. For the Z sector put H = HX and S = row HZ. A binary support vector z represents an undetectable operator when Hz = 0, and a nontrivial logical operator when also z ∉ S. Thus

Eq. 1

Interchanging X and Z gives dX, and the code distance is d = min(dX, dZ).

In words: the X-type checks catch Z errors; an undetectable Z error either is itself a stabilizer, which does nothing to the encoded information, or it is a logical operator, which silently corrupts it. The Z distance is the weight of the lightest corrupting one.

The condition HXHZT = 0 says every X-type generator overlaps every Z-type generator evenly, so all generators commute and can be measured together. It also means every row of HZ passes every check in HX, so S sits inside ker H. That is the one difference from Section 1: the minimum in Eq. 1 skips the nonzero vectors of S as well as zero. Stabilizers are undetectable but harmless, because the encoded state is defined to be unchanged by them. The paper puts it as: up to an overall phase, an undetectable Pauli acts trivially on the encoded information exactly when it belongs to the stabilizer group.

Code A becomes the Steane code by taking HX = HZ = H. Any two rows of H overlap in exactly two positions and each row has weight 4, so H HT = 0 and the code is valid, with k = 7 − 3 − 3 = 1. In the Z sector, ker H is the 16-vector Hamming code and S is the 8-vector row space: zero and seven vectors of weight 4. The vectors in ker H but not in S are the seven of weight 3 and the all-ones vector, so dZ = 3. The X sector is identical, so d = 3.

our checkWhy are the weight-4 kernel vectors exactly the stabilizers?

The row space of H has dimension 3, so it has 23 = 8 vectors. Each row has weight 4, and the sum of two rows has weight 4 + 4 − 2 · 2 = 4 because any two rows overlap in two positions. The sum of two rows is again a row (for instance rows 0 and 1 add to row 5, as the matrix above shows, and every other pair follows by shifting), so the zero vector and the seven rows are closed under addition and form the whole row space. All have weight 4, and ker H has exactly seven vectors of weight 4, so they coincide.

∎

Testing z ∉ S can be done by Gaussian elimination over 𝔽₂. The paper also describes a faster equivalent test. A logical detector matrix L has rows that represent a complete logical basis of the opposite sector, chosen so that the rows of L together with those of H span S⊥, the set of vectors orthogonal to all of S. Then

Eq. 2

so a zero-syndrome candidate is logically nontrivial exactly when Lz ≠ 0. In Code A, a single row works: L = (1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1). Then Lz is the parity of wt(z), and indeed the stabilizers all have even weight while the logicals have weight 3 or 7.

our sketchWhy does Eq. 2 hold?

Over 𝔽₂, as over the reals, a subspace equals the orthogonal complement of its orthogonal complement: S = (S⊥)⊥. The rows of H and L span S⊥, so z ∈ S exactly when z is orthogonal to every row of H and of L, which is the statement Hz = 0 and Lz = 0. In Code A, S⊥ is the Hamming code of dimension 4, spanned by the three independent rows of H plus the all-ones vector, which is the L chosen above.

∎

Code B lives on a torus. Draw a 5 × 5 grid of vertices and glue the right edge to the left and the bottom to the top, so the grid has 25 vertices, 25 horizontal edges, 25 vertical edges and 25 square faces. Put a qubit on each of the 50 edges. Each vertex gives an X-type check on its four edges (a "star"), and each face gives a Z-type stabilizer on its four edges (a "plaquette"). A star and a plaquette share either zero or two edges, so the CSS condition holds. Each family has rank 24 (the 25 stars add to zero, since every edge has two endpoints, and likewise the 25 plaquettes), giving k = 50 − 24 − 24 = 2.

In the Z sector a support z is a set of edges, and the star at a vertex is unsatisfied exactly when an odd number of chosen edges meet there. For a path of edges, the unsatisfied checks are its two endpoints. Undetectable supports are therefore sets of closed loops. A loop that bounds a region is a sum of the plaquettes inside it, hence a stabilizer; a loop that wraps around the torus is not, and is a logical operator. The shortest wrapping loop is a straight line of 5 edges, so dZ = 5, and by the symmetry between the grid and its dual dX = 5 too.

Background · the toric code (not from the paper)

The toric code is due to Kitaev (see Further reading). That every contractible loop is a sum of plaquettes, while a loop around the torus is not, is a standard topological fact about the torus that we use without proof; the 5 × 5 size and the edge numbering in the animation are ours.

In short: a CSS code is two binary check matrices whose rows overlap evenly; the Z distance is the smallest weight of a vector that passes every X check but is not a Z stabilizer (Eq. 1); Code A has d = 3 and Code B, whose errors are edge sets with syndromes at their endpoints, has d = 5.

3 · THE CERTIFICATION PROBLEM

Why is a lower bound so much harder than an upper bound?

To prove dZ ≤ w, it is enough to exhibit one vector of weight w that passes all checks and is not a stabilizer; anyone can verify it with one matrix product and one membership test. The paper calls such a vector a witness. To prove dZ ≥ W + 1, one must show that no nontrivial logical operator of weight at most W exists. That is a statement about every support of weight up to W.

Definition · exclusion and certification (Section 2.1)

Choose a cutoff W. A completed exclusion shows that no nontrivial logical operator of weight at most W exists, and so establishes dZ ≥ W + 1. Together with a checked logical operator of weight W + 1, it establishes dZ = W + 1. Both sectors must reach the required lower bound to certify the code distance, and a witness in either sector supplies an upper bound.

In words: an exact distance needs a witness from above and an exhaustive proof from below, and the two must meet.

The scale is what makes the proof hard. One benchmark code in the paper has n = 1768 qubits and Z distance 22, so its certificate is an exclusion through weight 21. The number of supports of weight exactly 21 among 1768 positions is C(1768, 21), about 2.7 × 1048 (our arithmetic). No computer will list them. For comparison, QEDist's search on this exclusion visits 23.6 million nodes (Section 4.2).

The codes in question are quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, whose checks each touch only a handful of qubits. For hypergraph-product codes the distance follows from smaller classical codes, but for lifted-product (LP) codes, a more flexible family that can reach larger distances, it does not, and published distances were often only upper bounds from randomized searches for witnesses. A reported upper bound leaves open the possibility of a substantially lighter logical operator, which, as the introduction notes, could change which finite-length code one chooses.

The sectors can also behave differently. For the [[1428, 186]] code, the paper finds dX = 18 and 19 ≤ dZ ≤ 28, which already gives d = 18 without pinning down dZ. For asymmetric codes, knowing both sector distances says more than d alone.

Fact · the survey (Table 1)

Of 95 tabulated lifted-product instances with d > 5, drawn from fifteen source families, QEDist verifies the exact distance of 88 and leaves 7 unresolved, all 7 from one "logical spectroscopy" study. Of the 88, 64 match upper bounds reported in the cited sources.

In short: a witness proves d ≤ w in one line, while d ≥ W + 1 needs a proof about every support up to weight W, a number like 1048 for real codes; QEDist supplies that proof by exhaustive but heavily pruned search.

4 · GROWING A SUPPORT THROUGH THE CHECKS

How can a search avoid looking at every subset?

The key is that sparse checks constrain how a candidate can grow. If a partial support T leaves some check unsatisfied, any undetectable support containing T must include another qubit of that check, so the search only ever needs to add qubits from unsatisfied checks. The paper describes this search in Section 3; the support-growth principle goes back to linked-cluster methods of Dumer, Kovalev and Pryadko, and QEDist's contribution is the bookkeeping and pruning built on top.

Definition · satisfied checks and irreducible supports (Section 3.1)

A check is unsatisfied if it overlaps the selected support in an odd number of qubits and satisfied if the overlap is even. A nonempty undetectable support is support-irreducible if it contains no smaller nonempty undetectable support.

In words: an unsatisfied check is one that currently fires, and an irreducible support is an undetectable error with no undetectable piece you could cut out of it.

Every shortest logical operator is support-irreducible. That is why the search can stop as soon as the syndrome becomes zero: any extension would contain the current undetectable support and hence could not be a shortest logical.

proofWhy must a shortest logical be irreducible?

This is the first step of the paper's proof of Theorem 1 (Appendix A). Let z be a minimum-weight logical with support U, and suppose a nonzero y ∈ ker H were supported on a proper subset of U. If y ∉ S, then y is itself a logical and is lighter than z. If y ∈ S, then z + y is in the same logical class as z, and since y sits inside U, adding it simply deletes the positions of y from U, so z + y is a lighter logical. Either way z was not of minimum weight.

∎

A search node records the selected support T, its syndrome s = H1T, and a set F of forbidden coordinates that this branch has promised never to use. For each check c, its available neighborhood is

Eq. 3

that is, the qubits of check c that are neither selected nor forbidden. If s ≠ 0, the search picks an unsatisfied check c; every completion must include an element of Nc. Order its available neighbors q1, …, qm. Child i includes qi and forbids q1, …, qi−1. To keep the number of children small, the check chosen is one with the fewest available neighbors. When s = 0, the search tests membership in S and ends the branch.

proofWhy does forbidding earlier siblings lose nothing and repeat nothing?

A completion of T is a set of extra qubits, disjoint from F, that makes the syndrome zero. It must contain at least one of q1, …, qm, so it has a first one in this order, say qi. It contains qi and none of q1, …, qi−1, which is exactly what child i requires, and it violates the requirement of every other child: child j < i requires qj, which it lacks, and child j > i forbids qi, which it has. The paper states this as: each possible completion is assigned to exactly one child, determined by its first neighbor in this order.

∎

Where does the search start? Every support contains some qubit, so in general it starts once from each of the n qubits, with all earlier qubits forbidden. Symmetry cuts this down. If a permutation of the qubits maps the check row spaces to themselves, it maps logicals to logicals of the same weight. For a cyclic translation of period P acting on blocks of P qubits, the paper shows it suffices to start once at position 0 of each block, excluding all earlier blocks, which reduces the starting coordinates from n to n/P. QEDist verifies the symmetry on the supplied matrices before using it.

proofWhy is one start per block enough?

Take any nonempty support and look at its first occupied block a. Translate the whole support until one of its qubits in block a sits at position 0. Translation moves all blocks together, so blocks before a stay empty. The translated support has the same weight and the same logical status, and it is compatible with the start at (a, 0) with all earlier blocks forbidden. The rule covers every orbit, including orbits shorter than P, and may cover an orbit more than once, which is harmless.

∎

In Code A, cyclic shift by one position is a symmetry: shifting maps row i of H to row i + 1. The seven positions form a single block with P = 7, so one start at qubit 0 suffices instead of seven. In Code B, horizontal and vertical translations of the torus are both symmetries, and the paper's rule for several generators (start at the smallest coordinate of each joint orbit and exclude earlier coordinates) leaves two starts: one horizontal edge with nothing forbidden, and one vertical edge with every horizontal edge forbidden. The paper reports the same count, two starting points, for the bivariate bicycle codes, which have the same two-translation structure.

Here is the whole search on Code A at cutoff W = 3, by hand. Start with T = {0}. Qubit 0 lies in rows 0, 3, 4 and 5, so those four checks fire. Each has three available neighbors, so take the lowest, row 0, with N = {2, 3, 4}. The children are T = {0, 2}; T = {0, 3} with 2 forbidden; and T = {0, 4} with 2 and 3 forbidden. In the first child, the syndrome is the sum of columns 0 and 2, which fires rows 2, 3, 4 and 6. Row 2 has N = {4, 5, 6}, giving children {0, 2, 4}, {0, 2, 5} and {0, 2, 6}. The first two still fire checks and have used the whole budget. The third has syndrome zero, weight 3, and is not one of the weight-4 stabilizers: a witness, found at the fifth node. At W = 2 the same tree stops one level higher: each child {0, q} has used the budget with checks still firing, so the search finishes after four nodes with no witness and proves dZ ≥ 3. Together with the witness, dZ = 3.

In short: the search adds only qubits of a firing check, gives each child a forbidden set so every completion lives in exactly one subtree, stops at zero syndrome because shortest logicals are irreducible, and uses verified symmetries to start from n/P coordinates instead of n.

5 · BOUNDING THE WEIGHT STILL NEEDED

When can a branch be abandoned before it runs out of budget?

The search above only stops a branch when it has used the whole weight allowance. Far better is to notice early that the firing checks cannot all be fixed within the remaining allowance. Section 3.2 gives three such tests; each one is a short counting argument.

The first applies before the search starts. If the all-ones vector lies in row H, every undetectable operator has even weight, so an odd cutoff W can be replaced by W − 1. Write Weff = W − 1 in that case and Weff = W otherwise. A list of check rows summing to the all-ones vector certifies the reduction.

proofWhy does the all-ones vector force even weight?

Appendix A writes the certificate as a binary vector α with αTH = 1T, meaning the rows selected by α add up to all ones. For z ∈ ker H, wt(z) ≡ 1Tz = αTHz = αT0 = 0 (mod 2). So no undetectable support has odd weight, and in particular no logical of weight exactly W when W is odd.

∎

Neither running example qualifies. Code A has logicals of weight 3. In Code B, rows summing to all ones would be a set of vertices containing exactly one endpoint of every edge, a two-coloring of the grid, and a 5 × 5 torus has odd loops of length 5, so none exists. On a 4 × 4 torus, by contrast, a checkerboard coloring works and every closed loop has even length (our example).

The second test counts. Let b = Weff − |T| be the number of further qubits permitted, and wc the largest column weight of H, the most checks any one qubit touches. If wt(s) > b wc, the remaining b qubits cannot touch every unsatisfied check, so the branch is pruned. An unsatisfied check with no available neighbor rules out completion immediately.

The third test looks at where the firing checks are. If p unsatisfied checks have pairwise disjoint available neighborhoods, each needs its own new qubit, so

Eq. 4

Such a collection is called a packing, and any packing gives a valid bound. QEDist builds one greedily, considering smaller neighborhoods first (Appendix A.1). In Code B the bound is vivid. A path of edges fires its two endpoints, and unless the endpoints are next to each other their stars share no edge, so the packing has size 2 and the path needs at least two more edges to close. With one edge of budget left it is pruned at once. When the endpoints are adjacent, their stars share the single edge between them, the packing drops to 1, and one edge can indeed close the loop.

our checkWhy is the syndrome-count bound weaker than the packing bound here?

In Code B each edge touches two stars, so wc = 2, and an open path fires two stars. The count test prunes only when 2 > 2b, that is, when b = 0, which the budget test already catches. The packing test prunes when 2 > b, that is, at b = 1, one level earlier. The count test knows only how many checks fire; the packing test also knows that no single edge can reach both endpoints.

∎

In short: parity can lower an odd cutoff by one, the number of firing checks over the column weight bounds the qubits still needed, and a packing of firing checks with disjoint neighborhoods gives a sharper bound (Eq. 4); a branch whose bound exceeds its budget b is cut.

6 · THE WEIGHTED-CHECK BOUND

Why should a check that is already satisfied matter?

The bounds of Section 5 look only at checks that fire. But adding a qubit to satisfy one check can violate another and force further additions. Section 3.3 gives the paper's own small example, which the animation below works through. Unsatisfied checks c1 and c2 have available neighborhoods {a, b} and {a, c}, and a satisfied check e has neighborhood {a, d}. The first two share a, so their disjoint-neighborhood bound is one. Adding a satisfies both but violates e, forcing the addition of d. Avoiding a requires both b and c. In either case, at least two additions are needed.

To turn that reasoning into arithmetic, let xv ∈ {0, 1} indicate whether available qubit v is added. Every completion satisfies two families of inequalities (Appendix A.2):

Eq. 8

Eq. 9

The first says a firing check needs at least one new qubit. The second says that if v is added to a satisfied check e, some other qubit of e must also be added to restore even parity. These replace the exact parity conditions with weaker linear inequalities, which the paper calls a parity relaxation.

Definition · the weighted-check bound (Eq. 10)

Add the inequalities of Eqs. 8 and 9 with nonnegative integer multipliers. The result has the form β ≤ Σv cvxv, where β is the sum of the multipliers on unsatisfied checks and the coefficients cv may have either sign. For any D ≥ 0 such that every cv ≤ D, a completion within budget b must satisfy

Eq. 10

Thus β > Db excludes the node.

In words: weight the firing checks, use satisfied checks to cancel any qubit that would count too many times, and if the total demand still exceeds what b qubits of capped value can supply, no completion fits.

proofWhy is each step of Eq. 10 valid?

A completion within budget gives a 0/1 vector x that satisfies every inequality of Eqs. 8 and 9; multiplying by nonnegative numbers and adding preserves ≥, so β ≤ Σ cvxv. Each xv is 0 or 1, so cvxv ≤ D xv whether cv is positive or negative. Finally Σ xv is the number of added qubits, at most b. The argument uses only that x describes some zero-syndrome completion, so, as the paper notes, it applies to every kernel completion, including stabilizers, and never removes a shortest logical.

∎

On the example, the multipliers 1 on c1, 1 on c2 and 1 on the inequality of e with v = a give

The inequality from e reduces the coefficient of xa from two to one and introduces xd, so each possible addition contributes at most one: D = 1 and β = 2. With one addition left, 2 > 1 · 1 and the node is cut. Without e, the coefficient of xa is 2, so D = 2 and the test 2 > 2 · 1 fails. The implementation keeps every coefficient at most two, so a combined requirement above 2b rules out completion. It raises multipliers greedily with bounded effort, because the bound is evaluated at many nodes; the effort limits choose which valid inequality is found, while Eq. 10 guarantees safety.

The same inequality can test a single proposed child. Conditioning on adding coordinate q gives β − cq ≤ D(b − 1), so a violation rules out that child without building it.

The animation computes all of this for the example: the exact minimum by checking all sixteen subsets of {a, b, c, d}, the greedy packing, and both combined inequalities.

Animation · the weighted-check bound on the paper's Fig. 3(c) example
unsatisfied checksatisfied checkchosen qubits
Fact · what satisfied checks buy (Section 4.2)

Across fourteen LP and PP sector problems, a bound using only unsatisfied checks speeds up the higher-check-weight examples but slows several others. Adding satisfied-check inequalities reduces median search time by factors of 1.37 to 5.28 relative to that bound, and with both types every one of the fourteen exclusions finishes faster than with the bound disabled. The 1112-qubit PP input takes 10.6 seconds with the bound disabled, 11.4 seconds with only unsatisfied checks, and 5.14 seconds with both.

In short: firing checks demand qubits (Eq. 8), satisfied checks charge for disturbing them (Eq. 9), and a nonnegative combination with demand β and coefficient cap D proves no completion fits in b qubits whenever β > Db (Eq. 10).

7 · USING STABILIZER EQUIVALENCE

Can a partial support already be provably too heavy?

The bounds so far apply to any undetectable completion. The last rule uses the quantum structure: multiplying a logical operator by a stabilizer preserves its encoded action and can reduce its weight. If the partial support T already covers more than half of some stabilizer, then any logical containing T can be made lighter by multiplying by that stabilizer, so the branch cannot contain a shortest logical.

Definition · the shortening rule (Section 3.4)

For every g ∈ S, a minimum-weight logical z satisfies

Eq. 5

since otherwise z + g is a lighter representative of the same nonzero logical class. Because the selected support only grows, a violation by T persists throughout its subtree, and the branch is pruned.

In words: a shortest logical never covers more than half of any stabilizer, because swapping the covered half for the uncovered half would shorten it.

our derivationWhere does "more than half" come from?

Adding two binary vectors cancels their common positions, so

This is less than wt(z) exactly when the overlap exceeds wt(g)/2. And z + g passes every check, since both terms do, and is not in S, since otherwise z = (z + g) + g would be in S. So z + g is a lighter logical, contradicting minimality. If T ⊆ supp(z) already overlaps g in more than wt(g)/2 positions, so does z.

∎

In Code A, stabilizer row 0 has support {0, 2, 3, 4}. The node T = {0, 2, 4} from the hand search overlaps it in three positions, more than 4/2, so any logical through that node would be shortened by row 0, and the rule discards it at once. In Code B every plaquette has weight 4, so a path that runs along three sides of a face is discarded: going around the fourth side instead is shorter. The rule is cheap because QEDist updates the overlaps with the supplied generators as each qubit is added or removed. It also has a limit the paper points out: the [[2970, 1188]] code's supplied generators have weight 22 or 23, so a partial support of weight at most 11 can never trip it, and the weighted-check bound must do the work.

With every rule in place, the animation below runs the search on Code B, exactly as the paper's pseudocode in Appendix A.1 orders the tests: the shortening rule first, then the zero-syndrome test, then the budget and the bounds, then branching on the firing check with the fewest available edges, children in increasing edge order. Edges are numbered h(i, j) for the edge leaving vertex (i, j) to the right and v(i, j) for the edge leaving it downward, row i and column j counted from the top left, with wrap-around. The first scenario excludes every logical of weight up to 4, which proves dZ ≥ 5. The second runs the same exclusion with the packing and shortening rules switched off, keeping only the budget. The third raises the cutoff to 5 and finds a witness.
