Running examples
  • Example A: three bits, X ≤ 4. Here X = 4x3 + 2x2 + x1 takes the values 0 to 7, and 5, 6, 7 are forbidden. The paper uses this case to introduce the trivial penalty (Eq. 1), and its own construction for it appears in Table 2. We also use it as a toy optimization problem in Section 9.
  • Example B: six bits, U = 53 and L = 17. Here X runs over 0 to 63. The paper's worked examples (Eqs. 12 and 16) and its Figure 3 use exactly these thresholds, and its numerical check evaluates all 64 assignments for them.
1 · CONSTRAINTS AS ENERGY

Why must a constraint be turned into a polynomial?

Quantum annealers, QAOA circuits and many classical "Ising machines" solve one kind of problem: minimize a polynomial in binary variables, with no side conditions at all. Real problems come with conditions (a knapsack has a weight limit, a schedule has a deadline), so before such a machine can be used every condition has to be folded into the polynomial itself, as an extra energy that is zero when the condition holds and positive when it fails.

Definition · QUBO and HUBO (Section 1.1; background from Glover et al.)

A quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem asks for the minimum of

over all 2n bit strings. A higher-order (HUBO) problem allows products of three or more variables as well. Because xi2 = xi for a bit, no variable ever needs to appear squared, so every such polynomial is a sum of products of distinct variables.

In words: a QUBO is a weighted count of which pairs of bits are on, a HUBO also counts triples, quadruples and so on, and the machine's job is to find the cheapest bit string.

QUBO is the native language of most current annealers, which have two-body couplings only. HUBO is the more natural language for many problems, and solvers that handle higher-order terms directly exist, for example the tensor-network solver HOBOTAN that the paper cites. The paper works in HUBO throughout.

Definition · penalty function (Section 2.1)

A penalty function for a constraint is a nonnegative function of the binary variables that is zero for every feasible assignment and strictly positive for every infeasible one. In this paper every penalty is a polynomial in the original binary variables.

In words: a penalty is an energy that costs nothing when the rule is obeyed and something when it is broken. Adding P times a penalty to an objective, with a large enough weight P, makes every rule-breaking bit string more expensive than the best rule-obeying one.

Equality constraints are easy. If the condition is g(x) = 0 for some polynomial g, then g2 is a penalty: it is zero exactly when g is zero and positive otherwise, and it uses no variables beyond those already in g. The paper makes exactly this point at the start of Section 1.1. Some inequalities have neat penalties too. The tutorial of Glover, Kochenberger and Du lists, for instance, the constraint x + y ≤ 1 with penalty xy: of the four assignments, only x = y = 1 breaks the rule, and only that one makes xy = 1.

A general inequality is harder, because "g(x) ≤ 0" has no squaring trick: a polynomial that is zero on a whole region and positive outside it has to be built by hand. The paper's question is how to do that for the most basic inequality on an integer stored in binary: X ≤ U.

Fact · what an exact penalty must do (Definition 1)

The four penalties studied in the paper are defined by their zero sets: Hupper(X, U) = 0 exactly when X ≤ U (Eq. 3), Hlower(X, L) = 0 exactly when L ≤ X (Eq. 4), Hin(X, L, U) = 0 exactly when L ≤ X ≤ U (Eq. 5), and Hout(X, L, U) = 0 exactly when X ≤ L or U ≤ X (Eq. 6), the last two for L ≤ U. Each must also be strictly positive everywhere else.

In short: annealers and QAOA minimize polynomials in bits without side conditions, so every constraint must become a penalty polynomial that is zero exactly on the feasible set; equalities have the squaring trick, inequalities do not.

2 · BINARY INTEGERS AND THE TWO STANDARD FIXES

What do people do today with X ≤ U?

An integer variable with values 0 to 2k − 1 is stored in k bits by the usual base-2 expansion,

and written X = (xk xk−1 ⋯ x1)2. The paper stresses that this encoding needs only O(log R) qubits for a range of size R, against O(R) for one-hot encoding with one bit per value, but that the encoding alone says nothing about how to penalize X > U. Two methods are standard.

The first is the slack variable. The inequality X ≤ U is rewritten as an equality X + s = U with a new integer s ≥ 0, the slack, which is itself stored in binary, and the squaring trick is applied to the equality. In Example A, the constraint X ≤ 4 becomes X + s = 4; the slack must reach 4, so it needs three bits s = s1 + 2s2 + 4s3, and the penalty is

This worked example is ours, built the way the Glover tutorial builds its knapsack example. The penalty is quadratic, which suits QUBO hardware, but three auxiliary bits have been added to a three-bit problem: the search space grows from 8 to 64 bit strings, and every feasible X now sits in a landscape of slack settings that the solver must also get right.

The second method, which the paper calls the trivial penalty, adds one product term for each forbidden bit string, a term that equals 1 on that string and 0 on every other. For Example A the forbidden values are 5 = (101)2, 6 = (110)2 and 7 = (111)2, and the trivial penalty is

It is exact and needs no new variables, but it has as many terms as there are forbidden values, namely 2k − U − 1, and every term involves all k bits.

Definition · literal, product term, product-term count, degree (Section 2.1)

A literal is a variable xi or its complement 1 − xi. A product term is a product of literals. A penalty written as a sum of product terms has product-term count equal to the number of products in the sum, where a factor written outside parentheses does not add to the count: the expression x6x5(x4 + x3x2) = x6x5x4 + x6x5x3x2 has two (Eq. 7), and (1 − x2)(1 − x1) has one (Eq. 8). A complemented literal is not expanded into 1 and −xi. The degree of a product term is its number of literals, and the degree of a penalty is the largest degree among its terms.

In words: count the products as the construction writes them, before multiplying anything out, and measure each by how many bits it ties together. The zero polynomial, which is the penalty for a vacuous constraint such as X ≤ 2k − 1, has count zero and no degree.

By these measures the trivial penalty for Example A has three terms of degree three. The paper lists four drawbacks of the trivial construction (Section 1.1): the term count grows linearly with the number of forbidden values, the degree is always the full k, no structure is shared between bit widths, and the construction does not reuse anything from the threshold's own binary digits. Degree matters in practice because current annealers have two-body couplings only, and every term of degree three or more has to be reduced to quadratic form, usually with extra auxiliary variables (Section 9 shows how).

In short: slack variables keep the penalty quadratic but add bits; the trivial penalty adds no bits but one degree-k term per forbidden value; the paper wants a penalty with neither cost.

3 · COMPARING BINARY NUMBERS

How do you tell, bit by bit, whether X exceeds U?

Everything in the paper rests on a fact so familiar from decimal numbers that it is rarely stated: to compare two numbers with the same number of digits, read from the left and stop at the first place they differ. This section states it for binary and proves it, because the recursion of the next section is this rule written as algebra. The statement and proof below are standard background, written out by us.

Fact · the highest differing bit decides (background)

Let X = (xk ⋯ x1)2 and U = (uk ⋯ u1)2 be different, and let m be the largest index with xm ≠ um. Then X > U exactly when xm = 1 and um = 0.

proofWhy can the lower bits never overturn the highest differing bit?

Above position m the two numbers agree, so those bits contribute the same amount to both. Suppose xm = 1 and um = 0. Then X − U equals 2m−1 plus the difference of the lower parts, and the lower part of U is at most

by the geometric series, while the lower part of X is at least 0. So X − U ≥ 2m−1 − (2m−1 − 1) = 1 > 0. The case xm = 0, um = 1 is the same argument with X and U exchanged.

∎

In Example B, with U = 53 = (110101)2, take X = 54 = (110110)2. Reading from the top, the bits agree at positions 6, 5, 4 and 3 and first differ at position 2, where x2 = 1 and u2 = 0, so X > U. Take instead X = 41 = (101001)2: the first difference is at position 5, where x5 = 0 and u5 = 1, so X < U, whatever the lower bits do.

Two consequences drive the construction. If the top bit of U is 0, then any X with top bit 1 is too big, and when the top bit of X is 0 the question passes unchanged to the lower bits. If the top bit of U is 1, then any X with top bit 0 is automatically small enough, and when the top bit of X is 1 the question again passes to the lower bits. "Too big already" is a condition to be added to the penalty; "fine already" is a condition that should switch the rest of the penalty off. Addition and multiplication are exactly the tools for those two jobs.

In short: X > U exactly when the highest bit where they differ is 1 in X and 0 in U; a 0 in U makes a 1 in X fatal, and a 1 in U makes a 0 in X safe.

4 · THE UPPER-BOUND RECURSION

How can a penalty for k + 1 bits be built from one for k bits?

The idea is to grow the penalty one bit at a time, from the least significant bit upwards. Split a (k + 1)-bit integer and threshold into their top bit and the rest: Xk+1 = 2kxk+1 + Xk and U = 2kuk+1 + U′, where Xk and U′ are the k-bit lower parts. The two consequences at the end of Section 3 then tell us what to do with a penalty Hk(Xk, U′) that already handles the lower parts.

Theorem 1 · exact recursive upper-bound penalty

For k = 1, set H1(X, 0) = x1 and H1(X, 1) = 0. For the step from k to k + 1 bits, define

Then Hk(X, U) is a nonnegative integer-valued polynomial in the original bits, and Hk(X, U) = 0 if and only if X ≤ U.

In words: walk up the threshold's bits; at a 0, add the new bit of X to the penalty (a 1 there is a violation on its own); at a 1, multiply the penalty by the new bit of X (a 0 there makes everything below irrelevant). The paper writes Hupper(X, U) for the result.

proofWhy does the recursion give exactly the right zero set? (the paper's induction)

Base case. With one bit, X = x1. For U = 0 the penalty x1 vanishes exactly when X = 0, which is exactly when X ≤ 0. For U = 1 the penalty is 0, and both values of X satisfy X ≤ 1.

Inductive hypothesis. For some k and every k-bit U′, the polynomial Hk(Xk, U′) is a nonnegative integer that is zero exactly when Xk ≤ U′.

Case A, uk+1 = 0 (Eq. 9: Hk+1 = xk+1 + Hk). Then U = U′ < 2k. A sum of two nonnegative numbers is zero exactly when both are zero, so Hk+1 = 0 exactly when xk+1 = 0 and Xk ≤ U′. Since U < 2k, any X with xk+1 = 1 is at least 2k > U, so these two conditions together are equivalent to Xk+1 ≤ U.

Case B, uk+1 = 1 (Eq. 10: Hk+1 = xk+1Hk). Then U = 2k + U′. If xk+1 = 0, the penalty is 0, and indeed Xk+1 = Xk < 2k ≤ U. If xk+1 = 1, the penalty equals Hk(Xk, U′), and Xk+1 ≤ U is equivalent to Xk ≤ U′, so the hypothesis gives the claim.

In both cases Hk+1 arises from a nonnegative integer polynomial by adding or multiplying by a bit, so it is again a nonnegative integer polynomial. By induction the theorem holds for every k.

∎

The paper's Table 1 runs the recursion for all two-bit thresholds: the threshold U = 0 = (00)2 gives x2 + x1, the threshold 1 gives x2, the threshold 2 = (10)2 gives x2x1, and the threshold 3 gives 0. Each can be checked against the four values of X directly. For example, x2x1 is nonzero only for X = 3, the only two-bit value above 2.

For Example A, U = 4 = (100)2. Start with u1 = 0, so H = x1. Next u2 = 0, so H = x2 + x1. Last u3 = 1, so

which is the entry for U = 4 in the paper's Table 2. Its values on X = 0, …, 7 are 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2: zero exactly on the feasible values, and positive on 5, 6 and 7. It has two product terms of degree two, against three of degree three in Eq. (1). It is already quadratic, so for this threshold no further reduction is needed for QUBO hardware.

Written as a loop, the recursion is the paper's Algorithm 1: initialize H = x1 if u1 = 0 and H = 0 if u1 = 1; then for i = 2, …, k replace H by xi + H when ui = 0 and by xiH when ui = 1. The animation runs it on Example B's threshold U = 53 = (110101)2. At each step it also evaluates the current penalty on every value of the lower bits, so the bars show the zero set taking shape: after step i, the bars are zero exactly up to the threshold formed by the lowest i bits of U.

Animation · Algorithm 1 for U = 53
bit being readpenalty valuezero (feasible)

The final expression is the paper's Eq. (12),

with two product terms and degree four. The trivial construction for the same constraint has 26 − 53 − 1 = 10 terms, each of degree six.

In short: reading U from the bottom, a 0 bit adds xi and a 1 bit multiplies by xi; induction on k proves the result is zero exactly when X ≤ U; for U = 4 this gives x3(x2 + x1) and for U = 53 it gives Eq. (12).

5 · THE UNROLLED FORMULA

What does each term of the penalty actually detect?

The recursion produces nested parentheses. Multiplying them out gives a flat formula that is easier to count and, as we show below, easier to interpret. Each zero bit of U starts a term, and each one bit above it multiplies that term by the corresponding variable.

Corollary 1 · explicit sum-product form

For U = (uk ⋯ u1)2,

with an empty product equal to 1 and an empty sum equal to 0.

In words: there is one term for each 0 in the threshold; the term for position i is xi times every xj sitting above a 1 of the threshold.

proofWhy does unrolling the recursion give Eq. (11)?

Follow Algorithm 1 as it reads the bits upwards and keep the penalty as a flat sum. A zero bit at position i appends a new term xi. A one bit at position j multiplies every term already present by xj, and those are exactly the terms started at zero bits below j. So the term started at position i ends up multiplied by xj for every j > i with uj = 1, and by nothing else. This is the paper's argument.

∎

For U = 53 = (110101)2, the zero bits sit at positions 2 and 4. The term for position 2 picks up the one bits above it at positions 3, 5 and 6, giving x6x5x3x2. The term for position 4 picks up positions 5 and 6, giving x6x5x4. Their sum is Eq. (12) multiplied out.

The following reading of Eq. (11) is ours; the paper proves correctness by induction and does not interpret the individual terms. The term for a zero bit i equals 1 exactly when xi = 1 and xj = 1 at every position j > i where uj = 1. In other words, at position i the number X has a 1 where U has a 0, and above position i, X has a 1 wherever U does. Such a term can only fire when X > U, and when X > U the term at the highest differing bit always fires.

our derivationWhy does a firing term force X > U, and why does some term fire when X > U?

Suppose the term for position i fires. Then xi = 1 ≠ 0 = ui, so X ≠ U; let m ≥ i be the highest differing bit. If m = i, Section 3 gives X > U at once. If m > i and um = 1, then xm = 0, but the firing term requires xm = 1 at every one bit of U above i, a contradiction. So um = 0, xm = 1 and X > U.

Conversely, if X > U, let m be the highest differing bit; Section 3 says xm = 1 and um = 0. Above m the bits agree, so xj = 1 wherever uj = 1. Hence the term for position m fires.

∎

So Hupper(X, U) counts the zero bits of U at which X "breaks through" while dominating U above. It is at least 1 off the feasible set and at most the number of zero bits of U, which is at most k. The animation evaluates both terms of Eq. (12) on six values of X, showing which literals are on and where the highest differing bit sits.

Animation · evaluating Hupper(X, 53)
highest differing bitliteral equal to 1term fires
Fact · bounded penalty values (Section 4.3)

Each single-bound penalty has smallest positive value 1 and largest value at most the bit width k, because each product term takes the value 0 or 1 and there are at most k terms. For Example B the largest value of Hupper(X, 53) is 2, reached at X = 62 and 63.

In short: unrolled, the penalty has one term per zero bit of U (Eq. 11); each term detects a specific way of exceeding U (our reading), so the penalty is a whole number between 1 and k whenever X > U.

6 · LOWER BOUNDS AND DUALITY

Does the same idea enforce X ≥ L?

A lower bound is the mirror image of an upper bound. Now a 1 in the threshold where X has a 0 is the danger, and a 0 in the threshold where X has a 1 makes X safe. The literal that signals danger at position i is therefore 1 − xi, which is 1 when the bit is off.

Theorem 2 · exact recursive lower-bound penalty

For k = 1, set H1(X, 0) = 0 and H1(X, 1) = 1 − x1. Writing L = 2kℓk+1 + L′, define

Then Hk(X, L) is a nonnegative integer-valued polynomial with Hk(X, L) = 0 if and only if L ≤ X. The paper writes Hlower(X, L).

In words: at a 1 of the threshold, add "this bit of X is off"; at a 0, multiply by "this bit of X is off", so that a 1 in X there switches everything below off.

proofWhy is the induction the same as before?

The base case is checked directly: 1 − x1 vanishes exactly when X = 1 ≥ 1. In Case A, ℓk+1 = 0 (Eq. 13), so L = L′ < 2k. If xk+1 = 1 then X ≥ 2k > L and the penalty is 0; if xk+1 = 0, the penalty equals Hk(Xk, L′) and L ≤ X is equivalent to L′ ≤ Xk. In Case B, ℓk+1 = 1 (Eq. 14), so L = 2k + L′. A sum of nonnegative terms is zero exactly when xk+1 = 1 and L′ ≤ Xk, which together say L ≤ X. Each step adds or multiplies by the nonnegative literal 1 − xk+1, so the result stays a nonnegative integer polynomial. This is the paper's proof, condensed.

∎

Unrolling gives the mirror of Eq. (11), one term for each one bit of L:

For Example B, L = 17 = (010001)2 has one bits at positions 1 and 5. Running Algorithm 2 upwards: ℓ1 = 1 gives 1 − x1; the zeros at positions 2, 3 and 4 multiply by 1 − x2, 1 − x3, 1 − x4; the one at position 5 adds 1 − x5; and the zero at position 6 multiplies everything by 1 − x6. The result is the paper's Eq. (16),

with two product terms and degree five, against seventeen terms of degree six for the trivial construction. On X = 0 both terms fire and the penalty is 2; on X = 1 to 16 it is 1; from X = 17 on it is 0.

The two constructions are linked by flipping bits. Flipping every bit of X gives X̄ = Σ (1 − xi)2i−1 = 2k − 1 − X, and flipping reverses order, so L ≤ X exactly when X̄ ≤ L̄.

Fact · one's-complement duality (Section 2.4)

Each literal xi of the upper-bound construction becomes 1 − xi, and each zero bit of the complemented threshold is a one bit of L. The paper stresses that this is a substitution on X and the threshold, not the Boolean negation 1 − Hupper.

As a check (ours), L̄ = 63 − 17 = 46 = (101110)2 has zero bits at positions 1 and 5. By Eq. (11), Hupper for threshold 46 has terms x1x2x3x4x6 (the one bits above position 1 are 2, 3, 4, 6) and x5x6. Replacing every xi by 1 − xi gives exactly the two terms of Eq. (16).

In short: the lower-bound penalty swaps the roles of 0 and 1 and uses the literals 1 − xi; it has one term per one bit of L (Eq. 15), and it is the upper-bound penalty applied to the bit-flipped number and threshold (Eq. 17).

7 · HOW SMALL ARE THE PENALTIES?

How many terms, and of what degree, compared with enumeration?

The paper's practical claim is a comparison of size, measured by product-term count and degree on the expressions as generated, before any simplification (Section 2.5). Both measures can be read straight off Eq. (11).

Term count. The upper-bound penalty has one term per zero bit of U, so at most k. The trivial construction has one term per forbidden integer, 2k − U − 1. The proposed count is strictly smaller for every U from 0 to 2k − 3; at U = 2k − 2 both have one term, and at the vacuous U = 2k − 1 both are zero. For lower bounds the count is the number of one bits of L against L for the trivial construction, with a tie only at L = 1.

Fact · average term counts (Section 2.5)

Averaged uniformly over all thresholds, the proposed construction has ½ log2 R product terms, while the trivial construction has (R − 1)/2, where R = 2k. The worst case is k = log2 R against R − 1.

our derivationWhere do the two averages come from?

The paper states the averages; this short computation is ours. As U runs over all 2k values, each of its k bits is 0 for exactly half of them, so the total number of zero bits is k · 2k−1 and the average is k/2 = ½ log2 R. For the trivial construction, 2k − U − 1 runs over 2k − 1, …, 1, 0 as U runs upward, and the average of 0, 1, …, R − 1 is (R − 1)/2. For k = 6 the averages are 3 and 31.5.

∎

Degree. In Eq. (11), the term for a zero bit i has degree 1 plus the number of one bits above i. The lowest zero bit has the most one bits above it, so the degree of the whole penalty is 1 plus the number of one bits of U above its lowest zero bit. This equals k only when the lowest zero bit is bit 1 and every bit above it is 1, that is, U = 2k − 2, where the penalty is xk ⋯ x1 and coincides with the trivial construction. For every smaller threshold the degree is less than k, while every trivial term has degree exactly k. For lower bounds the exceptional threshold is L = 1. The paper's Figures 1 and 2 plot both measures for all upper thresholds at k = 6.

For Example B, U = 53 has its lowest zero bit at position 2 with three one bits above (positions 3, 5, 6), giving degree four, as in Eq. (12). For Example A, U = 4 = (100)2 has its lowest zero at position 1 with one one bit above, giving degree two.

Fact · the comparison in one line (Sections 1.3 and 2.5)

Except at one non-vacuous boundary threshold per bound (U = 2k − 2 and L = 1), the proposed single-bound penalty has both fewer product terms and lower degree than the trivial construction, and its term count is O(log R) against O(R).

In short: term count is the number of zero bits of U (or one bits of L), averaging ½ log2 R against (R − 1)/2; degree is 1 plus the one bits above the lowest zero bit, below k except at U = 2k − 2.

8 · ADDING AND MULTIPLYING PENALTIES

How do you combine bounds into intervals and exclusions?

Many constraints are two-sided: a quantity must lie between two limits, or must avoid a middle range. Because the penalties are nonnegative, ordinary arithmetic combines their zero sets in exactly the logical way. A sum of nonnegative numbers is zero only when every summand is zero, so addition means "and". A product is zero as soon as one factor is zero, so multiplication means "or".

Theorems 3 and 4 · interval and exclusion penalties

For 0 ≤ L ≤ U < 2k,

is zero exactly when L ≤ X ≤ U, and

is zero exactly when X ≤ L or U ≤ X. Both are strictly positive everywhere else.

In words: to demand both bounds, add their penalties; to demand at least one of two conditions, multiply theirs. Note that the exclusion uses the upper-bound penalty at L and the lower-bound penalty at U.

proofWhy is the product strictly positive in the excluded middle?

For the interval: both summands are nonnegative, so the sum is zero exactly when both are zero, which by Theorems 1 and 2 means L ≤ X and X ≤ U. For the exclusion: if X ≤ L the first factor is zero, and if U ≤ X the second is. Conversely, a product of two numbers is zero only if one of them is, which by Theorems 1 and 2 gives X ≤ L or U ≤ X. Finally, if L < X < U, then X > L makes the first factor a positive integer and X < U makes the second a positive integer, so their product is at least 1. This is the paper's proof.

∎

Degrees combine predictably: the interval penalty has degree at most the larger of the two component degrees, and the exclusion penalty at most their sum. The animation reproduces the paper's Figure 3 for Example B by evaluating every penalty on all 64 values of X. The last frame is ours: it also reports the largest value of the exclusion penalty, which the paper does not state.

Animation · interval and exclusion for L = 17, U = 53
penalty valuezero (feasible)

The paper reports one numerical check (Section 4.1): all 64 assignments for k = 6, L = 17 and U = 53, on which all four penalties have exactly the predicted zero sets and are strictly positive elsewhere. The animation above performs the same check in the page.

In short: for nonnegative penalties, addition realizes "and" (intervals, Eq. 18) and multiplication realizes "or" (exclusions, Eq. 19); for Example B both have exactly the required zero sets.

9 · USING THE PENALTY

What happens when the penalty goes into an optimization problem?

A penalty only matters once it is added to an objective. This section is mostly ours: a toy problem that shows how the penalty weight is chosen, followed by the practical points the paper raises in Sections 4.3 and 4.4.

Take Example A as an optimization: find the largest 3-bit X with X ≤ 4. Written as a minimization, the objective is f = −X = −(4x3 + 2x2 + x1), and the constrained answer is X = 4. The unconstrained problem is

If P is too small, breaking the rule pays. With P = 1, the energies of X = 5, 6, 7 are −4, −5, −5, and the minimum −5 sits at the infeasible values 6 and 7. With P = 2 the energy of X = 6 is −6 + 2 = −4, tied with the feasible optimum. Any P > 2 works: then X = 5 costs −5 + P > −3, X = 6 costs −6 + P > −4, and X = 7 costs −7 + 2P > −3, all above −4. The animation computes all eight energies for several weights.

Animation · choosing the penalty weight (our example)
feasible X ≤ 4infeasibleminimum

The general rule behind the example (standard, and ours to state here) is that P must exceed the largest gain the objective can make by violating the constraint, divided by the smallest penalty an infeasible point can receive. The paper's point in Section 4.3 is that the second number is always 1 for its single-bound penalties and the largest penalty is at most k, so the scale of the penalty is predictable. It adds that this does not remove the need to choose an overall weight.

Penalties are not distances. The paper's third limitation (Section 4.4) is that the penalty value does not grow with the size of the violation. In Example B, Hupper(X, 53) equals 1 at X = 54 and also at X = 61, and 2 only at 62 and 63. A solver that follows the penalty downhill gets no signal pointing it back towards the feasible region; the construction is an exact yes-or-no test, not a measure of how far off a point is.

Higher degree still costs something. The second limitation is quadratization. Annealers with two-body couplings need degree-two polynomials, and a standard method from Dattani's review, due to Rosenberg, replaces a product xixj by a new bit y and adds a multiple of

which is zero exactly when y = xixj and at least 1 otherwise. Applying it to Eq. (12) is our worked example: substituting y for x6x5 turns the penalty into y x4 + y x3x2, and substituting z for x3x2 turns that into y x4 + y z. Two auxiliary bits plus two Rosenberg terms make the penalty quadratic. The ten degree-six terms of the trivial construction would need several reductions each. The paper notes that its slack-free property holds for the higher-order form and may not survive quadratization, and that the degree of the proposed penalty is not bounded independently of k.

Unused codes and fractions. Section 4.3 points out two uses beyond stated inequalities. A variable with N admissible values needs ⌈log2 N⌉ bits, and when N is not a power of two some bit strings mean nothing; the penalty Hupper(X, N − 1) excludes them. Example A is exactly this situation for N = 5 choices stored in three bits. And a quantity with fixed fractional resolution, such as multiples of 1/8, can be stored as an integer count of that unit, with the thresholds scaled the same way, so the same constructions apply unchanged.

In short: the penalty weight must beat the objective's gain from cheating, which on Example A means P > 2; the paper's penalties have a predictable range but are not distances, and their slack-free advantage is for higher-order solvers, since quadratization adds auxiliary bits back.

RESULTS

What the paper reports

The paper's results are theorems plus worked examples; its only numerical experiment is the exhaustive check of Section 4.1. The examples, as stated in the paper:

ASSESSMENT

What is shown, and what is claimed

Proved, and easy to trust. Theorems 1 to 4 and the two corollaries are complete, elementary inductions with no gaps that we could find. As an extra check, we evaluated Eq. (11) and Eq. (15) against the definitions for every k from 1 to 8, every threshold and every X, and found the zero sets exactly as claimed and the values never above k. The term-count and degree statements follow directly from the explicit formulas.

What the counts measure. All counts are taken on the expressions as generated, with complemented literals kept as single literals and nothing multiplied out. That is a fair convention for a solver that accepts such literals, but it matters for hardware that wants plain monomials or Ising spins. The following observation is ours, not the paper's: expanding a product of d complemented literals such as (1 − x4)(1 − x3)(1 − x2)(1 − x1) in Eq. (16) gives 2d monomials, and in spin variables si = 2xi − 1 both xi and 1 − xi are (1 ± si)/2, so any degree-d product term becomes up to 2d spin terms. The O(log R) count is therefore a count of generated product terms, not of Hamiltonian coefficients.

Claimed only as a possibility. The paper is careful, in Section 4.4, to say that it does not compare optimization performance with slack variables, unbalanced penalization or the trivial construction, and that fewer terms and lower degree should not be read as guarantees of higher feasibility rates, shorter time to solution or lower cost after quadratization. The statements that the construction "may" reduce evaluation work or embedding overhead are plausible but untested here.

Novelty in context. The paper positions itself honestly: the set of binary vectors below a threshold was already characterized in integer programming by Muldoon et al. and Adams et al. through valid inequalities and convex hulls, and the closest HUBO work, a preprint by Minato, was withdrawn and corresponds to the trivial baseline. The contribution is the exact nonnegative polynomial with the right zero set, its recursion and its arithmetic composition.

Context. The paper is short and was prepared for the journal Information Sciences. The first author lists a secondary-school affiliation alongside a company affiliation. The authors state that they used ChatGPT to improve language and readability, and that all claims and derivations are their own.

Our additions. The proof of the highest-differing-bit rule, the interpretation of each term of Eq. (11) and its proof, the derivation of the two averages, the duality check with threshold 46, the slack-variable formulation of Example A, the penalty-weight example, the Rosenberg quadratization of Eq. (12), the remark on expanding complemented literals, the exhaustive check up to k = 8, and all four animations are ours.

Cited by the paper for the squaring trick; the source here for the table of known penalties such as x + y ≤ 1 → P xy and for slack variables in a knapsack constraint.

N. Dattani, Quadratization in discrete optimization and quantum mechanics, arXiv:1901.04405. Cited by the paper for quadratization; a catalogue of methods for reducing higher-order terms to quadratic ones, including the Rosenberg substitution used in Section 9.

All four animations run real computations in the page: the first runs Algorithm 1 on the bits of 53 and evaluates each intermediate polynomial on every value of the lower bits; the second evaluates the product terms of Eq. (11) literal by literal; the third evaluates all four penalties of Example B on all 64 values of X; the fourth computes the energy of all eight bit strings of Example A for each penalty weight. The running examples come from the paper; the derivations and examples marked as ours are ours.

How Should Candidates Be Weighted under Open-List Proportional Representation? Harmonic Weights and Dirichlet Order Statistics

Daria Boratyn, Dariusz Stolicki · posted Nov 19, 2026 · physics.soc-ph, cross-listed in math.PR · arXiv 2611.26337

Overview

If a party's vote is split among its candidates at random, and you do not know how lopsided the split tends to be, not even its order of magnitude, then the share you should expect for the candidate in position k falls off like 1/k, and this paper proves it. The question comes from political science: under open-list proportional representation a few candidates collect most of a list's personal votes, so anyone who counts candidates (how many women a party nominates, how many incumbents return) needs a weight for each list position before any votes are cast. The authors model the split with the symmetric Dirichlet distribution, the standard family of random points on a simplex, and show that no single member of the family gives sensible weights: the uniform split is too even, and every fixed concentration makes the top of the list too flat and the bottom too steep. Averaging over the concentration with the scale-invariant prior dθ/θ, however, turns geometric profiles into a 1/k profile, and the result sits within 1.4 to 3.4 percent of the simple harmonic weights 1/(kHn). Along the way the paper uses some of the most useful tools in probability: the gamma representation of the Dirichlet distribution, order statistics and their gaps, hazard rates, Poisson processes, and the Poisson–Dirichlet limit that also describes the cycle lengths of a random permutation. This chapter builds each of those from the ground up, with a three-candidate example small enough to check by hand.

By the end you'll be able to explain
  • why counting candidates on party lists needs weights, and what the paper means by the weight of a list position (Definitions 1 and 3, Assumption A1);
  • what the probability simplex and the symmetric Dirichlet distribution are, and how the parameter α controls how concentrated a random split is;
  • the gamma trick: a Dirichlet vector is a vector of independent gamma variables divided by their sum, and why that turns expected shares into expected order statistics (Lemma 1);
  • how to compute the expected gap between the k-th and (k+1)-th largest of n random numbers from a tail integral, and what a hazard rate is (Eq. 4);
  • why, for the uniform split, the expected largest of three shares is 11/18, and why the harmonic weights appear exactly as normalized expected margins (Proposition 1);
  • why every fixed α gives a profile that is flat at the top and collapses at the bottom (Definition 5, Proposition 2);
  • the sparse limit, the Poisson–Dirichlet distribution, and its connection to the longest cycle of a random permutation (Proposition 3, Remark 6);
  • why averaging geometric profiles over a scale-invariant prior produces 1/k decay (Theorem 1, Proposition 4), and how far the result is from the harmonic weights (Tables 1 to 3).

V = (V1, …, Vn)

the k-th largest coordinate of a vector x, so x(1) ≥ ⋯ ≥ x(n)
α
the symmetric Dirichlet parameter, per candidate; α = 1 is the uniform distribution on Δn
θ
the total concentration nα (Definition 2)
π(n)k(α)
the expected share of the k-th largest candidate, E(V(k)) (Definition 1)
Hn

w(n)k
the harmonic weight 1/(kHn) (Definition 3)

G1, …, Gn

fα, Fα, Qα, hα

Running examples
  • Example A: three candidates, uniform split. A list of n = 3 candidates divides its vote by a point chosen uniformly from the triangle Δ3 (α = 1). This is the same as breaking a stick of length 1 at two uniformly random points. We will compute by hand that the expected shares of the first, second and third candidates are 11/18, 5/18 and 2/18, compare them with the harmonic weights 6/11, 3/11 and 2/11, and simulate the split in the page. The paper's Table 3 contains this case (n = 3, α = 1) as its first row.
  • Example B: unknown concentration with θ0 = 1. The total concentration θ is drawn from the prior dθ/θ on [1, ∞), and the list is long. The paper's Table 1 gives the resulting weights relative to the leader, 1, 0.533, 0.356, 0.263, 0.206, …, and the page recomputes them from Eqs. (8), (13) and (14).
1 · WEIGHTING LIST POSITIONS

Why would anyone need a weight for each place on a list?

In open-list proportional representation each party presents an ordered list of candidates. Voters cast preference votes for individual candidates; the votes of all of a party's candidates are pooled to decide how many seats the party wins, and the individual votes decide which of its candidates fill those seats (the empirical studies the paper cites look at elections of this kind in Italy, Poland and Finland). The paper's Section 1.1 makes the empirical point that those individual votes are divided very unevenly: a few candidates attract most of the list's vote, many attract almost none.

That unevenness is a problem for anyone who counts candidates. A study of how many women a party nominates, or how many of last election's candidates return, has to decide whether the leader of a list counts the same as the candidate in position 30. Section 2 of the paper reviews the existing answers: cut-offs that count only the top positions, weights that fall linearly with rank, estimated probabilities of being elected, logistic curves, and the reciprocal weights 1/k of Flis and coauthors, used before this paper without a derivation. Most of these need information beyond the list itself, such as the party's result at the previous election, and none is derived from a model of how a list's vote is divided.

The authors want weights that depend on list position alone and can be assigned before the election. Their definition of the weight of a position is the share of the list vote its occupant can be expected to receive. To connect positions with shares they make one idealizing assumption.

Assumption A1 · sorting

The candidates appear on the list in nonincreasing order of their vote shares: the share of the candidate in position k is V(k), the k-th largest of the shares V1, …, Vn.

In words: the party ranks its candidates exactly by how well they will do. Real lists are sorted imperfectly, and Section 7 of the paper returns to this.

Definition 1 · expected-share profile

For a random vector V of shares, the expected-share profile is the vector π(n) with coordinates

In words: the k-th weight is the average, over all possible splits of the vote, of the k-th largest share. Under A1 it is the weight an analyst who knows the model but not the result would give to position k. The coordinates sum to 1, because V(1) + ⋯ + V(n) = 1 for every split.

The candidate answer the paper ends up recommending has no free parameters at all.

Definition 3 · harmonic weights

For a list of n candidates, the harmonic weights are

Eq. 2

In words: weight position k in proportion to 1/k, and divide by Hn so the weights sum to 1. The ratio of any two weights, wk/wl = l/k, does not depend on the length of the list; only the normalization does, and the leader's weight is 1/Hn.

For Example A, H3 = 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 = 11/6, so the harmonic weights are 6/11, 3/11 and 2/11, about 0.545, 0.273 and 0.182. The paper's Remark 3 notes that the sequence 1, 1/2, 1/3, … is also the sequence of divisors in the D'Hondt method of seat allocation: on a closed list, the k-th candidate is elected exactly when the list's vote divided by k is among the M largest quotients of all lists, where M is the number of seats.

To say how close two weight profiles are, the paper uses one measure throughout.

Definition 4 · total variation distance

In words: the share of the total weight that would have to be moved from some positions to others to turn one profile into the other. A distance of 0.03 means three percent of the weight is in the wrong place.

In short: the weight of a list position is defined as the expected share of the k-th largest candidate under a random split of the vote (Definition 1, Assumption A1); the candidate answer is the harmonic profile 1/(kHn), and profiles are compared by total variation distance.

2 · DIVIDING A VOTE AT RANDOM

What does it mean to choose a split of the vote at random?

A split of a list's vote among n candidates is a point of the probability simplex

which is a segment for n = 2, a triangle for n = 3 and a tetrahedron for n = 4. To speak of an expected share we need a probability distribution on this set, and since the weights are meant to be assigned before anything is known about the individual candidates, the distribution should treat all candidates alike. The paper's choice is the standard one.

Assumption A2 · symmetric Dirichlet shares

The vector V has the symmetric Dirichlet distribution with parameter α > 0, the distribution on Δn with density proportional to

In words: every candidate is treated the same (the distribution is exchangeable), and the single number α sets how concentrated a typical split is. For α = 1 the density is constant, so every split is equally likely. For α < 1 the density blows up near the corners of the simplex, so the vote typically goes to a few candidates; for α > 1 the mass moves towards the center, where all shares are close to 1/n (Remark 2).

The paper also notes that this family arises as the large-electorate limit of the Pólya–Eggenberger urn, a model in which each new voter tends to copy earlier ones. To compute anything with it we need one more family of distributions, which we review as background.

Background · the gamma distributionThe gamma distribution with shape α > 0 and unit scale has density fα(x) = xα−1e−x/Γ(α) on x > 0, where Γ(α) = ∫0∞ tα−1e−t dt is the gamma function, so that Γ(m) = (m − 1)! for whole numbers. Its mean is α and its variance is α, so E(G2) = α(α + 1). For α = 1 it is the exponential distribution, density e−x. The key closure property is that a sum of independent gamma variables with shapes α1, …, αn is gamma with shape α1 + ⋯ + αn. The upper incomplete gamma function Γ(a, x) = ∫x∞ ta−1e−t dt gives the tail: 1 − Fα(x) = Γ(α, x)/Γ(α).

The bridge between the two families is the most useful fact in this paper, quoted in the proof of Lemma 1 from the reference book of Kotz, Balakrishnan and Johnson.

Fact · the gamma trick (used in the proof of Lemma 1)

Let G1, …, Gn be independent gamma variables with shape α and let S = G1 + ⋯ + Gn. Then (G1/S, …, Gn/S) has the symmetric Dirichlet distribution with parameter α, and S is independent of that vector.

In words: to split a vote at random, give each candidate an independent random "strength", and hand out the vote in proportion to strength. The total strength S carries no information about how the vote is divided. For Example A this means: draw three independent exponential numbers and divide each by their sum. The three resulting shares are uniformly distributed on the triangle.

Independence of S from the shares is what makes the trick so effective, because it lets expectations factor. Since G(k) = V(k) S and E(S) = nα,

This is the first half of Lemma 1. In words: the expected k-th largest share is the expected k-th largest of n independent gamma numbers, divided by their expected total. A question about a distribution on a simplex has become a question about independent random numbers, which is much easier.

The same factoring measures how concentrated a split is. Political scientists use the effective number of candidates of Laakso and Taagepera, one over the sum of squared shares: it equals n when all shares are equal and 1 when one candidate takes everything. Evaluated at the expected sum of squares, the paper states that

derivationWhere does the expected sum of squares come from? (our derivation)

The paper states the formula without proof; this derivation is ours and uses only the gamma trick. Write Gi = ViS. Because S is independent of V,

The left side is α(α + 1), the second moment of a gamma variable with shape α. The total S is gamma with shape nα, so E(S2) = nα(nα + 1). Dividing,

∎

For the uniform split, α = 1, this gives Neff = (n + 1)/2: about half the list is effectively in play, whatever the list. For Example A it gives Neff = 2. The formula also shows that α alone is not the natural way to describe concentration on lists of different lengths, which motivates the second parameterization.

Definition 2 · total concentration

The total concentration of a list is θ := nα, the sum of the Dirichlet parameters of its candidates.

In words: α measures concentration per candidate, θ for the list as a whole. If θ is held fixed while n grows, Eq. (1) gives Neff = (θ + 1)/(θ/n + 1) → 1 + θ, so the effective number of candidates stays bounded however many names are added at the bottom.

In short: a random split is a symmetric Dirichlet point of the simplex, with α setting its concentration; dividing independent gamma variables by their sum produces it, which turns expected shares into expected gamma order statistics (Eq. 3) and gives Neff = (nα + 1)/(α + 1) (Eq. 1).

3 · ORDER STATISTICS AND THEIR GAPS

How do you compute the expected k-th largest of n random numbers?

Eq. (3) reduces everything to E(G(k)), the expected k-th largest of n independent gamma variables. Computing it directly from the density of G(k) is messy. The paper instead computes the expected gaps between neighbors, using two standard tools: the tail-integral formula for expectations and the hazard rate.

The tail-integral formula says that for a nonnegative random variable X, E(X) = ∫0∞ Pr(X > x) dx. (It follows by writing X = ∫0∞ 1{x < X} dx and taking expectations inside the integral.) The hazard rate of a distribution is

the density at x divided by the probability of having survived past x. In words, it is the instantaneous rate at which a variable that has already passed x is about to stop. For the exponential distribution f1(x) = e−x and 1 − F1(x) = e−x, so h1 ≡ 1: the exponential has a constant hazard, which is the memoryless property.

Lemma 1 · gamma representation, second half

Let G(n+1) := 0. For every k ∈ [n],

Eq. 4

In words: the expected gap below the k-th largest value equals 1/k times the average reciprocal hazard rate at that value. Where the hazard is high, values are packed together; where it is low, they spread out.

proofWhy is the gap an integral of "exactly k exceed x"? (the paper's proof)

By the tail-integral formula applied to both order statistics,

The event G(k) > x means at least k of the n variables exceed x, and G(k+1) > x means at least k + 1 do. Their difference is the probability that exactly k exceed x, which is a binomial probability with success chance 1 − Fα(x):

That gives the first equality. For the second, substitute u = 1 − Fα(x). Then du = −fα(x) dx, so dx = −du/(u hα(x)), and the integral becomes

The function C(n, k) uk−1(1 − u)n−k is 1/k times the density of the beta distribution with parameters k and n − k + 1, which is the distribution of 1 − Fα(G(k)) (the k-th smallest of n uniform numbers). The integral is therefore 1/k times the expectation of 1/hα(G(k)).

∎

For the exponential distribution the hazard is identically 1, so the expected gap is exactly 1/k. (This is also the memoryless picture: once k variables are still above some level, the time until the next of them stops is the minimum of k independent exponentials, which has mean 1/k. That intuition is ours; the paper's route is Eq. 4.) Adding gaps from the bottom up,

For Example A, with n = 3: the smallest of three exponentials has mean 1/3, the middle one is 1/2 above it on average, and the largest a further 1 above that. So E(G(3)) = 1/3, E(G(2)) = 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6 and E(G(1)) = 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 = 11/6. Dividing by nα = 3 as Eq. (3) says, the expected shares are

In stick-breaking language: break a stick at two uniform points, and the longest piece is on average 11/18 of the stick. The animation below checks this by simulation in the page, generating each split exactly as the gamma trick prescribes, and then looks at the gaps between the averaged shares, which will matter in the next section.

In short: the expected gap below the k-th largest of n variables is 1/k times the expected reciprocal hazard there (Eq. 4); for exponentials the hazard is 1, the gaps are 1, 1/2, …, 1/n, and for Example A the expected shares are 11/18, 5/18 and 2/18.

4 · THE UNIFORM SPLIT

Does the "know nothing" distribution already give harmonic weights?

The uniform distribution on the simplex is the obvious model for complete ignorance about a split: every division of the vote is equally likely. The paper notes that it is the counterpart of the "impartial anonymous culture" of social choice theory and that its expected ordered coordinates have been used as average player weights in weighted voting games. This section asks what weights it gives and whether they are reasonable.

Combining Eqs. (3) and (4), for every α the expected margin by which the k-th candidate leads the next one is

with π(n)n+1 := 0. In words: the margins are harmonic, proportional to 1/k, up to the correction factors ρk, the expected reciprocal hazard rates at the ordered values.

Proposition 1 · expected margins

(i) If α = 1, then ρ(n)k(1) = 1 for every k, and consequently

(ii) If α < 1, then ρ(n)k(α) < 1 and it is strictly decreasing in k; if α > 1, then ρ(n)k(α) > 1 and it is strictly increasing in k. In either case the normalized expected margins are not harmonic.

(iii) For every α > 0 and every fixed k, ρ(n)k(α) → 1 as n → ∞.

In words: under the uniform split, the harmonic weight of position k is exactly the expected lead of its occupant over the next candidate, measured as a fraction of the leader's expected share. This identity holds for α = 1 and no other α, although the margins near the top of a long list are approximately harmonic for every α.

proofWhy does the identity hold only for the uniform split? (the paper's proof)

(i) The exponential hazard is h1 ≡ 1, so every ρk is 1. Summing Eq. (5) from position k to position n telescopes to the first formula. In particular π1(1) = Hn/n, and dividing the margin 1/(kn) by Hn/n gives 1/(kHn) = wk.

(ii) The gamma hazard rate is strictly decreasing when α < 1 and strictly increasing when α > 1, with limit 1 at infinity in both cases (a classical fact from reliability theory, cited from Barlow and Proschan). Take α < 1. Then 1/hα is strictly increasing and smaller than 1. Since G(k+1) < G(k) almost surely, ρk+1 < ρk < 1. The case α > 1 is symmetric. Finally, π1(α) is the sum of all margins, Σj ρj/(jnα), so the normalized margins are proportional to 1/k only if ρk does not depend on k, which (ii) rules out.

(iii) As n grows, G(k) tends to infinity in probability, and 1/hα(x) → 1 as x → ∞. For α < 1 the function 1/hα is bounded by 1 and the bounded convergence theorem applies; for α > 1 it is decreasing, the quantity is monotone in n for nested samples, and monotone convergence applies.

∎

For Example A the margins are 11/18 − 5/18 = 6/18, 5/18 − 2/18 = 3/18 and 2/18. Dividing by the leader's 11/18 gives 6/11, 3/11 and 2/11, exactly the harmonic weights of Section 1, as the last frame of the animation above also shows numerically. The expected shares themselves, 11/18, 5/18 and 2/18, are not harmonic: the paper's Table 3 puts them at total variation distance 0.071 from the harmonic weights, and the hand computation gives 14/198 ≈ 0.0707. The paper's Remark 5 quantifies how fast the identity breaks away from α = 1: for n = 10, ρk(1/2) falls from 0.81 at the top of the list to 0.12 at the bottom, ρk(2) rises from 1.24 to 4.66, and in both cases the normalized margins are at distance 0.12 from the harmonic weights.

The uniform split is nevertheless not a good model of real lists, and the paper gives three reasons, all in Section 4.

One concentration for every list. By Eq. (1) the effective number of candidates is (n + 1)/2, about half the list, whatever the country, party or election.

Leaders become alike as lists grow. The expected share of the second candidate relative to the leader is π2/π1 = (Hn − 1)/Hn = 1 − 1/Hn, which rises from 0.66 on a list of ten to 0.81 on a list of one hundred, while the leader's expected share Hn/n falls from 0.293 to 0.052, a factor of 5.6. Adding weak candidates at the bottom of a list should not change how the top two compare, yet here it does.

Too even. Under the uniform split, the variance of a candidate's share relative to the list average (that is, of nVi) is (n − 1)/(n + 1), below one. The lognormal distribution that Fortunato and Castellano fitted to exactly this quantity for elections in Italy, Poland and Finland has variance about 1.9. (The variance formula follows from the derivation under Eq. (1): with α = 1, E(Vi2) = 2/(n(n + 1)), so Var(nVi) = 2n/(n + 1) − 1 = (n − 1)/(n + 1); that check is ours.)

Fact · harmonic weights hide inside the uniform model (Proposition 1(i))

Under the uniform split, the harmonic weight of position k equals the expected lead of position k over position k + 1, divided by the leader's expected share. Within the symmetric Dirichlet family this holds only for α = 1.

In short: the uniform split gives expected shares (1/n)(1/k + ⋯ + 1/n), not harmonic ones, though its normalized margins are exactly harmonic (Eq. 6); it is unrealistic because it fixes Neff at (n + 1)/2, makes leaders more alike on longer lists, and divides votes more evenly than real elections do.

5 · A FIXED CONCENTRATION

Can a better choice of α fix the uniform model?

If the uniform split is too even, the obvious repair is a smaller α, which pushes mass towards the corners of the simplex. The choice of α then matters a great deal: on a list of thirty candidates the leader's expected share is 0.27, 0.19, 0.13 and 0.10 for α = 1/4, 1/2, 1 and 2. The paper shows that two defects remain for every fixed α. The first concerns the shape of the profile, measured by how fast it falls in proportional terms.

Definition 5 · elasticity

For a weight profile p with positive coordinates and pm+1 := 0, the elasticity at position k is

In words: the percentage drop from position k to k + 1, multiplied by k. A power law pk ∝ k−s has elasticity tending to s, so on doubly logarithmic axes it is a straight line of slope −s. For the harmonic weights εk = k/(k + 1) for every k < n, close to 1 except at the very top.

For Example A the harmonic elasticities are 1/2 and 2/3, and the uniform profile (11, 5, 2)/18 has ε1 = 6/11 ≈ 0.55 and ε2 = 2·3/5 = 1.2: flatter than harmonic at the top, steeper below (our computation from the definition). By Lemma 1 the elasticity of a Dirichlet profile is

For large n the k-th largest observation concentrates near the quantile xk = Qα(1 − k/(n + 1)), so the right side is approximately 1/(xkhα(xk)). Everything therefore depends on the function x hα(x).

Proposition 2 · shape of the profile

For every α > 0 the function x ↦ x hα(x) is strictly increasing on (0, ∞), with limit 0 at zero and ∞ at infinity.

In words: the approximate elasticity 1/(x h(x)) runs from ∞ at the bottom of the list (small x) down to 0 at the top (large x). Every fixed-α profile is nearly flat among the leaders and collapses among the trailing candidates.

proofWhy is x h(x) increasing for every shape α? (the paper's proof)

Since the derivative of log(1 − Fα) is −hα, and log fα(x) = (α − 1) log x − x − log Γ(α), the logarithmic derivative is

If α ≤ 1 the hazard is nonincreasing with limit 1, so hα ≥ 1 and the derivative is at least α/x > 0. If α > 1, integration by parts gives Γ(α, x) = xα−1e−x + (α − 1)Γ(α − 1, x), and Γ(α − 1, x) ≤ Γ(α, x)/x (because tα−2 ≤ tα−1/x for t ≥ x). Hence

and the derivative is again positive. The limits follow from hα(x) ~ xα−1/Γ(α) as x → 0 and hα(x) → 1 as x → ∞.

∎

The elasticity equals 1, the harmonic value, at a single point, the fraction u*α = 1 − Fα(x*) of the way down the list, where x*hα(x*) = 1. The paper reports u* = 0.14, 0.23, 1/e ≈ 0.37 and 0.52 for α = 1/4, 1/2, 1 and 2. (For α = 1 this is easy to check: h ≡ 1, so x* = 1 and u* = e−1.) Lowering α steepens the top of the profile only by moving the collapse higher up the list. On log-log axes a Dirichlet profile is concave, and it can only touch the straight harmonic line, never follow it.

The second defect concerns length. By Proposition 1(iii) and Eq. (5), E(G(1)) − E(G(k)) tends to Hk−1 as n → ∞, while E(G(1)) itself grows like log n (the maximum of n gamma variables, a standard extreme-value fact the paper cites). So the leader's share vanishes at the rate (log n)/(nα), and the ratios between the top few expected shares tend to 1: the "leaders become alike" problem of the uniform split is shared by every fixed α.

In short: for any fixed α the elasticity rises from 0 at the top to ∞ at the bottom (Proposition 2), so the profile is too flat among leaders and too steep among the rest, and the leaders' shares become equal as the list grows.

6 · THE SPARSE LIMIT

What happens if the list's total concentration, not α, stays fixed?

Both defects come from tying concentration to the individual candidate. If each new name at the bottom of a list brings its own α, the list as a whole becomes more even as it grows. The paper's remedy is to fix the total concentration θ = nα instead, so α = θ/n. By Definition 2 the effective number of candidates then tends to 1 + θ, and the paper calls this limit the sparse regime: most of the vote goes to a bounded number of candidates, however long the list.

The limiting profile has an explicit formula in terms of the exponential integral E1(x) = ∫x∞ t−1e−t dt, which decreases from +∞ at x = 0 to 0 at infinity.

Definition 6 and Proposition 3 · sparse profile

For θ > 0 define

Eq. 8

If A2 holds with α = θ/n, then for every k

Moreover the ℓk(θ) sum to 1 over k, and

with the ratio of the two sides tending to 1 as k → ∞.

In words: with the total concentration fixed, the expected shares of the leaders settle down to fixed numbers ℓ1, ℓ2, … that no longer depend on the length of the list, and far down the list they fall off geometrically, with ratio θ/(1 + θ).

The proof introduces two more classical objects, which we sketch as background before the details.

Background · Poisson processes and Poisson–DirichletA Poisson process on (0, ∞) with intensity λ(x) dx is a random scatter of points such that the number of points in any interval is Poisson distributed with mean ∫ λ(x) dx over that interval, independently for disjoint intervals. Kingman's theorem (1975), quoted in the proof, says that as n → ∞ with α = θ/n, the ordered Dirichlet shares converge to the Poisson–Dirichlet distribution with parameter θ: take the points J1 ≥ J2 ≥ ⋯ of a Poisson process with intensity (θ/x)e−x dx, which has infinitely many tiny points but a finite total S = J1 + J2 + ⋯, and divide each point by S. It is the n = ∞ version of the gamma trick, and once more S is gamma distributed (with shape θ) and independent of the normalized sequence.
proofWhere does the E1 formula come from? (the paper's proof of Eqs. 8 to 10)

The ordered shares are bounded, so convergence in distribution to Poisson–Dirichlet implies convergence of their expectations. As in Eq. (3), independence of S gives the limit E(Jk)/E(S) = E(Jk)/θ. The number of points above x is Poisson with mean ∫x∞ (θ/t)e−t dt = θE1(x). The k-th largest point lies in [x, x + dx] when one point falls there (probability (θ/x)e−x dx) and exactly k − 1 lie above, which gives the density

for Jk. Multiplying by x, integrating and dividing by θ gives Eq. (8). Summing over k inside the integral, the series Σ (θE1)k−1/(k − 1)! equals eθE1, which cancels the exponential and leaves ∫ e−x dx = 1.

For the bound (10), let Tk be a sum of k independent unit exponentials. By the same Poisson property Jk has the distribution of E1−1(Tk/θ): the k-th point from the top is reached when the Poisson count θE1(x) has accumulated k unit-exponential waiting times. The expansion E1(x) = −γ − log x + Ein(x), with Ein(x) = ∫0x t−1(1 − e−t) dt ≥ 0, from the NIST handbook, rearranges to

Each exponential X has E(e−X/θ) = 1/(1 + 1/θ) = θ/(1 + θ), so E(e−Tk/θ) = (θ/(1 + θ))k, and dividing by θ gives (10). For the asymptotic statement, the paper shows that the correction factor eEin(Jk) has expectation tending to 1 under the appropriately tilted distribution of Tk, using Jk → 0 and a uniform integrability bound.

∎

The case θ = 1 is famous in combinatorics, as the paper's Remark 6 notes: Eq. (8) and the asymptotic form of (10) were found by Shepp and Lloyd in 1966 for the cycle lengths of a uniformly random permutation. Write a random permutation of n objects as a product of cycles; the longest cycle has expected length about ℓ1(1) n, and ℓ1(1) = 0.62433… is the Golomb–Dickman constant, which the paper's appendix recovers to five decimals as a check on its numerics. The cited preprint of Mendonça and Negret extends this to the Ewens measure, which weights a permutation by θ raised to its number of cycles, and its integral formula for the longest cycle, ∫0∞ exp(−t − θE1(t)) dt, is Eq. (8) with k = 1.

The animation evaluates Eq. (8) in the page by numerical integration for four values of θ, plots the first ten ℓk against the geometric lower bound (10), and then compares the θ = 3 profile with the harmonic weights, as the paper's Table 1 does.

Animation · the sparse profile ℓk(θ), Eq. (8)
ℓk(θ)lower bound (10)harmonic 1/k

The sparse limit cures the length problem: the top shares no longer depend on n. It does not by itself give harmonic weights. Its tail is geometric, so for any fixed θ it eventually falls far below 1/k. The paper reports that for θ = 3 the sparse profile is within d = 0.010 of the harmonic weights over the top three positions, but even the best-fitting θ has distance growing from 0.007 over three positions to 0.173 over one hundred.

In short: fixing θ = nα keeps Neff near 1 + θ and makes the top expected shares converge to ℓk(θ) of Eq. (8), the Poisson–Dirichlet profile (for θ = 1, the longest cycles of a random permutation); its tail is geometric with ratio θ/(1 + θ) (Eq. 10), so no single θ is harmonic.

7 · NOT KNOWING THE CONCENTRATION

What if θ itself is unknown, even in order of magnitude?

An analyst assigning weights before an election knows how concentrated a list's vote will be no better than how it will be divided. The concentration also varies across countries, parties and elections, since electoral rules shape the incentive to cultivate a personal vote. So the paper treats θ as random, with a distribution that does not depend on the length of the list.

For a positive quantity whose order of magnitude is unknown, the classical choice (Jeffreys, 1946; Jaynes, 1968) is the scale-invariant measure dθ/θ. It gives equal mass to [1, 10], [10, 100] and [0.1, 1], and, up to a constant factor, it is the only measure on (0, ∞) that looks the same after θ is multiplied by any constant: under θ = cφ, dθ/θ = dφ/φ (standard background). Equivalently, log θ is uniform. The measure has infinite total mass, so the paper restricts it to an interval and takes limits.

Assumption A3 · random concentration

The total concentration θ has density proportional to θ−1 on [θ0, Θ], where 0 < θ0 < Θ < ∞, and A2 holds conditionally on θ with α = θ/n.

In words: first pick the list's concentration log-uniformly between θ0 and Θ, then split the vote with that concentration.

Definition 7 and Theorem 1 · random concentration

The mixture weight of position k is

(ii) for every k ≥ 2,

and in particular ∫0∞ ℓk(θ) θ−1 dθ = 1/(k − 1); (iii) the leader's mixture weight is finite and equals

Eq. 14

In words: averaged over a scale-invariant range of concentrations, the expected share of position k ≥ 2 is 1/(k − 1) times a partial sum of a series whose total is 1. Since that series has a geometric tail, the partial sum is essentially 1 after the first few positions, and the weights decay like 1/(k − 1), that is, like 1/k.

proofHow does integrating over θ produce 1/(k − 1)? (the paper's proof of Eqs. 13 and 14)

All integrands are nonnegative, so the θ integral in (11) and the x integral in (8) can be swapped. For fixed x, write y = E1(x). The θ integral for k ≥ 2 is

The factor yk−1 cancels the E1(x)k−1 of Eq. (8). Next comes the gamma–Poisson identity, valid for whole numbers: with λ = θ0y,

(It says that a gamma variable with shape k − 1 exceeds λ exactly when a rate-one Poisson process has fewer than k − 1 points in [0, λ].) The j-th term, integrated against e−x dx, is exactly ℓj+1(θ0) by Eq. (8), and the factor 1/(k − 1) comes from (k − 2)!/(k − 1)!. This gives (13). Letting θ0 → 0, every ℓj(θ0) with j ≥ 2 tends to 0 and ℓ1(θ0) to 1, so the sum tends to 1/(k − 1). For k = 1 the θ integral is ∫θ0∞ θ−1e−θy dθ = E1(θ0y), which gives (14); the paper bounds E1 to show this integral is finite.

For (i), under A3 the expected share is the log-uniform average of π(n)k(θ/n) over [θ0, Θ]. By Proposition 3 and bounded convergence, as n → ∞ it tends to (gk(θ0) − gk(Θ))/log(Θ/θ0). The normalizing logarithm cancels in the ratio, and gk(Θ) → 0 as Θ → ∞ because every gk(θ0) is finite.

∎

The mechanism has a one-line prototype, given in the paper's Remark 7: ∫01 rk−1 dr = 1/k. Averaging geometric sequences rk−1 over their ratio r produces a harmonic one. Here each fixed θ gives a profile with geometric tail ratio θ/(1 + θ), and the paper's intuition is that averaging such geometric profiles over a scale-invariant range of concentrations produces the harmonic rate. The paper places this within a general principle (citing Newman's review of power laws): mixtures of exponentially decaying terms with scale-free rates decay polynomially. The exponent comes from the prior.

Proposition 4 · power priors

For every s ∈ (0, 1) and every k,

Eq. 15

In words: a prior proportional to θ−s gives weights proportional to Γ(k − s)/Γ(k), which behaves like k−s for large k. The harmonic rate k−1 belongs specifically to the scale-invariant prior.

The leader is special. Formula (13) does not apply to k = 1, and g1 depends strongly on the lower bound: Remark 8 reports g1(θ0) = 1.17, 3.04 and 5.28 for θ0 = 1, 1/10 and 1/100, growing like log(1/θ0). The reason is that for small θ the leader takes nearly the whole vote, and dθ/θ puts infinite mass near zero. A positive lower bound is indispensable, and it fixes the leader's weight relative to everyone else. The paper's natural choice is θ0 = 1, which by Neff → 1 + θ admits all lists with at least two effective candidates. This is Example B.

For Example B, Eq. (13) is easy to evaluate from the θ = 1 sparse profile computed in the previous animation: ℓ1(1) = 0.6243, ℓ2(1) = 0.2096, so g2(1) = 0.6243, g3(1) = (0.6243 + 0.2096)/2 = 0.4170, and with g1(1) = 1.171 the ratios are 0.533 and 0.356, matching Table 1. The products k gk(1), which would be constant for an exactly harmonic profile, are 1.17, 1.25, 1.25, 1.23 and 1.20 for k = 1 to 5 and tend to 1. Fact · random concentration gives 1/k decay (Theorem 1)

If the total concentration has the scale-invariant prior on [θ0, ∞), the limiting expected share of position k ≥ 2 is proportional to (1/(k − 1)) Σj<k ℓj(θ0), which is 1/(k − 1) up to a geometrically small correction; the leader's weight is finite and set by θ0.

In short: averaging the sparse profile over θ with dθ/θ turns geometric tails into 1/k decay (Theorem 1, Eq. 13), just as ∫ rk−1 dr = 1/k; a prior θ−s would give k−s instead (Eq. 15), and the lower bound θ0 = 1 sets the leader's weight at g1 = 1.171.

8 · HOW CLOSE IS "CLOSE TO HARMONIC"?

Should an analyst just use 1/(kHn)?

Theorem 1 gives decay like 1/(k − 1) below the leader, and the harmonic weights decay like 1/k. The practical question is how much weight is misplaced if the analyst uses the simple closed form instead of the mixture. The paper answers with total variation distances after renormalizing both profiles over the top m positions (Table 2). With θ0 = 1 the distance is between 0.014 and 0.034 for every m from 2 to 100: at most about three percent of the weight is in the wrong place. The best lower bound θ0* lies between 0.77 and 1.16, and the distance rises to between 0.02 and 0.09 for θ0 = 1/2 and to between 0.04 and 0.06 for θ0 = 2.

Remark 9 describes the residual pattern: relative to the leader, the mixture puts up to 7 percent more weight than the harmonic profile on positions 2 to 5 and up to 15 percent less on distant ones, because it follows 1/(k − 1) rather than 1/k.

A single well-chosen Dirichlet parameter does not do as well, as Table 3 shows. On a list of exactly n candidates with fixed α, the best-fitting α gives distance 0.028 for n = 3, 0.092 for n = 10 and 0.217 for n = 100, and neither the best α nor the corresponding nα is stable across lengths. For n = 2 alone one parameter suffices, as π(2)1(α) = 2/3 for α ≈ 2.60. (For comparison, the uniform split with n = 2 gives the expected larger share 3/4, the mean of the larger of U and 1 − U for uniform U, against the harmonic 2/3; that example is ours.) The cause is Proposition 2: a concave log-log profile can only touch the harmonic line.

Remark 10 adds an honest caveat. Theorem 1 treats the list as the top of an unbounded pool of candidates, so its bottom positions are not squeezed by the end of the list. On a list of exactly n candidates with α log-uniform on [1/n, A], the distance from the harmonic weights depends on the upper bound A: 0.16 to 0.19 for n between 5 and 50 when A = 1, and 0.035 to 0.058 when A is between 8 and 32, that is, when the prior reaches splits much more even than the uniform one. So the approximation rests on the same premise as the harmonic scheme itself: ratios between positions should not depend on list length.

For Example A, the uniform model's own expected shares sit at distance 0.071 from the harmonic weights, as computed in Section 4, while Table 3 shows that the best fixed α for n = 3, α* = 1.81, brings this down to 0.028.

In short: with θ0 = 1 the mixture and the harmonic weights differ by 1.4 to 3.4 percent of total weight over any top 2 to 100 positions (Table 2), while no fixed parameter comes close on long lists (Table 3); the agreement requires a prior that reaches nearly even splits when a list is taken in isolation.

ASSESSMENT

What is shown, and what is claimed

Proved. Lemma 1, Propositions 1 to 4 and Theorem 1 are complete proofs built on classical results (the gamma representation of the Dirichlet distribution, Kingman's Poisson–Dirichlet limit, monotonicity of the gamma hazard, and standard bounds on E1), each cited. The mathematics is the solid part of the paper. The in-page computations reproduce the paper's Table 1 rows for θ = 3 and for θ log-uniform on [1, ∞), the Table 2 distances at θ0 = 1 to three decimals, and the values of g1 in Remark 8; our hand computation for Example A matches Table 3's entry 0.071.

Numerical, not proved. Tables 2 and 3, the best-fitting parameters, Remark 10 and the u* fractions are numerical results from one-dimensional quadrature; the appendix reports cross-checks (sums to one within 10−13, agreement with Monte Carlo within 2 × 10−4, recovery of the Golomb–Dickman constant). The statement that "no fixed value of the parameter yields similar weights" rests on these tables plus the qualitative argument from Proposition 2, not on a theorem.

Modeling choices that carry the conclusion. The harmonic rate is specific to the scale-invariant prior: Proposition 4 shows that θ−s would give k−s. The leader's weight is fixed by the lower bound θ0, chosen as 1 by the "at least two effective candidates" argument; Table 2 shows the agreement is best for θ0 near 1, so this choice is doing real work. Assumption A1 (perfect sorting) is an idealization, and the authors note that imperfect sorting would flatten the profile by position. Theorem 1 is a long-list limit, and on a single finite list the approximation needs a prior reaching nearly even splits (Remark 10). The symmetric Dirichlet family is only one exchangeable model; the two-parameter Poisson–Dirichlet family gives decay with exponent above one.

Empirical fit. The paper is theoretical. Its comparison with the empirical lognormal regularity of Fortunato and Castellano finds agreement within about 5 percent of total weight for lists of up to ten candidates but not for long lists, where the lognormal model implies a faster decline of the leaders' shares (distance growing from 0.05 to 0.19), while the uniform profile stays below 0.08. The authors argue that the lognormal regularity was established on pooled data and has been reported to fail on long lists, but no direct test of harmonic weights against list-level electoral returns is carried out. The recommendation to use harmonic weights is therefore an argument from a principled prior, supported by approximation results, rather than an empirically validated finding.

Our additions. The derivation of E(ΣVi2) and of the variance (n − 1)/(n + 1) via the gamma trick, the memoryless reading of the exponential gaps, all of Example A's hand computations (shares, margins, elasticities, distance 14/198), the n = 2 comparison, the check u* = 1/e, the explanation of the gamma–Poisson identity and of the scale invariance of dθ/θ, and the three animations are ours. The animations evaluate the paper's formulas; the simulation in the first one is our own.

Feasible Sub-Replicating Portfolios for Basket Options via the Block Rearrangement Algorithm

Mohamad Hassan Abou Daya, Carole Bernard, Steven Vanduffel · posted Nov 19, 2026 · q-fin.CP · arXiv 2611.26119

Overview

If you know exactly how each of three stocks can end up, but nothing about how they move together, the cheapest possible price of an option on their sum is pinned down by two numbers that squeeze it from both sides, and this paper makes the squeeze tight to within 0.1 percent using only two option strikes per stock. The question is a classic of model-free finance: market prices of ordinary options on each stock reveal each stock's distribution, but they say nothing about the dependence between stocks, so a basket option has a whole interval of prices consistent with the market. The top of that interval has been understood for two decades. The bottom is hard, because for three or more assets nobody knows which dependence makes the basket cheapest. The authors attack it from two directions at once. From above, a numerical method called the block rearrangement algorithm shuffles samples of the stocks into a dependence that makes the basket as cheap as it can find. From below, they build an explicit portfolio of ordinary options and cash whose payoff never exceeds the basket's payoff in any state of the world, so its price is a guaranteed lower bound. When the two numbers agree, a one-line inequality called weak duality proves both are optimal. Along the way the paper uses ideas that run all through optimization and probability: linear programming duality, couplings with fixed marginals, rearrangement inequalities, and the fact that a piecewise linear function attains its minimum at a corner. This chapter builds each of them on a three-stock example small enough to check with a pencil.

By the end you'll be able to explain
  • what a basket call is, why the market's option prices fix each stock's distribution but not their dependence, and how that turns pricing into an optimization over couplings (problem (1));
  • what a sub-replicating portfolio is, why its price is a lower bound for every dependence at once, and how matching it with an upper bound certifies optimality (weak duality, Corollary 2.6);
  • why, for two assets, pairing large values of one with small values of the other gives the cheapest basket, and why nothing so simple exists for three;
  • how the rearrangement algorithm searches for a cheap dependence one column at a time, and why each step can only lower the price (Remark 2.9);
  • how the paper reads option strikes off the functions φi of Eqs. (2) to (4) by pairing each asset with the sum of the others (Eq. 5);
  • why the cash part of the portfolio can be computed exactly by checking finitely many corner points (Proposition 2.3, Eq. 8);
  • the three cases with closed-form answers: deep in the money, one dominant asset, and jointly mixable marginals (Propositions 3.1, 3.2, 3.4);
  • how the bounds are transferred from discretized samples back to the true distributions (Proposition 2.11, Corollary 2.12), and what the log-normal examples show (Tables 2 to 6).
