Running examples
  • Example A: three toy stocks, four scenarios each. Stocks 1 and 2 each end at 1, 2, 3 or 4, each value with probability 1/4. Stock 3 is a long shot: it ends at 0, 1, 2 or 13, again with probability 1/4 each. The basket call has strike K = 10, above the basket's mean mX = 2.5 + 2.5 + 4 = 9. The example is ours, built so that every step of the paper's construction can be done by hand; the page recomputes everything in it.
  • Example B: the paper's three log-normal stocks. Three stocks start at 100, have volatilities 35.5%, 20% and 25%, mature in half a year, and enter the basket with weight 1/3 each, so the basket's forward value is 100. The paper's Table 2 reports the lower bound of the basket call at strikes from 100 to 120, and the page reprices the paper's tabulated portfolios from scratch.
1 · BASKET OPTIONS AND MISSING DEPENDENCE

What can market prices say about an option on a sum of stocks?

A European call option on a stock gives its holder the right to buy the stock at a fixed price k, the strike, on a fixed date T. If the stock ends at X, the holder buys only when X > k, and gains X − k, so the payoff is (X − k)+. A put pays (k − X)+. A basket call pays the same kind of amount on a sum of stocks: with prices X1, …, Xn at time T (already multiplied by their weights in the basket) and basket strike K, its payoff is

Pricing theory says that, in a market without arbitrage, there is a probability measure ℚ, the risk-neutral measure, under which the price of any payoff is its expected value (after discounting, which disappears because the paper assumes zero interest rates). So the price of a call on stock i at strike k is a function of k alone.

Definition · call price function

In words: the market price of a call on stock i, viewed as a curve in the strike. The paper assumes that the full curve is known, a continuum of strikes, which is the idealization of a liquid options market.

The curve determines the whole distribution of Xi. The paper's standing assumption records the first step of that fact.

Assumption 2.1 · marginals with densities

Each Xi has a density on (0, ∞) with full support and finite mean. Then CXi is strictly positive, strictly decreasing, strictly convex and continuously differentiable, with

In words: raising the strike by a small amount h lowers the payoff by h exactly in the states where the option is in the money, so the slope of the price curve is minus the probability of finishing above the strike.

Differentiating once more gives the density of Xi as the second derivative of the call price curve, a classical observation known as the Breeden–Litzenberger formula. That second step is our addition; the paper only needs the first derivative. Either way, the vanilla market fixes each marginal law. What it does not fix is the joint law of (X1, …, Xn), and the basket price depends on it. Any joint law with the right marginals, a coupling, gives a price consistent with every quoted option. The lowest of them is the subject of the paper.

Problem (1) · the primal problem

where Π is the set of probability measures on ℝ3+ whose marginals reproduce every call price, ∫(xi − ki)+ dμ = CXi(ki) for all ki ≥ 0 and each i. In words: among all ways the three stocks could depend on each other that the market cannot rule out, find the one that makes the basket call cheapest. The paper writes the problem for n = 3 for ease of exposition and notes that it extends to any n (Remark 2.8).

The paper calls (1) a multi-marginal optimal transport problem: the unknown is a joint law with prescribed marginals, and the cost is the basket payoff. The highest price, the matching supremum, is described in the introduction as well understood, with super-replicating portfolios known since the work of Hobson, Laurence and Wang. The infimum is not, and the introduction lists two reasons: earlier methods use finitely many option prices rather than whole marginals, and the dependence that attains the infimum is unknown in closed form for more than two assets.

For Example A the call price functions can be read off directly. For stock 1,

linear in between. For stock 3 the price falls from CX3(0) = 4 to CX3(2) = 11/4 and then, since only the value 13 lies above, along a straight line of slope −1/4, so CX3(6) = 7/4 and CX3(8) = 5/4. Each slope is minus the probability of finishing above the strike, as Assumption 2.1 says (for discrete stocks the slope jumps at each possible value, which is why the paper later works with one-sided derivatives). The three marginals are fixed, but the basket price is not: if the stocks move together, pairing 1 with 1 with 0, 2 with 2 with 1, and so on, the basket sums are 2, 5, 8 and 21, and the basket call is worth (0 + 0 + 0 + 11)/4 = 11/4. If they are independent, averaging over all 64 combinations gives 2. Section 3 shows that the cheapest coupling gives 5/4.

In short: vanilla option prices fix each stock's distribution through the call price curve (Assumption 2.1) but leave the dependence free, so the lowest arbitrage-free basket price is an optimization over couplings (problem 1); in Example A that price can be anywhere from 5/4 up to 11/4.

2 · PORTFOLIOS THAT NEVER PAY TOO MUCH

How can one number be a lower bound for every possible dependence at once?

Problem (1) minimizes over an enormous set. The way to bound a minimum from below without searching that set is to find something that is cheaper than the basket in every single state of the world. Hold a stock, some calls on single stocks and some cash. If the portfolio's payoff never exceeds the basket's payoff, whatever the three prices turn out to be, then its price is below the basket's price under any coupling. And because each piece of the portfolio depends on only one stock, its price depends only on the marginals, which are known.

Written as an optimization, this is the linear programming dual of (1). It maximizes the price of a static position, cash λ plus calls with strike profile νi, over all such positions that stay below the basket payoff pointwise:

The νi are signed measures: a point mass +1 at strike k means one long call at k, −1 a short call. The portfolios the paper builds are all of the following form.

Definition · sub-replicating portfolio (Theorem 2.4)

A portfolio f1(x1) + f2(x2) + f3(x3) + λ̄ sub-replicates the basket call if

In words: whatever the three prices are at maturity, the portfolio pays at most what the basket pays. Each fi is a payoff on stock i alone, and λ̄ is cash.

Any continuous piecewise linear payoff with finitely many kinks can be bought with stock and calls: start with the right slope at zero, and at each kink add (x − k)+ times the change of slope there. The payoff min(x, 2), for example, is x − (x − 2)+: one share of stock and one short call at 2. This is the background fact behind the paper's remark that every continuous piecewise linear function of xi with finitely many kinks is a static call position.

Fact · weak duality (proof of Corollary 2.6)

If (6) holds, then for every coupling μ ∈ Π,

for any particular coupling μ̂ ∈ Π. If HV = BV, then μ̂ attains the infimum and the portfolio is an optimal sub-replicating portfolio.

proofWhy are both inequalities true, and why does equality certify optimality?

Fix any μ ∈ Π. Taking μ-expectations of both sides of (6) preserves the inequality. The left side's expectation is Σ Eμ[fi(Xi)] + λ̄, and since each fi depends on Xi alone and every μ ∈ Π has the same marginals, this is the same number HV for every μ. So HV ≤ Eμ[(ΣXi − K)+] for all μ, and hence HV is at most the infimum. The second inequality holds because μ̂ is one of the couplings over which the infimum is taken. If HV = BV, the infimum is squeezed between two equal numbers, so it equals both: μ̂ attains it, and no sub-replicating portfolio can be worth more than this one, since by the first inequality every such portfolio is worth at most the infimum.

∎

The paper stresses that only this weak form of duality is used anywhere in its proofs. A deeper theorem of Kellerer (1984), cited in Section 2, says the gap closes in general: the best dual value over integrable functions of single assets equals the infimum. The paper does not claim the same for the restricted class of call positions, and it does not need to.

For Example A, take the portfolio

It is sub-replicating: if x3 ≤ 6, it is at most 2 + 2 + 0 − 4 = 0, which is at most the basket payoff; if x3 > 6, it is min(x1, 2) + min(x2, 2) + x3 − 10, which is at most x1 + x2 + x3 − 10, and so again at most the basket payoff. Its price uses only the marginals. Since min(X1, 2) takes the values 1, 2, 2, 2, its expectation is 7/4, the same for stock 2, and E[(X3 − 6)+] = 7/4 because only the value 13 exceeds 6. So

No coupling of the three toy stocks can price the basket below 5/4. Section 3 exhibits one that prices it at exactly 5/4, which by weak duality makes both optimal. Sections 5 and 6 show that this portfolio is exactly what the paper's construction produces.

In short: a portfolio of single-stock options and cash that never pays more than the basket (Eq. 6) has a price that depends only on the marginals and bounds the basket price below for every coupling; matching it with the basket price under one coupling proves both optimal (Corollary 2.6). In Example A the portfolio min(x1, 2) + min(x2, 2) + (x3 − 6)+ − 4 is worth 5/4.

3 · DEPENDENCE AS A MATRIX

Which coupling makes a sum as cheap as possible?

To search for the cheapest coupling, it helps to see couplings concretely. If every marginal is discretized into N equally likely values, a coupling can be stored as an N × n matrix: column i lists the N values of stock i, each row is one equally likely scenario, and the basket in that scenario is the row sum. Reordering the entries within a column changes the dependence but not the marginal, so searching over couplings means searching over permutations of each column. The basket value is the average of (row sum − K)+. This is the representation the rearrangement algorithms use (Section 2.2 of the paper), with N = 50,000 rows in the numerical examples.

The basket payoff is a convex function of the sum. Convex functions punish spread: by Jensen's inequality, E[(S − K)+] ≥ (E[S] − K)+, and the less the sum S varies, the closer the price gets to that floor. So the cheapest coupling should make the row sums as equal as possible, pairing large values of one stock with small values of the others. For two assets this intuition is exactly right.

Fact · two assets (Tchen 1980, Rüschendorf 1983, as cited in Remark 2.9)

For two random variables U and V with fixed marginals, the antimonotone coupling, which pairs the k-th largest value of U with the k-th smallest of V, minimizes E[φ(U + V)] over all couplings, for every convex function φ.

proof sketchWhy does pairing large with small help every convex function? (our argument)

This exchange argument is ours, for the discrete matrix picture; the paper cites the result. Take two rows with u1 < u2 and v1 < v2, paired in the same order, so the row sums are s = u1 + v1 and t = u2 + v2. Swapping v1 and v2 gives sums p = u1 + v2 and q = u2 + v1. Both new sums lie between s and t, and p + q = s + t. A convex φ lies below its chord on [s, t], and writing p = (1 − w)s + wt, q = ws + (1 − w)t for some w in [0, 1] gives

So every swap that undoes a same-order pair can only lower Σ φ(row sum), and repeating swaps ends at the antimonotone arrangement.

∎

Hobson, Laurence and Wang used this antimonotone structure, the lower Fréchet copula, to build optimal sub-replicating portfolios for two-asset baskets in 2005. With three or more assets the idea breaks down: no arrangement can make every column antimonotone to every other one, and the formula that would describe such an arrangement, the lower Fréchet bound max(u1 + ⋯ + un − n + 1, 0), is not a valid copula for n ≥ 3 (the paper cites Nelsen, Section 2.10). The paper adds that the sum has no minimum in convex order in general for n ≥ 3 (Bernard, Jiang and Wang 2014): the coupling that is cheapest at one strike K need not be cheapest at another, and none is known in closed form.

The extreme favorable case has its own name. The marginals are jointly mixable if some coupling makes the sum constant. Then, by Jensen's inequality, nothing can beat it, and the basket's lowest price is just (mX − K)+ (Proposition 3.4, Section 7). Three columns each containing 1, 2, 3 are jointly mixable, for instance: the rows (1, 2, 3), (2, 3, 1), (3, 1, 2) all sum to 6.

Example A is not mixable, since 13 cannot be balanced by values of at most 4. With N = 4 rows there are 4! × 4! = 576 ways to arrange columns 2 and 3 against a fixed column 1, and the page checks all of them (that brute force is ours, possible only because the example is tiny). The minimum basket value is 5/4, attained for instance by the rows

Stocks 1 and 2 move together here, and stock 3 moves against their sum. All the "excess" is concentrated in a single scenario: the long shot pays off while the other two are at their lowest.

In short: a coupling of discretized marginals is a matrix whose columns can be permuted; convexity of the payoff rewards equal row sums, and for two assets the antimonotone pairing is optimal for every strike, but for three or more no such universal arrangement exists. In Example A the cheapest of all 576 arrangements is worth 5/4.

4 · THE REARRANGEMENT ALGORITHM

How do you search for a cheap coupling when N is 50,000?

Brute force is hopeless beyond toy sizes: with N rows and n columns there are (N!)n−1 arrangements. The rearrangement algorithm (RA) of Puccetti and Rüschendorf (2012) uses the two-asset fact as a local move. Pick one column, call it U, and let V be the sum of all the other columns, row by row. Rearrange column U to be antimonotone to V: the largest entry of U goes to the row where V is smallest, and so on. By the two-asset fact, this step cannot increase E[φ(U + V)] for any convex φ, and U + V is the full row sum. Cycle through the columns until nothing changes.

Remark 2.9 · every step is a descent step

Each rearrangement step replaces the coupling of two block sums U and V by their antimonotone coupling, which minimizes E[φ(U + V)] over couplings of U and V for every convex φ. Each step is therefore non-increasing in E[φ(ΣXi)] for every convex φ, whichever objective is used to monitor convergence.

In words: one rearrangement move never makes any convex function of the basket larger, so it never raises the basket call price at any strike at all.

The block rearrangement algorithm (BRA) of Bernard and McLeish and of Boudt, Jakobsons and Vanduffel, which the paper uses, generalizes the move: the columns are split into two blocks, chosen at random, and the coupling of the two block sums U and V is replaced by their antimonotone coupling (Remark 2.9). By default it monitors the variance of the row sums, as a proxy. Because the true target is E[(ΣXi − K)+], and for n ≥ 3 the two objectives need not have the same minimizer, the authors also run it with this "K-aware" objective. Both RA and BRA are heuristics and can stall in a local minimum, so the paper runs them many times from random starting arrangements and keeps the output whose hedging portfolio is worth the most (Section 2.2; the tables use 64 restarts for the three-asset example and 20 for the six-asset one).

The animation runs the plain RA on Example A, starting from the comonotone arrangement in which all three stocks move together (basket value 11/4). At each step it shows the column being rearranged, the sums of the other columns that decide the new order, and the basket value. Starting from any of the 576 arrangements, RA reaches 5/4 on this example (the page checks this); the paper's warning about local minima concerns realistic sizes.

Animation · rearrangement algorithm on Example A
column being rearrangedsum of other columnsrow pays (sum > K)

After the first sweep stocks 1 and 2 are sorted the same way and stock 3 is sorted against their sum. That is the coupling Section 3 found by brute force, up to the order of the rows. The algorithm gives an upper bound BV for the infimum, because its output is a genuine coupling of the discretized marginals. Whether that upper bound is the infimum is a separate question, which the next three sections answer from the other side.

In short: the rearrangement algorithm makes one column (or block) antimonotone to the sum of the rest, a move that can never raise the price of any convex payoff of the basket (Remark 2.9); it is a fast heuristic for the cheapest coupling, and on Example A it reaches the true minimum 5/4 in one sweep.

5 · STRIKES FROM TWO-ASSET PROBLEMS

Where should the options in the lower-bound portfolio be struck?

Weak duality turns any sub-replicating portfolio into a lower bound, but a bad portfolio gives a bad bound. The paper's central idea is how to choose strikes. For each asset i, lump all the other assets into one aggregate,

computed under the coupling μ̂ from the rearrangement algorithm. The basket is Xi + Yi, a basket of two assets, and for two assets Hobson, Laurence and Wang (2005a) know the optimal sub-replicating portfolio. Its strikes on Xi are where a certain function changes sign. Define, for each i,

Here CYi is the call price function of Yi under μ̂, which is piecewise linear because μ̂ lives on a finite sample (Remark 2.2), so the paper takes the right derivative for Xi and the left derivative for Yi. Using the slope formula of Assumption 2.1, the appendix rewrites this as

In words: φi(x) compares the probability that stock i finishes at or below x with the probability that the rest of the basket finishes high enough to bring the total to K. Let Ai = {x : φi(x) > 0}. It is a union of intervals, all inside [0, K), because for x ≥ K the second probability is 1. Its boundary points, in increasing order, are the strikes Ki1 < Ki2 < ⋯ < Ki2ni, with the convention Ki1 = 0 when Ai starts at 0. The payoff held on stock i is then

Definition · the asset leg fi

Equation (5) describes one share of stock i, a short call at each odd-numbered strike and a long call at each even-numbered strike. In words: fi rises with slope 1, goes flat across each interval of Ai, and rises with slope 1 again after it. So fi(0) = 0, 0 ≤ fi(z) ≤ z, and beyond the last strike fi(z) = z − Li, where Li is the total length of Ai.

The intuition behind the flat stretches, which is our gloss rather than the paper's wording, is that on Ai stock i is more likely to be low than the rest of the basket is to make up the difference, so a dollar of exposure to stock i there would cost more than it can be guaranteed to deliver. From each two-asset portfolio the paper keeps only the leg on Xi; the legs on the aggregates Yi, which are not traded, are discarded, and a single cash amount λ̄ (Section 6) restores pointwise feasibility. One practical adjustment comes from Algorithm 1, line 16: if the last strike lies above the largest sample value of Xi, it is moved to K, where the long call is worthless on the sample.

Two remarks in the paper temper this. For a discrete Yi, as here, optimality of the two-asset triplet is not asserted; and even with the exact optimal coupling the inherited strikes are not guaranteed to be optimal for the three-asset problem (Remark 2.5, Section 4). The paper therefore follows the construction with a derivative-free local search over the strike values (Nelder–Mead alternated with Powell's method), keeping the number of strikes and their pattern fixed. Every candidate it visits is a valid sub-replicator, so the search can only raise a valid lower bound.

For Example A, use the coupling from the rearrangement algorithm, rows (4, 4, 0), (3, 3, 1), (2, 2, 2), (1, 1, 13). For stock 1 the aggregate Y1 = X2 + X3 takes the values 4, 4, 4, 14. By Eq. (15), on [2, 3) one gets φ1 = 1/2 − 1/4 = 1/4 (half the values of X1 are at most 2, and only Y1 = 14 reaches 10 − x), on [3, 4) φ1 = 1/2, and on [4, 6) φ1 = 3/4; from x = 6 on, every value of Y1 reaches 10 − x and φ1 = 0, while on [0, 2) it is −1/4 or 0. So A1 = [2, 6), with strikes 2 and 6. The strike 6 exceeds the largest value of X1, so line 16 moves it to 10, and

For stock 3, Y3 = X1 + X2 takes the values 8, 6, 4, 2, and φ3 equals 1/4, 1/2, 1/2, 1/4 on [0, 1), [1, 2), [2, 4), [4, 6), then 0 on [6, 8) and −1/4 after. So A3 = [0, 6), K31 = 0 and K32 = 6, and f3(z) = z + (z − 6)+ − z = (z − 6)+, a single call. These are the legs of the portfolio of Section 2; the call at 10 on stocks 1 and 2 is worthless and changes nothing.

In short: pairing each asset with the sum of the others gives n two-asset problems whose solutions place strikes at the boundary points of {φi > 0} (Eqs. 2 to 4 and 15); the resulting leg fi alternates slopes 1 and 0 (Eq. 5). In Example A this produces min(z, 2) on stocks 1 and 2 and a call at 6 on stock 3.

6 · THE CASH COMPONENT, EXACTLY

How much cash must be subtracted so the portfolio never overpays?

The legs fi come from separate two-asset problems, so their sum may exceed the basket payoff somewhere. The fix is to subtract the largest overshoot. Define

and set the cash to its smallest value,

Then (6) holds by definition, whatever strikes were used. The infimum is finite: where the basket is below K, Ψ ≥ −Σfi(xi) ≥ −Σxi ≥ −K, and where it is above, Ψ = Σ(xi − fi(xi)) − K ≥ −K. A simulation-based estimate of this infimum would carry sampling error into the bound, and the paper instead computes it exactly.

Proposition 2.3 · exact computation of λ̄

Let each asset's strikes be ordered, so fi has slopes in {0, 1}, and let 𝓑i := {0} ∪ {Ki1, …, Ki2ni} ∪ {K}. Then

In words: to find the worst overshoot over a continuum of price combinations, it is enough to try every combination in which each stock sits at one of its own strikes, at 0, or at K.

proofWhy is checking a finite grid enough?

Cut ℝn+ by the hyperplanes {xi = b} for every breakpoint b of every fi (and b = 0), together with the hyperplane {Σxi = K}. These cut the orthant into finitely many closed polyhedral cells, and Ψ is affine on each cell, because each fi is affine between its breakpoints and the basket payoff is affine on each side of {Σxi = K}. Each cell lies in the orthant, so it contains no full line, and Ψ ≥ −K on it. By the fundamental theorem of linear programming, an affine function bounded below on such a polyhedron attains its minimum at a vertex. So λ̄ is the minimum of Ψ over all cell vertices.

A vertex is the intersection of n independent hyperplanes from the family. If all of them have the form {xi = b}, each coordinate is a breakpoint, and the vertex is in 𝓑1 × ⋯ × 𝓑n. Otherwise one of them is {Σxi = K} and the others fix n − 1 coordinates, leaving one coordinate vm = K − Σi≠m vi in [0, K]. If vm is not a breakpoint, slide it. If fm has slope 1 there, moving vm up to the next element b of 𝓑m (which exists, because K ∈ 𝓑m) raises the basket payoff and fm by the same amount, so Ψ does not change. If fm has slope 0, moving vm down to the previous element (which exists, because 0 ∈ 𝓑m) keeps the payoff at 0 and fm constant, so again Ψ does not change. Either way the slid point lies in the grid and has the same value. Hence the grid minimum is at most λ̄, and it is at least λ̄ because the grid is part of the orthant.

∎

The proof also explains why 0 and K are added to the grid: they are the stopping points of the slide. The paper notes that the ordering assumption can be dropped, with the same sliding argument showing Ψ(v′) ≤ Ψ(v). The grid has at most ∏(2ni + 2) points. With one pair of strikes per asset that is 4n: 64 for three assets, 4,096 for six, and, the paper reports, 49 = 262,144 for nine assets, still under a second. Every row of the paper's tables has one pair of strikes per asset.

Theorem 2.4 · feasible sub-replicating portfolio

Under Assumption 2.1, with f1, f2, f3 from Eq. (5) and λ̄ from Eq. (7), the portfolio Πsub = f1(x1) + f2(x2) + f3(x3) + λ̄ sub-replicates the basket call on ℝ3+, and its expected cost under any μ ∈ Π is Σ Eμ[fi(Xi)] + λ̄, which depends only on the marginals.

In words: whatever coupling the strikes came from, even a poor one, the result is a valid lower bound. The coupling affects only how good the bound is.

For Example A, 𝓑1 = 𝓑2 = {0, 2, 10} and 𝓑3 = {0, 6, 10}, a grid of 27 points. At (2, 2, 6), for instance, the basket sum is exactly 10, the payoff is 0, and the legs pay 2 + 2 + 0, so Ψ = −4. Checking all 27 points gives λ̄ = −4, attained at six of them (ties of this kind are common; the paper mentions several tied vertices in its own optimal portfolios). This matches Proposition 3.2 below, which predicts λ̄ = −(2 + 2). The hedging value is HV = 7/4 + 7/4 + 7/4 − 4 = 5/4, equal to the basket value of the coupling from Section 4. By Corollary 2.6, both are optimal.

The animation builds this certificate step by step, computing φi from the rearranged matrix, reading off the strikes, scanning all 27 grid points for λ̄, and finally comparing the portfolio with the basket scenario by scenario.

Animation · building the lower-bound portfolio for Example A
φ > 0, flat legportfoliobasket payoff

In the final frame the portfolio equals the basket payoff in every row of the optimal coupling. That is no accident: the portfolio is never above the payoff, and the two have the same average, so they must agree wherever the optimal coupling puts mass.

In short: the cash component is the minimum of a piecewise linear function, which is attained on the finite grid of breakpoints plus 0 and K (Proposition 2.3, Eq. 8), so it is computed exactly with 4n evaluations for one strike pair per asset; in Example A it is −4, giving HV = 5/4 = BV and a certificate of optimality.

7 · THREE CASES WITH CLOSED FORMS

When can the lower bound be written down without any search?

Section 4 of the paper explains why the construction cannot be proved optimal in general: the strikes are inherited from two-asset problems that need not match the n-asset dual, and the optimal coupling has no closed form, so the rearrangement algorithm might miss it. Section 3 of the paper identifies three regimes in which one or both obstructions disappear and the answer is explicit.

Case 1: deep in the money. The simplest sub-replicating portfolio is the linear one, x1 + x2 + x3 − K, because a ≤ a+. It is worth mX − K.

Proposition 3.1 · no active strikes

If Ai = ∅ for at least one i (computed from any coupling in Π), then the linear portfolio Π1sub = x1 + x2 + x3 − K is optimal, and the lower bound equals mX − K. The proposition also holds for discrete marginals.

In words: if some stock's φi is never positive, the stocks can be arranged so that the basket always finishes at or above K, and then the call is just a forward contract.

proof sketchHow does an empty Ai produce a coupling with basket always at least K?

The appendix argues in two steps. First, Ai = ∅ means Fi(x) ≤ ℚ(Yi ≥ K − x) for all x ≥ 0 by Eq. (15). Pair Xi = Fi−1(U) antimonotonically with Y′ = G−1(1 − U), where G is the distribution function of Yi and U is uniform. If some u gave Fi−1(u) + G−1(1 − u) < K, a chain of inequalities forces G to be constant on a non-degenerate interval at level 1 − u; a monotone function has only countably many such flat levels, so this happens for countably many u, a set of probability zero. Second, the other assets are kept with their joint law, and Xi is attached to their sum through the distributional transform, so the sum Xi + Yi is at least K almost surely while all marginals are preserved. Under that coupling the call pays exactly ΣXi − K, worth mX − K, which matches the linear portfolio.

∎

In the paper's log-normal examples this regime covers all strikes below 99.89 (three assets) and below 99.66 (six assets), just under the basket forward of 100. In Example A it does not apply: mX − K = −1 < 0, and both A1 and A3 are non-empty.

Case 2: one dominant asset. Suppose stock 3 is spread so widely that it dominates the others. Consider the coupling μc in which stocks 1 and 2 move together (comonotone) and stock 3 moves against their sum. Along it the basket is a function of one uniform variable u,

large near u = 0, where the dominant stock is large. For a1, a2, c ≥ 0 with a1 + a2 + c = K, the paper proposes the vanilla portfolio

long the two small stocks capped by short calls, long a call on the dominant stock, and short cash a1 + a2.

Proposition 3.2 · one dominant asset

(i) For every such a1, a2, c, the portfolio (12) is sub-replicating, −(a1 + a2) is its exact cash component, and its cost is CX3(c) − PX1(a1) − PX2(a2), so

(ii) If Sc(u*) = K, the choice ai = FXi−1(u*), c = FX3−1(1 − u*) has a1 + a2 + c = K and cost ∫0u* (Sc(u) − K) du.

(iii) If moreover Sc ≥ K on (0, u*] and Sc ≤ K on [u*, 1), a single crossing from above, then μc is optimal and the portfolio of (ii) is an optimal sub-replicating portfolio.

In words: when the basket along μc drops through K exactly once, the cheapest coupling is "small stocks together, big stock against them", and the matching hedge is two capped positions plus one call, struck where the crossing happens.

proofWhy is portfolio (12) never above the basket payoff?

Write d1 = x1 − a1, d2 = x2 − a2, d3 = x3 − c. Since a1 + a2 + c = K, the basket payoff is (d1 + d2 + d3)+ and the portfolio is min(d1, 0) + min(d2, 0) + max(d3, 0). If d3 ≤ 0 the portfolio is at most 0, which is at most the payoff. If d3 > 0 it is min(d1, 0) + min(d2, 0) + d3 ≤ d1 + d2 + d3, again at most the payoff. At (a1, a2, c) both vanish, so the cash −(a1 + a2) cannot be raised. The cost follows from E[min(Xi, ai)] = ai − PXi(ai). For (iii), under μc the event u ≤ u* has X1 ≤ a1, X2 ≤ a2, X3 ≥ c, where the portfolio equals Sc − K = (Sc − K)+; the event u ≥ u* has the reverse inequalities, where both are 0. So portfolio and payoff agree μc-almost surely, their prices agree, and weak duality finishes the argument.

∎

Example A is a case of this kind. Along μc, ordered from the top of stock 3 down, the basket takes the values 1 + 1 + 13 = 15, then 2 + 2 + 2 = 6, 3 + 3 + 1 = 7 and 4 + 4 + 0 = 8: one crossing of K = 10, from above. With a1 = a2 = 2 and c = 6, the bound (13) is CX3(6) − PX1(2) − PX2(2) = 7/4 − 1/4 − 1/4 = 5/4, which is V(μc) = (15 − 10)/4. The general construction of Sections 5 and 6 and the closed form of Case 2 land on the same portfolio, as the paper's identification of (12) with strikes K11 = a1, K31 = 0, K32 = c says they should. (Proposition 3.2 is stated for continuous marginals; applying the same choice to our discrete example is our step, and Corollary 2.6 confirms it.)

The paper adds that the single-crossing condition is a condition on the marginals alone, and that it requires the two dominated stocks to be bounded. For log-normal marginals, which are unbounded, it holds only up to the small mass near u = 1 where Sc rises above K again, so the certificate in Table 4 refers to the discretized problem. When Sc crosses K twice, μc is no longer optimal in general, yet the bound (13) can still be attained by some other coupling, and Table 4 shows an instance. Remark 3.3 explains why the earlier route through the two-asset problem on (X1 + X2, X3) does not give a vanilla hedge: it needs calls on the sub-basket X1 + X2, and replacing them with calls on the single stocks destroys pointwise sub-replication.

Case 3: jointly mixable marginals. If some coupling makes X1 + X2 + X3 constant, the constant must be mX.

Proposition 3.4 · joint mixability

The optimal portfolio is the linear one when K ≤ mX and the zero portfolio when K > mX. In words: if the stocks can perfectly offset each other, the cheapest basket call is the one on a sum that never moves.

The proof is Jensen's inequality for the convex function z ↦ (z − K)+, with equality under the mixing coupling. The appendix also notes a numerical subtlety: in this regime the φi carry no information (the basket is almost constant, so they are dominated by noise), which is why Algorithm 1 first tries the two portfolios without strikes, the linear one and Σ(xi − K)+, and returns one of them if it already matches BV (Remark 2.10).

In short: the lower bound is explicit when the basket can be kept above K (Case 1, linear portfolio), when one asset dominates and the basket along "small together, big against" crosses K once (Case 2, Eqs. 11 to 13), or when the sum can be made constant (Case 3, Jensen). Example A falls in Case 2.

8 · FROM SAMPLES BACK TO REAL DISTRIBUTIONS

Do bounds computed on 50,000 sample points say anything about the true log-normal stocks?

The rearrangement algorithms only work on discretized marginals: each log-normal law is replaced by N = 50,000 equally likely atoms at its mid-point quantiles. The certificate HV = BV of Corollary 2.6 is then a statement about that discrete problem (Remark 2.7). The paper reports that discretization alone moves the values by more than the final precision, by about 11% of the option value at K = 120 in the three-asset example, so the authors carry both bounds back to the original laws.

Lower bound. The portfolio sub-replicates on all of ℝn+, not just on the sample, so its price under the true marginals is a valid lower bound for problem (1):

For log-normal stocks every call price here comes from the Black formula. The paper does not just evaluate this at the sample-refined strikes; it maximizes it again over the strikes, and it releases long calls that had been parked at K because they were worthless on the sample.

Background · the Black formulaIn the paper's model Si,T = Si,0 exp(σiWi,T − σi2T/2) with Wi a Brownian motion, so log Si,T is normal and E[Si,T] = Si,0. For a log-normal X with mean F and log-volatility σ√T, a direct integration against the normal density gives the standard formula C(k) = F Φ(d1) − k Φ(d2), with d1 = [ln(F/k) + σ2T/2]/(σ√T) and d2 = d1 − σ√T, where Φ is the standard normal distribution function. For the weighted stock xi = Si/3 in Example B, F = 100/3. This formula is textbook background, not a result of the paper.

Upper bound. The rearranged sample is a coupling of the discretized marginals, not of the true ones, so BV is not yet an upper bound for (1). It becomes one after each atom is spread back over the slice of the true distribution it stands for.

Proposition 2.11 · reassembly with the original marginals

Let the rearranged rows be (x1(π1(m)), …, xn(πn(m))), m = 1, …, N, where πi are permutations. Let M be uniform on {1, …, N} and T uniform on (0, 1), independent, choose an orientation for each row and asset, put Ti = T or 1 − T accordingly, and set

Then (X̃1, …, X̃n) has exactly the original marginals, so

In words: each atom of each stock is replaced by the whole slab of the true distribution between two consecutive quantile levels, and within a row all n slabs are traversed together by one uniform variable, forwards or backwards.

proofWhy does the reassembled vector have the right marginals?

Fix i. Given M = m, Ti is uniform on (0, 1) whichever orientation was chosen, so Ui = (πi(M) − 1 + Ti)/N is uniform on the interval ((πi(m) − 1)/N, πi(m)/N). Since πi is a permutation and M is uniform, each of the N intervals is chosen with probability 1/N, and together they tile (0, 1). So Ui is uniform on (0, 1), and Fi−1(Ui) has the law of Xi, the standard inverse-transform fact. Equation (10) is the basket value under this coupling, written row by row.

∎

Each row integral is one-dimensional, so BVex is computed by quadrature rather than simulation (Gauss–Legendre, with adaptive quadrature on the at most 2n rows containing the lowest or highest slab of some asset, where the quantile function or its derivative is unbounded), and the orientation pattern can be chosen per row to make the integral smallest. This construction is the one-dimensional case of the reassembly of Neufeld and Xiang (2022).

Fact · the bracket (Corollary 2.12)

For any strikes, any rearranged sample and any orientations,

The width BVex − HVex bounds at once the errors from discretization, from a possibly suboptimal rearrangement and from possibly suboptimal strikes. Its relative size is ε := (BVex − HVex)/BVex (Eq. 14).

The animation reprices the paper's tabulated three-asset portfolios (Table 2) from scratch: Black-formula prices for each leg, the exact cash component by enumerating the 64 grid points of Proposition 2.3, and the resulting HVex, compared with the paper's bracket. The computation is ours; the strikes and the bracket are the paper's.

stock 1 legstock 2 legstock 3 leg

The repricing recovers the tabulated cash components to all four decimals and the lower bounds 0.10218, 0.01810, 0.00404 and 0.00102 at K = 100 to 115. At K = 120 the strikes as printed give about 0.00018 rather than 0.00028; the paper warns that its strikes are rounded to four decimals, that several tied vertices determine the cash of an optimal portfolio, and that rebuilding from the rounded strikes can lower the value by up to 10−4, which is the size of this gap.

In short: pricing the portfolio under the true marginals gives a valid lower bound HVex, spreading each rearranged atom back over its quantile slab gives a valid upper bound BVex computed by quadrature (Eqs. 9 and 10), and the two bracket the true answer for the original problem (Corollary 2.12).

ASSESSMENT

What is shown, and what is claimed

Proved. Every portfolio the method outputs sub-replicates the basket call on all of ℝn+, for any strikes and any coupling used to pick them (Theorem 2.4, Corollary 2.6). The cash component is computed exactly by a finite enumeration (Proposition 2.3). The reassembled coupling has the original marginals (Proposition 2.11), so HVex and BVex are genuine lower and upper bounds for the original problem (Corollary 2.12). The three closed-form regimes are proved in the appendix (Propositions 3.1, 3.2, 3.4). All of these proofs rest on weak duality and elementary arguments, and they are short enough to check line by line.

Shown numerically. The tightness of the bracket, at most 0.1% (three assets) and 0.02% (six assets) of the bound, is an outcome observed in the paper's log-normal examples, not a guarantee. The bracket itself is rigorous up to the accuracy of the quadrature for BVex, which the authors check by quadrupling the nodes (a change below 10−10). The page's repricing of Table 2 matches the reported lower bounds at four of five strikes, and the fifth differs by the rounding effect the paper describes.

Not claimed. Section 4 states plainly that optimality cannot be guaranteed in advance for n ≥ 3: the inherited strikes need not be dual optimal, and the rearrangement algorithm is a heuristic. The authors describe the method as "verifiably optimal rather than provably optimal". Its costs grow exponentially with n, through the 4n grid and the 2n−1 orientation patterns, and the examples stop at six assets, with one pair of strikes per asset in every reported row. The comparison with Neufeld and Xiang ran their code with substitute linear programming solvers in place of the commercial one, so their running times are not reported, and the paper notes that their method handles general costs and many more marginals. The pair-decomposition intuition explains where strikes go, but the paper gives no theorem saying why two strikes per asset suffice in these examples.

Why it matters. The lower end of the arbitrage-free price range for a basket option is what a seller can be sure of collecting without knowing correlations. The paper turns a hard infinite-dimensional problem into a small, checkable object: six options and a cash amount whose validity anyone can verify with a 64-point check, plus an upper bound that shows how much room is left.

FURTHER READING

Further reading

M. H. Abou Daya, C. Bernard and S. Vanduffel, Feasible sub-replicating portfolios for basket options via the block rearrangement algorithm, arXiv:2611.26119 (2026). The paper itself; numbering in this chapter follows its HTML version.

A. Neufeld and Q. Xiang, Numerical method for feasible and approximately optimal solutions of multi-marginal optimal transport beyond discrete measures, arXiv:2203.01633 (2022). The grid-based method the paper compares against in Tables 5 and 6, and the source of the reassembly idea used in Proposition 2.11; its abstract describes the relaxation by finitely many linear constraints and the computed upper and lower bounds.

T. Koike, L. Lin and R. Wang, Joint mixability and notions of negative dependence, arXiv:2204.11438 (2022). Background on joint mixes, random vectors with constant sum, the structure behind Case 3; its abstract describes the joint mix as a concept of extremal negative dependence that minimizes the variance of the sum.

Built from a full read of arXiv 2611.26119v1. Assumption, remark, proposition, theorem, corollary, table and equation numbers match the paper. Example A is ours. All three animations compute in the page: the first runs the rearrangement algorithm on Example A and checks all 576 arrangements by brute force; the second computes φi, the strikes, the exact cash component by grid enumeration and the scenario-by-scenario comparison; the third reprices the paper's Table 2 portfolios with the Black formula and the 64-point enumeration of Proposition 2.3.

Ancilla-Free Exact Dicke-State Synthesis with Optimal Size and Depth

Yunqi Huang, Wei Zi, Jianhao He, Zekun Ye, Shenggen Zheng · posted Nov 20, 2026 · quant-ph · arXiv 2611.27640

Overview

Every Dicke state, the equal superposition of all n-bit strings with exactly k ones, can be built exactly from n qubits in their ground state with O(n) gates in O(log n) layers and not one spare qubit, which matches the known lower bounds on both counts and refutes a recent conjecture that the balanced case needs depth proportional to k. The trick is to stop amplifying a weak starting state many times and instead start from one that already overlaps the target by a constant: a layer of tilted qubits, a sign correction that depends only on how many qubits are 1, and a small reverse tilt. A constant number of amplitude amplification steps, finished by one exactly tuned phase step, then lands on the target with probability one. The sign correction needs arithmetic on the Hamming weight, and the paper finds room for that arithmetic inside the output register itself, by squeezing each block of 31 symmetric qubits into a 5-bit count.

By the end you'll be able to explain
  • what the Dicke state |Dnk⟩ is, why the symmetric subspace has the Dicke states as a basis, and what the lower bounds Ω(n) gates and Ω(log n) depth mean (Theorem 1, Table I);
  • why the natural product state has overlap only Θ(k−1/4) with the target, from its binomial weight distribution and Stirling's formula (Eq. 7);
  • how amplitude amplification rotates a state in a two-dimensional plane, and how one final phase-matching step with tuned phases u and v makes the result exact (Section V);
  • why a weight-dependent sign correction followed by a small inverse rotation turns the overlap into a sum of absolute values (Eq. 6), and how the signs are computed exactly from an integer recurrence (Eq. 13);
  • why that overlap never falls below the constant η = 1/128, by comparing the rotation with a quantum walk whose amplitudes are Bessel functions (Eqs. 8 to 12, Lemma 2);
  • how a phase depending only on the Hamming weight is applied with no ancillas, by compressing blocks (Eq. 1), adding block weights with carry-save adders (Eq. 2) and counting qubits (Eqs. 3 to 5, Lemma 1);
  • what is proved, what is only asymptotic, and what remains open.

  • Example A: four qubits, weight two. The target is |D42⟩ = (|0011⟩ + |0101⟩ + |0110⟩ + |1001⟩ + |1010⟩ + |1100⟩)/√6. Everything in the construction can be done by hand here: the product state, the signs, the overlaps and the final phases all come out in closed form. The example and its closed forms are ours; the page simulates it on a 16-amplitude state vector.
  • Example B: the paper's Figure 2. n = 128 qubits and weight k = 32. The paper reports that the product state alone has overlap F0 ≈ 0.2850, and that the sign-corrected state at d = 1 has F1 ≈ 0.8384. The page recomputes both from scratch.
1 · THE TARGET AND THE LIMITS

What is a Dicke state, and how cheaply could one possibly be built?

A register of n qubits has a basis of 2n states |x⟩, one for each bit string x = (x1, …, xn), and a general state is a unit vector of complex amplitudes on those strings. Measuring the register returns string x with probability equal to its squared amplitude. The register starts in |0n⟩, all zeros, and a circuit is a sequence of gates applied to it. The model in the paper allows arbitrary single-qubit gates and the two-qubit CNOT, which flips its target qubit when its control qubit is 1. The size of a circuit counts these gates, and its depth counts layers, where each layer consists of gates on disjoint qubits that can run at the same time.

Definition · Dicke state

In words: the equal superposition of all n-bit strings that contain exactly k ones. There are C(n, k) such strings, so each gets amplitude C(n, k)−1/2 and the state has length one.

For Example A there are C(4, 2) = 6 strings of weight two, each with amplitude 1/√6. Two Dicke states of different weights share no strings, so they are orthogonal, and each has length one. The n + 1 Dicke states of an n-qubit register are therefore orthonormal. They span the symmetric subspace 𝒮n, the states that do not change when the qubits are permuted, because a permutation-invariant state must give equal amplitude to strings that are permutations of each other, and strings are permutations of each other exactly when they have the same weight.

The paper cites two uses. In the decoded quantum interferometry algorithm a Dicke state is a uniform superposition over all sets of k error positions in a codeword, and in quantum metrology the balanced state |Dnn/2⟩ is a probe for small collective spin rotations. The states at k = 0 and k = n are trivial: |0n⟩ is already the target, and n parallel X gates make |1n⟩. The paper calls the other weights, 1 ≤ k ≤ n − 1, nontrivial, and for those, two lower bounds are known.

Fact · lower bounds the paper cites

For every nontrivial weight, the reduced state of any pair of qubits of |Dnk⟩ is entangled (Wang and Mølmer). Huang et al. show that preparing any n-qubit state with this property needs Ω(n) CNOT gates, and Yuan and Zhang show that preparing any nontrivial Dicke state needs depth Ω(log n).

The intuition behind the depth bound, in our words rather than the paper's: every pair of qubits ends up correlated, and with two-qubit gates the set of qubits that can influence a given qubit at most doubles with each layer, so information has to spread across all n qubits, which takes about log n layers. Previous constructions met both bounds only when r = min{k, n − k} is a constant. For balanced states, with r near n/2, their bounds give O(n2) gates and O(n) depth, and Yuan and Zhang conjectured that depth Ω(k) is necessary. The paper asks the following question.

Problem 1 · exact Dicke-state preparation

Can every n-qubit Dicke state be prepared exactly using O(n) single-qubit gates and CNOTs, with O(log n) depth and without ancillary qubits? In words: build the target with probability one, no more gates than qubits up to a constant factor, logarithmic time, and no workspace beyond the n output qubits.

Theorem 1 · the main result

For every n ≥ 2 and 1 ≤ k ≤ n − 1, there is an ancilla-free circuit that prepares |Dnk⟩ exactly using O(n) arbitrary single-qubit gates and CNOTs, with O(log n) depth. For k = ⌊n/2⌋ this rules out the Ω(k) depth lower bound conjectured by Yuan and Zhang.

The proof has three parts, and the chapter follows them: a starting state with constant overlap (Sections 2, 4 and 5 here), exact amplitude amplification (Section 3), and a circuit that applies a phase depending only on the Hamming weight, built inside the output register (Section 6).

In short: |Dnk⟩ is the uniform superposition of the C(n, k) strings of weight k; the Dicke states form an orthonormal basis of the symmetric subspace; any nontrivial one needs Ω(n) gates and Ω(log n) depth, and Theorem 1 meets both bounds with no ancillas.

2 · A FREE FIRST GUESS

How close does one layer of single-qubit rotations get?

The cheapest possible attempt is to tilt every qubit by the same amount, so that each one reads 1 with probability p = k/n. The number of ones is then a binomial random variable with mean k, which puts the most weight near the target weight. The tilt is a rotation about the y axis of the Bloch sphere,

a real rotation matrix acting on the amplitudes of |0⟩ and |1⟩. Applied to |0⟩ it gives cos(α/2)|0⟩ + sin(α/2)|1⟩, so the angle φ = 2 arcsin √p makes the probability of 1 equal to sin²(φ/2) = p. The paper writes Ra := Ry(a)⊗n for the same rotation on every qubit, one layer of n gates.

Definition · the product state

In words: every qubit is independently tilted towards 1 by the same amount; grouping strings by weight, the coefficient of the Dicke state of weight w is the square root of the binomial probability of w ones.

whyWhy is the Dicke coefficient the square root of a binomial probability?

Expanding the tensor product, the string x gets amplitude √p for each 1 and √(1 − p) for each 0, so every string of weight w has amplitude pw/2(1 − p)(n−w)/2. The sum over those C(n, w) strings is C(n, w)1/2 times |Dnw⟩, by the definition of the Dicke state. Multiplying gives aw = (C(n, w)pw(1 − p)n−w)1/2, and the squares aw2 are the binomial probabilities, which sum to one.

∎

In Example A, p = 1/2 and φ = π/2, so each qubit is (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2 and all 16 strings have amplitude 1/4. The Dicke coefficients are aw = (C(4, w)/16)1/2, that is 1/4, 1/2, √6/4, 1/2, 1/4. The overlap with the target is a2 = √6/4 ≈ 0.6124, so a measurement of the weight would succeed with probability 6/16.

For large n the overlap shrinks. The binomial weight has standard deviation σ := √(k(1 − k/n)), which lies between √(k/2) and √k when k ≤ n/2. The probability mass near the mean spreads over about σ weights, so the central probability ak2 is of order 1/σ and the amplitude ak is of order σ−1/2 = Θ(k−1/4). The paper makes this quantitative near the centre.

proofWhere does the constant 1/3 come from?

Stirling's formula, n! ≈ √(2πn)(n/e)n, comes with explicit error bounds: the ratio of n! to √(2πn)(n/e)n lies between 1 and e1/(12n). At w = k the paper uses these bounds to get ak2 ≥ e−1/6/(√(2π)σ), and e−1/6/√(2π) ≈ 0.338 > 1/3.

For w = k + j, define the relative-entropy-like function

Applying Stirling's bounds to n!, w! and (n − w)! gives

Because σ ≤ √k and k ≥ 16, a shift of |j| ≤ σ/4 ≤ k/16 keeps w/k and (n − w)/(n − k) in [15/16, 17/16]. Hence w, n − w ≥ 15 and w(1 − w/n) ≤ (17/16)2σ2. The second derivative is g″(w) = 1/w + 1/(n − w) ≤ 4/(3σ2) on this range, and g(k) = g′(k) = 0, so Taylor's theorem gives g(w) ≤ 2(w − k)2/(3σ2) ≤ 1/24. The two Stirling corrections add up to at most 1/90. Using e−x > 1 − x and √(2π) < 8/3, the paper concludes

∎

In Example B, σ = √(32 · 3/4) = √24 ≈ 4.90. The page computes a32 ≈ 0.2850, matching the paper's F0, and a322 ≈ 0.0812 is indeed above 1/(3σ) ≈ 0.0680.

Fact · the product state is not enough

The overlap of |P⟩ with |Dnk⟩ is ak = Θ(σ−1/2) = Θ(k−1/4), so amplifying it directly takes Θ(k1/4) steps as k grows. With O(log n) depth per step this would give depth growing like k1/4 log n, more than the target O(log n).

In short: one layer of Ry(φ) gates makes the binomial state |P⟩, whose Dicke coefficients are square roots of binomial probabilities; its overlap with the target decays like k−1/4 (Eq. 7), which is 0.6124 in Example A and 0.2850 in Example B.

3 · EXACT AMPLITUDE AMPLIFICATION

How does a partial overlap become an exact preparation?

Suppose a circuit B makes a state |ψ⟩ = B|0n⟩ whose overlap with the target is a real number F between 0 and 1. Amplitude amplification, the generalization of Grover search due to Brassard, Høyer, Mosca and Tapp, raises that overlap by rotating the state inside a plane. Put α := arcsin F and write

where |⊥⟩ is a unit vector orthogonal to the target. The two vectors |Dk⟩ and |⊥⟩ span a plane, and |ψ⟩ sits in it at angle α above the |⊥⟩ axis. Two reflections of that plane are available. The first, Zk(−1), flips the sign of the |Dk⟩ component, a reflection across the |⊥⟩ axis. The second flips the sign of the |ψ⟩ component: since Z0(−1) flips the sign of |0n⟩ and B maps |0n⟩ to |ψ⟩, the operator BZ0(−1)B† flips the sign of |ψ⟩ and fixes everything orthogonal to it. One amplification step is

whyWhy does Q rotate the state by 2α?

This is the standard argument, in our words. On the plane, Zk(−1) is the reflection across the |⊥⟩ axis, and −BZ0(−1)B† = 2|ψ⟩⟨ψ| − I is the reflection across the line through |ψ⟩. Two reflections across lines meeting at angle α compose to a rotation by 2α. Starting at angle α from |⊥⟩, the state after t steps is at angle (2t + 1)α, and its target component is sin((2t + 1)α).

∎

The paper takes t := ⌊π/(4α) − 1/2⌋ steps, the largest number that does not rotate past the target. With β := (2t + 1)α ≤ π/2,

Unless β lands exactly on π/2, a residue cos β remains on |⊥⟩. The fix, which the paper takes from Høyer's work on arbitrary phases, replaces the two sign flips of one last step by two general phases. First Zk(u) multiplies the target component by a unit complex number u. Then BZ0(v)B† multiplies the |ψ⟩ component by v, which adds (v − 1)ξ|ψ⟩ to the state, where ξ is the current overlap with |ψ⟩. After Zk(u),

The added multiple of |ψ⟩ contributes (v − 1)ξ cos α to the |⊥⟩ coefficient, which was cos β. Cancelling it requires

Phase matching · the two conditions

In words: choose u on the upper unit semicircle with this real part, then set v = −ξ̄/ξ. The |⊥⟩ coefficient vanishes, and the target coefficient becomes u sin β − tan α cos β, a complex number of modulus one, which a single-qubit gate proportional to the identity turns into exactly 1.

proofWhere do the two conditions come from?

Write c := cos β/cos α, a real number. Since |v| = 1, the right side ξ − c must have the same modulus as ξ. Squaring, |ξ − c|2 = |ξ|2 − 2c Re ξ + c2, so the condition is c2 = 2c Re ξ, that is 2 cos α Re ξ = cos β (when c ≠ 0). Then v = (ξ − c)/ξ, and since Re ξ = c/2 the number ξ − c is −ξ̄, giving v = −ξ̄/ξ.

For u, substitute ξ. Its real part is F sin β Re u + cos α cos β, which must equal cos β/(2 cos α). Rearranging (this algebra is ours),

and since 2F cos α = 2 sin α cos α = sin 2α, Re u = −cot(2α) cot β.

The paper then checks that this is a legitimate real part. For α < π/4 the choice of t gives β > π/2 − 2α, which puts Re u in (−1, 0). For α ≥ π/4, t = 0 and β = α, so Re u = −cos 2α/(2 sin2α) = 1 − 1/(2F2), which lies in [0, 1/2). With u in the upper half plane, Re ξ > 0, so ξ ≠ 0 and v is well defined.

∎

Example A, starting from the product state alone, needs no full steps. Here F = √6/4, so F2 = 3/8 and α ≈ 37.76°, below 45°, and t = ⌊45/37.76 − 1/2⌋ = 0, so β = α. In closed form (our calculation), cos 2α = 1 − 2F2 = 1/4, sin 2α = √15/4 and cot α = √(5/3), so Re u = −(1/√15)√(5/3) = −1/3. Then u = −1/3 + (2√2/3)i, ξ = 1/2 + (√2/4)i ≈ 0.5 + 0.354i, and v = −ξ̄/ξ comes out equal to u. The animation below carries this out on the full 16-amplitude state of four qubits.

The second chip uses the starting state of the next section, whose overlap 0.9853 is so large that again t = 0 and only the phase-matching step is needed, now with Re u = 1 − 1/(2F2) ≈ 0.4850. In both runs the state never leaves the symmetric subspace: every operation used is either a collective rotation or a phase that depends only on the weight.

The step count is what matters for the main theorem. If F is at least a constant η, then α ≥ arcsin η and t ≤ π/(4 arcsin η), a constant. For Example B starting from the product state, F0 ≈ 0.2850 gives α ≈ 16.56° and t = 2 full steps before phase matching, which is what the paper reports in its Figure 2.

In short: amplification rotates by 2α per step in the plane of target and residue; t = ⌊π/(4α) − 1/2⌋ steps plus one step with tuned phases u and v (Re u = −cot 2α cot β, v = −ξ̄/ξ) reach the target exactly, and a constant lower bound on F makes the number of steps constant.

4 · SIGN CORRECTION AND A SMALL REVERSE TILT

How can a cheap circuit raise the starting overlap to a constant?

The product state's overlap is small because its weight distribution is spread over about σ weights while the target sits on one. The paper's idea is to compare |P⟩ not with the target itself but with a slightly rotated copy of it, Rθ|Dk⟩, whose weight distribution is also spread out, and then to undo the rotation. The coefficients of the rotated target are

with the sign at zero set to +1. The collective rotation keeps the symmetric subspace in place, because applying the same gate to every qubit commutes with permuting the qubits, so Rθ|Dk⟩ is a combination of Dicke states with real coefficients βw. The operator S multiplies each Dicke component by the sign of the matching βw, a phase that depends only on the weight.

Definition · the starting circuit (Eq. 6)

In words: make the product state, fix the sign of each weight component to agree with the rotated target, then rotate every qubit back by θ. The overlap with the target is the sum of aw times |βw|, every term nonnegative.

proofWhy is the overlap a sum of absolute values?

Ry(θ) is a real orthogonal matrix, so R−θ = Rθ† = RθT and ⟨Dk|R−θ|Dw⟩ = ⟨Dw|Rθ|Dk⟩ = βw. Expanding S|P⟩ = Σw aw sgn(βw)|Dw⟩,

A remark of ours: for any other choice of signs sw = ±1, the overlap would be Σ awswβw ≤ Σ aw|βw|, so S is the best weight-dependent sign pattern for this rotation. Without S, the overlap is Σ awβw, and terms of opposite signs cancel.

∎

Why a rotation helps, informally: rotating |Dk⟩ spreads it over neighbouring weights, so Rθ|Dk⟩ has many coefficients of size about σ−1/2 near k, matching the spread of |P⟩, but with oscillating signs. The sign correction aligns them, and the inner product of two spread-out vectors with aligned signs can be of order one. Section 5 makes this precise.

The algorithm tries four angles, θd := 2 arctan(d/(2√n)) for d ∈ {0, 1/4, 1, 2}, and keeps the one with the largest Fd (Algorithm 1). At d = 0 there is no rotation, all signs are +1 and F0 = ak. The angle is chosen so that tan(θ/2) = d/(2√n), which makes cos2(θ/2) = q/(q + 1) and sin2(θ/2) = 1/(q + 1) with q := 4n/d2, an integer for the three positive candidates. That is what lets the paper compute every sign exactly with integers (Section VI).

Exact signs · Section VI

In words: βw is a positive factor times an integer Hw, so sgn(βw) = sgn(Hw). The sum runs over j, the number of positions where a weight-k input string and a weight-w output string both have a 1.

proofWhere do the binomials and the sign (−1)k−j come from?

Each qubit is rotated by Ry(θ), whose entries are ⟨0|R|0⟩ = ⟨1|R|1⟩ = cos(θ/2), ⟨1|R|0⟩ = sin(θ/2) and ⟨0|R|1⟩ = −sin(θ/2). The amplitude from an input string to an output string is the product of one entry per qubit. Fix an output string of weight w. Among the weight-k input strings, exactly C(w, j)C(n − w, k − j) share j ones with it. Such an input has k − j transitions 1 → 0, each contributing −sin(θ/2), giving the sign (−1)k−j; it has w − j transitions 0 → 1, each contributing sin(θ/2); and n − w − k + 2j unchanged bits, each contributing cos(θ/2). Factoring out (q + 1)−n/2, each unchanged bit contributes √q and each changed bit contributes 1, which produces the factor qj inside Hw and the prefactor q(n−w−k)/2. Normalizing the two Dicke states gives the square root of binomials.

∎

Computing Hw term by term would be slow, so the paper uses a three-term recurrence. Starting from H0 = (−1)kC(n, k),

with the last term omitted at w = 0. The Hw are values of Krawtchouk polynomials, a classical family of orthogonal polynomials, and (13) is their difference relation.

proofHow does the recurrence follow from a generating function?

The paper observes that Hw is the coefficient of tk in Pw(t) := (1 + qt)w(1 − t)n−w: choosing j of the w factors to contribute qt and k − j of the n − w factors to contribute −t gives exactly the j-th term of Hw. Differentiating Pw and comparing gives the polynomial identity

and taking the coefficient of tk, where tP′w contributes k times the coefficient of tk in Pw, gives (13).

∎

In Example A with d = 1, q = 16 and θ = 2 arctan(1/4) ≈ 0.4900, so cos(θ/2) = 4/√17 and sin(θ/2) = 1/√17. The recurrence (13), started at H0 = 6, gives H = (6, −45, 193, 720, 1536), so only the weight-1 component changes sign. The prefactors make (our closed form) β = (16√6, −60√6, 193, 60√6, 16√6)/289 ≈ (0.1356, −0.5085, 0.6678, 0.5085, 0.1356). Pairing with a = (1/4, 1/2, √6/4, 1/2, 1/4),

whereas without the sign correction the middle term enters with a minus sign and the overlap is (8 − 60 + 193/4)√6/289 ≈ −0.0318, almost nothing. For the other candidates the page computes F1/4 ≈ 0.7542 and F2 ≈ 0.8083 in Example A, so the algorithm picks d = 1.

5 · WHY THE OVERLAP STAYS CONSTANT

Why does the sign-corrected overlap not decay as n grows?

The numbers above are for particular sizes. The theorem needs a single constant that works for all n and k. The paper proves one.

Lemma 2 · constant overlap

There is a constant η > 0 such that max{F0, F1/4} ≥ η for all 1 ≤ k ≤ n/2. The proof gives η = 1/128.

The plan of the proof is a product of two estimates. Near weight k, on a window of width of order σ, every aw is at least of order σ−1/2 by (7). If the absolute values |βw| on the same window add up to at least of order σ1/2, the sum Σ aw|βw| is at least a constant. The second estimate is the hard one, and the paper gets it by comparing the rotation with a simpler process whose amplitudes are known in closed form.

The rotation as a walk on weights. In the Dicke basis the generator of Rθ only connects neighbouring weights: a small rotation of every qubit moves a weight-w state to weights w ± 1. After a diagonal change of phases, the paper writes the generator as −iH, where H is a real symmetric tridiagonal matrix indexed by j = w − k with off-diagonal entries

A particle hopping along the integers with these rates is a continuous-time quantum walk. Near j = 0 the rates are almost constant, equal to h := √(k(n − k))/2, so the paper compares H with the walk K := h(T + T†) on all of ℤ, where T shifts j to j + 1. Its Figure 3 draws the two chains side by side.

The walk with constant rates is solved by Bessel functions. For integer j the Bessel function of the first kind has the integral representation

Starting at j = 0, the walk K run for time s has amplitudes

whyWhy does a Fourier transform solve the walk?

Represent a sequence (vj) on ℤ by its Fourier series v(t) = Σ vje−ijt. The shift T multiplies the series by e−it and T† by eit, so K acts by multiplication by h(e−it + eit) = 2h cos t. The walk e−isK therefore multiplies by e−i2hs cos t, and the starting point j = 0 has Fourier series 1. The j-th amplitude is the j-th Fourier coefficient of e−i2hs cos t, which the Jacobi–Anger expansion identifies as (−i)jJj(2hs). Parseval's identity, the statement that the squared lengths of a sequence and of its Fourier series agree, then gives Σj Jj(z)2 = 1 and, applied to the derivative in t, Σj j2Jj(z)2 = z2/2.

∎

The two walks stay close. With z := 2hθ and βw extended by zero outside 0 ≤ w ≤ n, the paper proves

proofHow is the gap between the two walks controlled?

First the rates are compared: for every integer j, |hj − h| ≤ λ(|j| + 1) with λ := n/(2√(k(n − k))). Inside the range this follows from (k + j + 1)(n − k − j) − k(n − k) = (n − 2k − j)j + (n − k − j) and the bounds |n − 2k − j| ≤ n and 0 < n − k − j ≤ n; outside, |j| + 1 ≥ k and λk ≥ h.

Next, the walk φ(s) = e−isK|0⟩ stays concentrated: ‖φ(s)‖ = 1 and ‖Mφ(s)‖ = √2 hs, where M multiplies the j-th entry by j (both from Parseval, as above). Shifting indices and the triangle inequality give

Duhamel's formula, the quantum analogue of variation of constants for differential equations, bounds the difference of two evolutions by the integral of the generator difference along one of them:

Substituting h and λ gives the right side of (9), and taking absolute values entry by entry cannot increase the distance.

∎

In Example B with d = 1/4 (our computation, shown in the animation above), θ ≈ 0.02210, h ≈ 27.71 and z ≈ 1.225. The left side of (9) is about 0.0104 and the right side about 0.0986, so the bound holds with room to spare.

Bessel amplitudes spread like σ−1/2. The paper sets τ := 11/12 and Kτ := √(2/π)(1 − τ2)−1/4. A bound of Krasikov, together with |J0(z)| ≤ √(2/(πz)) and |J−j| = |Jj|, gives

By a Chebyshev-type step (our name for it) applied to Σ j2Jj2 = z2/2, the window |j| ≤ τz holds probability at least 1 − 1/(2τ2) = 49/121. A sum of squares that is at least 49/121, with each term at most Kτ/√z in absolute value, forces the sum of absolute values to be large:

proofHow do these pieces give η = 1/128?

If σ < 48, then (7) gives F0 = ak > (1/(3 · 48))1/2 = 1/12. The w = k part of (7) comes from the Stirling bound ak2 ≥ e−1/6/(√(2π)σ), which holds for every k, small or large.

Otherwise σ ≥ 48, so k ≥ 16; take θ = θ1/4. Since x/2 ≤ arctan x ≤ x on [0, 1], the paper gets 1/8 ≤ z/σ = √n θ ≤ 1/4, so the window |j| ≤ τz lies inside |j| ≤ σ/4 where (7) applies. Multiplying (7), (12) and using Kτ < √2,

By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, (9) and ‖a‖ = 1, this sum differs from F1/4 by at most 1/(32√2) + 3/(8σ). Hence F1/4 > 1/(32√2) − 3/(8σ) > 1/128, and the two cases give η = 1/128.

The constant 1/128 is far below the overlaps in the examples, 0.8384 and 0.9853; it is a proof constant, not a performance figure.

In short: near the target weight the collective rotation is a quantum walk with almost constant hopping rates, whose amplitudes are Bessel functions (Eqs. 8, 10); the two walks differ by little (Eq. 9), Bessel amplitudes are spread evenly over a window of width of order σ (Eqs. 11, 12), and multiplying by the product-state coefficients (Eq. 7) gives F ≥ 1/128 for every n and k (Lemma 2).

6 · WEIGHT-DEPENDENT PHASES WITHOUT ANCILLAS

Where does the arithmetic happen if there are no spare qubits?

Everything so far needs one primitive: multiply each Dicke component |Dw⟩ by a phase eif(w) that depends on the weight. The sign correction S uses f(w) ∈ {0, π}, and Zk(u) and Z0(v) put a phase on a single weight. The natural way to do this is to compute the Hamming weight into a fresh register, apply the phase, and uncompute, but fresh registers are ancillas. The paper's observation is that on the symmetric subspace the register is far from full: a symmetric state of s qubits is a combination of only s + 1 Dicke states, so its information fits in ⌈log(s + 1)⌉ qubits.

Lemma 1 · phases on the symmetric subspace

For every function f : {0, …, n} → ℝ there is an n-qubit circuit Uf with O(n) gates and O(log(n + 1)) depth satisfying Uf|Dnw⟩ = eif(w)|Dnw⟩ for 0 ≤ w ≤ n.

Step 1: compress blocks. For n ≤ 31 a constant-size circuit exists by exact synthesis. For n ≥ 32, split the qubits into Q := ⌈n/31⌉ blocks, all of size 31 except possibly the last. For each block size s there is a unitary Vs that writes the block's weight in binary and empties the rest:

for every block weight j ∈ {0, …, s}. One Vs acts coherently on all the weights at once. Since s ≤ 31, five qubits hold the count and the other 26 return to |0⟩, and each Vs has constant size; the paper builds it from the coherent Dicke transform of Bärtschi and Eidenbenz followed by a unary-to-binary conversion.

Compression works on the whole symmetric state because a Dicke state of the full register splits into Dicke states of the blocks,

so after compression each block holds a superposition of binary counts ji, and the counts add up to w. As a small check of ours with Example A, split four qubits into two blocks of two: |D42⟩ = √(1/6)|D20⟩|D22⟩ + √(4/6)|D21⟩|D21⟩ + √(1/6)|D22⟩|D20⟩, and the squared weights 1/6 + 4/6 + 1/6 add to one. A block of two qubits holds three Dicke states, which still need two qubits, so the saving only appears for larger blocks; at s = 31 it is 26 qubits per block.

Step 2: add the block counts with carry-save adders. The Q counts are five-bit rows to be added. The basic gadget is the full adder, which uses one fresh qubit for the carry:

The sum bit a ⊕ b ⊕ c and the carry bit ab ⊕ ac ⊕ bc (the majority of the three) satisfy a + b + c = (a ⊕ b ⊕ c) + 2(ab ⊕ ac ⊕ bc). For a = b = c = 1 the sum bit is 1 and the carry is 1, and 3 = 1 + 2. The paper implements the carry with the identity ab ⊕ ac ⊕ bc = a ⊕ (a ⊕ b)(a ⊕ c), which needs one Toffoli gate; checking it by cases (our check), a = 0 gives bc, the majority of 0, b, c, and a = 1 gives 1 ⊕ (¬b)(¬c) = b ∨ c, the majority of 1, b, c.

Applied column by column to three rows, full adders produce two rows, a sum row and a carry row shifted one place left, with the same total. Repeating on disjoint triples in parallel shrinks Mt rows to Mt+1 = Mt − ⌊Mt/3⌋ rows, about two thirds as many, so about log3/2 Q rounds bring Q rows down to two. This is the Wallace-tree idea from classical hardware. Each round has constant depth, and the paper counts the total cost:

where gt = ⌊Mt/3⌋ is the number of triples in round t and round t has at most 5 + t columns. So the carry-save stage uses O(Q) gates, O(Q) fresh qubits, and O(log Q) depth.

proofWhy is the total number of carry qubits only linear in Q?

Each round turns gt triples into pairs, so the rows drop by gt and Σt gt = Q − 2. Since Mt+1 − 2 ≤ (2/3)(Mt − 2), the remaining excess shrinks geometrically. Summing from round u onward gives Σt≥u gt = Mu − 2, and summing that over u,

Therefore Σ(5 + t)gt ≤ 5(Q − 2) + 2(Q − 2) = 7(Q − 2).

∎

The two remaining rows A and B are added by an ordinary ripple-carry adder into an m-qubit register W, with m := ⌈log(n + 1)⌉, using m − 1 temporary carries that are uncomputed afterwards. The paper checks that the register is large enough to hold all of this at once:

The first inequality uses m ≤ Q + 4, which follows from n + 1 ≤ 32Q.

Animation · carry-save addition of eight block weights
rows in a triple this roundnew sum and carry rows

The block weights in the animation are our choice, eight blocks of 31 qubits (n = 248); the rounds, the bits and the carry count are computed in the page with equation (2).

Step 3: apply the phase and undo everything. With the total weight w held in W, the phase eif(w) is applied by a tree of flags. The paper splits W into its three high-order bits and ℓ := m − 3 low-order bits, sets L := 2ℓ, and makes 2j − 1 extra copies of low-order bit j with CNOT trees. For each of the eight high-order values it raises a flag when the high bits match, then splits the flag down a binary tree, one level per low-order bit, using a Toffoli gate and a CNOT to replace (p, 0) by (p ∧ ¬y, p ∧ y). Exactly one leaf is marked, the leaf for the actual weight, and a single-qubit gate diag(1, eif(w)) on leaf w applies the phase; leaves with w > n get angle zero. The tree is then reversed. The space count is

using 2L = 2m−2 ≤ n/2 and n ≥ 31Q − 30 ≥ 24Q − 20 for Q ≥ 2. This stage uses O(L) = O(n) gates and depth O(ℓ + 1) = O(log n). Finally the arithmetic is uncomputed and the blocks are decompressed, leaving eif(w)|Dw⟩.

For a phase on a single weight, as in Zk(u), it is enough to test whether W equals that weight, put one phase gate on the test flag and reverse the test. For weight zero, as in Z0(v), the paper skips the summation entirely and tests that every block count is zero with a balanced AND tree, which needs B0 − 1 free qubits, where B0 is the number of bits holding the block counts, and 2B0 − 1 ≤ 10Q − 1 ≤ n.

In short: symmetric blocks of 31 qubits compress into 5-bit counts (Eq. 1), freeing 26 qubits each; carry-save adders (Eq. 2) sum the counts in O(log Q) rounds with O(Q) carries (Eq. 3); a flag tree applies the phase; the space bounds (Eqs. 4, 5) show it all fits in n qubits, giving any weight-dependent phase with O(n) gates and O(log n) depth (Lemma 1).

7 · ASSEMBLY AND COMPILATION

How do the pieces add up to O(n) gates and O(log n) depth?

The proof of Theorem 1 in Section V of the paper assembles the parts. After complementing bits, assume 1 ≤ k ≤ n/2. The circuit B = R−θSRφ consists of two layers of single-qubit rotations and one phase circuit from Lemma 1. By Lemma 2, F ≥ η, so the number of amplification steps t is bounded by a constant. Each step uses B, B† and two single-weight phase circuits, and the final phase-matching step uses the same ingredients with tuned phases. Every collective rotation and every weight-dependent phase keeps the state in 𝒮n, which is the only place Lemma 1 has to work. A constant number of pieces, each with O(n) gates and O(log n) depth, gives O(n) gates and O(log n) depth in total. For k > n/2 a final layer of X gates flips every bit.

The paper also shows how to produce the circuit as an explicit list of gates.

Algorithm 1 · generating the circuit

For 0 < k < n, set r = min{k, n − k} and p = r/n. Start with d⋆ = 0 and F = ar. For d = 1/4, 1, 2, compute H0, …, Hn by (13) with q = 4n/d2, compute Fd by (14), and keep d if Fd2 is strictly larger. Build S from the signs of Hw, form B from Rφ, S and R−θ, append the amplification steps if F < 1, and append X⊗n if k > n/2. In words: try four angles, keep the best overlap, and wire up the circuit around it.

The overlaps are compared exactly, not in floating point. Splitting even and odd weights in (6) gives

where b := p/(q(1 − p)) and A := (1 − p)nqn−k/(C(n, k)(q + 1)n) are rational. Since √b = dσ/(2(n − k)), every Fd2 lies in the field ℚ(σ) of numbers x + yσ with x, y rational (σ2 is rational), and comparing them is exact. The paper bounds the integers involved by |Hw| ≤ qkC(n, k) ≤ qk2n, so all numbers have O(n log(n + 1)) bits and the whole computation takes Õ(n2) bit operations.

Proposition 1 · classical generation

Algorithm 1 generates the circuits of Theorem 1 in time polynomial in n. The gate matrices have algebraic entries described exactly; adjoining cos α, √(1 − (Re u)2) and i to ℚ(F) gives a field of degree at most 32, in which the amplification parameters are computed.

The number of full amplification steps is also found exactly, without computing α. Starting from (x, y) = (F, cos α), each application of the rotation matrix with entries 1 − 2F2 and ±2F cos α adds 2α to the angle; updates are accepted while y stays nonnegative, and the final pair is (sin β, cos β).

In short: a constant number of blocks, each one O(n) gates and O(log n) depth, proves Theorem 1; Algorithm 1 picks the best of four angles by exact arithmetic in ℚ(σ) (Eq. 14) and emits the gates in polynomial time (Proposition 1).

ASSESSMENT

What is shown, and what is claimed

Proved. Theorem 1: every nontrivial Dicke state has an exact, ancilla-free circuit with O(n) gates and O(log n) depth, which is optimal on both counts given the cited lower bounds. The constant overlap (Lemma 2, η = 1/128), the weight-dependent phase circuit (Lemma 1) and the exact phase-matching formulas are proved in full, and Proposition 1 shows that the circuits can be generated in polynomial time with exact algebraic gate entries. The balanced case refutes the Ω(k) depth conjecture of Yuan and Zhang. The proofs are short and checkable; this chapter recomputed the paper's two Figure 2 overlaps and checked bound (9) at one instance.

Not reported. The constants hidden in O(n) and O(log n) are never computed, and the paper gives no gate counts or depths for any concrete n. The constants are likely large: each Lemma 1 call compresses blocks of 31 qubits with exactly synthesized 31-qubit unitaries, runs a carry-save tree and a flag tree, and undoes all of it, and B is used several times per amplification step. For the sizes of current hardware, the older O(nr) circuits may well be shorter in practice; the paper does not compare. The authors list reducing the gate count, by optimizing the phase circuits and the rotation angle, as future work.

Model assumptions. The gate set allows arbitrary single-qubit rotations with exact algebraic angles and CNOTs between any two qubits. Adapting the construction to finite gate sets, as used in fault-tolerant computing, and to restricted qubit connectivity is stated as future work; the Yuan–Zhang paper, by contrast, also treats grid connectivity.

A note on authorship. The paper states that OpenAI ChatGPT (Codex) assisted with all sections, including proof development and checking, and that the authors take responsibility for all claims. The arguments followed in this chapter are short enough to check line by line, and the two numbers in Figure 2 reproduce.

Why it matters. Dicke states are a basic resource for symmetric algorithms, metrology and decoded quantum interferometry, and the paper closes their asymptotic circuit complexity in the standard model. The method, a good starting state plus a constant number of exact amplification steps, with arithmetic done in space freed by compression, looks reusable for other symmetric states.

The Rotation Strategy Wins Penney's Game for Permutations

Himaghna Roy Choudhury · submitted Nov 11, announced Nov 24, 2026 · math.CO · arXiv 2611.28063

Overview

Watch a stream of random numbers and wait for three consecutive ones to fall in a chosen up-and-down shape: if your opponent picks a shape, you can always pick one that is more likely to show up first, by taking the opponent's shape and moving its last entry to the front. Elizalde and Lin conjectured this rotation rule for shapes of every length k; this paper proves it for every k ≥ 3 and shows that for k ≥ 8 the edge is at least about 0.0053/(k + 1). The proof rewrites the winning margin as a positive number times a difference of two signed sums over chains of overlapping occurrences, called clusters, proves that the clusters living on any single ordering cancel down to −1, 0 or 1, and then shows that the first nonzero term of the difference favors the rotation and outweighs everything after it. For k ≥ 8 that comparison is a page of inequalities; for 3 ≤ k ≤ 7 it is finished by exact rational arithmetic on a computer.

By the end you'll be able to explain
  • what Penney's game for permutations is, why the answer does not depend on the distribution of the numbers, and what the rotation R(A) does (Theorem 1.3, Conjecture 1.2);
  • how first-occurrence probabilities become counts of orderings and exponential generating functions, and why the margin equals F(1)D, the expected game length times a difference of cluster series (Lemma 2.2, Proposition 3.4, Eqs. 1 to 3 and 6);
  • why the signed clusters on any one ordering add up to −1, 0 or 1, through a telescoping partial-sum trick (Lemma 3.1), and how that tames the infinite tail (Lemmas 3.2, 3.3, Eq. 5);
  • how to count orderings with two overlapping occurrences by shuffling chains inside gaps (Lemma 4.1, Eq. 9), and why the first nonzero term dk+1 is at least 1 for the rotation (Lemma 4.2);
  • how a geometric majorant proves D > 0 for every k ≥ 8 (Proposition 5.1, Eqs. 12 to 14), and how exact certificates finish k = 3 to 7 (Section 6, Table 1);
  • what is proved, what is computed, and which questions remain open (Questions 7.1 and 7.2).
