Running examples
  • Example A: 123 against 312. The first player waits for three increasing numbers; the reply is R(123) = 312, a high number followed by a low and a middle one. This is the paper's Example 1.1. Elizalde and Lin computed that 123 comes first with probability about 0.342, so the rotation wins about 0.658 of the time.
  • Example B: 213 against 321. The reply R(213) = 321 is monotone, and for k = 3 this is the closest race among the rotation pairs: Elizalde and Lin's table gives 0.450 for 213 coming first. In the paper's Table 2 it is the pair with the smallest certified bound. All counts for Example B below were computed by us by listing permutations.
1 · THE GAME

What is Penney's game for permutations, and what does the conjecture claim?

The original game, proposed by Penney in 1969, uses a fair coin. Each player names a word of three letters over {H, T}, the coin is tossed until one of the two words shows up as three consecutive tosses, and the owner of that word wins. The surprise is that the second player can always choose a word that wins more than half the time, so the relation "beats" is not transitive: there are words X, Y, Z with Y beating X, Z beating Y and X beating Z. Conway found a formula for the odds, Li proved a general version with martingales, and Guibas and Odlyzko showed from the overlap structure of words that the second player always has a winning reply. As Elizalde and Lin recount, Guibas and Odlyzko and, later, Felix showed that the winning reply can be taken of the form b a₁⋯ak−1: drop the opponent's last letter and put a suitable letter in front.

The permutation version replaces coin tosses by real numbers. A sequence X₁, X₂, … of independent random variables with a common continuous distribution is observed, so no two are equal, and each player names a permutation of length k. What matters about k consecutive numbers is only their relative order, recorded by the standardization: replace each entry by its rank among the k. For instance st(0.62, 0.30, 0.45) = 312, since 0.62 is the largest, 0.30 the smallest and 0.45 in the middle.

Definition · consecutive occurrence and waiting time

In words: Tπ is the first time at which the last k observations are in the same relative order as π. A window of k adjacent observations with that order is a consecutive occurrence of π; in this paper every occurrence is consecutive.

The game between patterns A and B ends at min(TA, TB), and A wins if TA < TB. The two times are never equal, because a single window has only one pattern.

Fact · the distribution does not matter

For independent observations with a common continuous law, the relative order of X₁, …, Xn is a uniformly random permutation: each of the n! orderings has probability 1/n!. Every first-occurrence probability is therefore a sum of counts of permutations divided by factorials, and is the same for uniform, normal or any other continuous law.

whyWhy is every ordering equally likely?

This is the standard argument, not specific to the paper. The joint distribution of (X₁, …, Xn) is unchanged when the variables are permuted, because they are independent with the same law. Permuting the variables maps the event "the ordering is σ" onto the event "the ordering is τ" for any pair σ, τ, so all n! orderings have the same probability. Ties have probability zero for a continuous law, so these n! events cover everything and each has probability 1/n!.

∎

The second player's proposed reply is a rotation.

Definition · the rotation

In words: move the last entry of A to the front. For A = 123 this gives B = 312, and for A = 213 it gives B = 321.

Here is the intuition, which is ours and not the paper's. The last k − 1 entries of B are a₁⋯ak−1, so they have the same relative order as the first k − 1 entries of A. Whenever an occurrence of A at some window is preceded by the right observation, B has already occurred one step earlier, ending the game before A gets its turn. The rotation copies the coin-game reply: drop the last symbol of A and put something in front.

Conjecture 1.2 (Elizalde and Lin) and Theorem 1.3

For every k ≥ 3 and every A ∈ 𝔖k,

Elizalde and Lin verified the conjecture for k = 3 and supported it numerically for k = 4; this paper proves it for every k ≥ 3. The theorem does not say the rotation is the best reply. Elizalde and Lin give cases where another reply does better: 2134 beats 2341 by more than 1234 does, and finding an optimal reply is their open Problem 6.2.

Example A can be started by hand. At n = 3 the game ends with A for the single ordering 123 and with B for 312, each with probability 1/6. At n = 4 the game must not have ended at n = 3, and the last three of four numbers must form a target. The paper lists them: the game ends with A only for 2134, and with B for 1423, 2413, 3412 and 4312. The orderings 1234, 3124 and 4123 also end with an occurrence of 123, but their first three entries already form 123 or 312, so the game was over earlier. Hence

The ordering 4123 shows the rotation at work: 412 is an occurrence of B and 123 follows one step later, too late. For Example B the same count (ours) gives 1 ordering for each player at n = 3, and 2 orderings ending with A against 3 ending with B at n = 4.

The animation plays the game on actual numbers. Each step draws one observation, standardizes the last three, and stops at the first target. The first preset is built so that B appears one step before an increasing run would have completed A; the second lets A win; the third draws fresh random numbers.

Animation · one game, 123 against 312
current windowearlier observationsnumber under a bar: its rank inside the window

For k = 3, Elizalde and Lin computed every pairwise probability exactly as a convergent series. Their table gives, for the six rotation pairs, Pr(A first) = 0.342 for 123 against 312 and for 321 against 132, 0.461 for 132 against 213 and for 312 against 231, and 0.450 for 213 against 321 and for 231 against 123. All six are below one half, which is the case k = 3 of the conjecture.

For words, Conway's formula gives the odds from how the two words overlap themselves and each other. For example (our evaluation of the formula as stated by Elizalde and Lin), the coin word 100 comes before 000 with probability 7/8. No such formula is known for permutations, because an overlap between two occurrences fixes only the relative order of the shared entries, not their values, and the race depends on arbitrarily long chains of overlapping occurrences.

In short: the game waits for the first window of k consecutive observations whose relative order is A or B; every ordering of n observations has probability 1/n!, so the problem is counting permutations; the conjecture, now Theorem 1.3, says the rotation B = aka₁⋯ak−1 wins with probability above 1/2 for every A.

2 · FROM PROBABILITIES TO COUNTS

How do the winning probabilities become sums over permutations?

Because each ordering of the first n observations has probability 1/n!, the probability that the game ends at time n with pattern A is a count divided by n!. The paper names three counts. Call a window a target if its pattern is A or B, and number window starts from zero, so start i is the window Xi+1⋯Xi+k.

Definition · the three counts

αn counts permutations of length n that contain no target, with α₀ = 1. The numbers uAn and uBn count permutations of length n whose only target is the final window, with pattern A or B respectively. In words: αn counts orderings where the game is still running after n observations, and uAn counts orderings where it ends at exactly time n with A winning.

So Pr(T > n) = αn/n! with T = min(TA, TB), and

Sums of the form Σ an zn/n! are exponential generating functions. They are the natural bookkeeping device here for two reasons. Setting z = 1 turns counts into probabilities, as above. And multiplying two of them corresponds to splitting a permutation into a left part and a right part: if bm and cj count two kinds of structure, then the coefficient of zn/n! in the product is Σj C(n, j) bn−j cj, where C(n, j) chooses which j of the n values go to the right part. The paper defines

Then UA(1) = Pr(TA < TB) and UB(1) = Pr(TB < TA), and F(1) = Σn Pr(T > n) = E[T], the expected length of the game, a fact the paper uses at the end.

For Example A, listing all permutations up to length 8 (our computation) gives

and α₀, α₁, α₂ = 1, 1, 2. The columns n = 3 and n = 4 are the counts of Example 1.1. B leads at every n in this table, which is the pattern behind Question 7.1 at the end of the chapter.

Listing every permutation becomes slow beyond about n = 11, where there are almost 40 million, but the probabilities can be computed exactly by building orderings one observation at a time, which is also how the paper's Section 6 computes its certificates. To append an observation to an ordering of length n, insert it at a rank r ∈ {0, …, n} and raise every existing rank that is at least r by one. Every permutation of length n + 1 arises exactly once, from the ordering of its first n entries and the rank of its last entry. For k = 3 the only thing needed to recognize the next window is the ranks of the last two entries, so the state of a still-running game is that pair of ranks, and each of the n + 1 insertion ranks has probability 1/(n + 1).

The animation runs this recursion in the page for both running examples. Each step adds one observation and shows the probability that the game ends at that time with each pattern, together with the running totals. The method is the paper's; the run on these two examples is ours.

For Example A the totals settle at 0.3421 and 0.6579, and for Example B at 0.4497 and 0.5503, matching Elizalde and Lin's table to its three digits. The recursion also gives E[T] = F(1) ≈ 5.18 for both examples; these values are ours.

In short: Pr(T > n) = αn/n! and Pr(game ends at n with A) = uAn/n!; exponential generating functions F, UA, UB package these counts, evaluate to probabilities at z = 1, and multiply when permutations are split into a left and a right part.

3 · SIGNED CLUSTERS

How can "the only target is the last one" be counted without tracking everything before it?

The direct count uAn asks that no earlier window be a target, and conditions of the form "nothing happens" are hard to count. Inclusion and exclusion trades them for conditions of the form "these things happen", which are easier, at the price of signs. The basic identity is that for any finite set of size r,

by the binomial theorem. So if every ordering is counted once for each set M of its target occurrences that it chooses to "mark", with sign (−1)|M|, then orderings with no targets count 1 and all others cancel to 0. The clusters of Goulden and Jackson organize these marked sets, and Elizalde and Noy adapted them to consecutive patterns.

Definition 2.1 · marked occurrences and clusters

A marked occurrence of σ ∈ 𝔖n is a target occurrence whose start has been selected. A cluster of length n is a permutation σ ∈ 𝔖n together with a set of marked occurrences such that the first marked start is 0, the last marked start is n − k, and successive marked starts differ by less than k. A cluster with s marks has weight (−1)s.

In words: a cluster is a chain of marked windows covering the whole permutation, each overlapping the next, with sign + for an even number of marks and − for an odd number.

The paper's example: for A = 123 and B = 312, the permutation 4123 has B at start 0 and A at start 1. Marking both gives a cluster of length 4 with weight (−1)² = 1 whose last mark is A. Marking only start 1 is not a cluster, because a cluster's first mark is at start 0. Because A and B are distinct patterns of the same length, each marked start carries exactly one of the two labels.

Let cAn and cBn be the total weights of clusters of length n whose last marked occurrence is A or B, and form

The single-mark clusters are A and B themselves, each with weight −1, so cAk = cBk = −1. The differences change sign and grow, so whatever argument decides the sign of their weighted sum has to control the whole tail, not just the first terms. The link between clusters and the game is Lemma 2.2.

Lemma 2.2 · first occurrences from clusters

For every n ≥ k,

Equivalently, as formal power series,

proofWhy does a first occurrence factor as "anything avoiding" times "a cluster"?

The paper proves the identity for A; B is the same with labels exchanged. Consider pairs (σ, M) where σ ∈ 𝔖n ends with A and M is a set of target occurrences of σ containing the final one, with weight (−1)|M|−1. If σ has r earlier target occurrences, its weights sum to (1 − 1)r, which is 1 if r = 0 and 0 otherwise. So the total weight of all pairs is uAn.

Now cut each pair. List the marked starts in increasing order, and let s be the smallest marked start from which all successive marked starts differ by less than k. Every marked start before s is at most s − k, so its window lies inside the first s positions. Let π = st(σ₁⋯σs) carry the marks before s, and γ = st(σs+1⋯σn) carry the rest, shifted by s. Standardization preserves the relative order inside each window, so all marks remain target occurrences. Then γ is a cluster of length j = n − s with last pattern A, and π is any permutation of length n − j with any set of marked occurrences.

Conversely, choose which n − j of the values {1, …, n} go to the left (C(n, j) ways), a marked permutation π of length n − j and a cluster γ of length j. Arranging the chosen values in the order of π followed by the others in the order of γ gives a unique pair (σ, M), and cutting it returns π and γ because the marks of π end at least k starts before the first mark of γ. The weight factors as

For a fixed π, the weights (−1)|Mπ| sum to 1 if π avoids both targets and 0 otherwise, so the total over all π of length n − j is αn−j. Summing over j gives (2), and multiplying by zn/n! and summing over n gives (3).

∎

As a check at n = 4 for Example A, with α₁ = 1 and α₀ = 1, Eq. (2) gives uA4 = −(C(4,3)·1·(−1) + 1·1·3) = −(−4 + 3) = 1 and uB4 = −(−4 + 0) = 4, the two counts of Example 1.1. We checked (2) the same way through n = 8, and the paper reports the same check against direct counts for every pattern of length 3 and 4.

Setting z = 1 in (3) turns the identity into a statement about the game. Subtracting the two halves gives the paper's central reduction.

Proposition 3.4 · the margin as a product

Let D = CA(1) − CB(1). Then

So B wins with probability above 1/2 exactly when D > 0.

proofWhy can the power series be evaluated at z = 1?

The windows at starts 0, k, 2k, … use disjoint observations, so they are independent, and avoiding all targets requires each of the first ⌊n/k⌋ of them to miss, giving

Hence F(1) is finite, and F(1) ≥ α₀ = 1. The same estimate shows that some target appears with probability one. The event that the game ends at time n with A has probability uAn/n!, so UA(1) = Pr(TA < TB) and UB(1) = Pr(TB < TA). Section 4 shows that CA(1) and CB(1) converge absolutely (Lemma 3.3). For absolutely convergent series, Mertens' theorem says the Cauchy product (2) converges to the product of the sums, so evaluating (3) at 1 is legitimate, and subtracting gives (6).

∎

For Example A, the recursion of Section 2 gives F(1) ≈ 5.1838 and a margin of 0.6579 − 0.3421 ≈ 0.3157, so D ≈ 0.0609 and 3!·D ≈ 0.365 (our numbers). The paper certifies 3!·D ≥ 0.3018 for this pair (Table 2), consistent with that value.

In short: signed clusters, chains of overlapping marked occurrences with weight (−1)marks, turn "the last window is the first target" into U = −F·C (Lemma 2.2); evaluated at 1 this says the rotation's margin is E[T] times D = CA(1) − CB(1) (Eq. 6), so the whole theorem is the inequality D > 0.

4 · CANCELLATION ON ONE ORDERING

Why can the cluster series be controlled at all, when its terms grow?

The cluster counts in the table above grow, and the number of marked sets on a long ordering grows exponentially. The paper's key observation is that on any one ordering almost all of them cancel. Fix an ordering σ ∈ 𝔖k+d whose first and last windows are targets, and list its actual target starts as 0 = t₁ < t₂ < ⋯ < tr = d. For 1 ≤ j ≤ r, let wj be the total weight of the marked sets that contain t₁ and tj, lie inside {t₁, …, tj}, and have successive differences less than k. Then wr is the total weight of all clusters on σ.

Lemma 3.1 · near-total cancellation

For each ordering, wr ∈ {−1, 0, 1}. Moreover wr = 0 unless the actual target starts connect 0 to d with successive differences less than k.

The proof sorts marked sets by their second-to-last mark ti, which must lie within k − 1 of tj. Adding one more mark flips the sign, so

The sum runs over a contiguous block of indices, which makes it a difference of partial sums. Set S₀ = 0 and Sj = w₁ + ⋯ + wj, and let ℓ(j) be the largest index with tℓ(j) ≤ tj − k, or 0 if there is none. Then wj = −(Sj−1 − Sℓ(j)), and therefore

proofWhy does Sj = Sℓ(j) force every weight into {−1, 0, 1}?

Each Sj with j > 1 equals an earlier partial sum, because ℓ(j) < j. Starting from S₀ = 0 and S₁ = −1, induction on j shows Sj ∈ {0, −1} for every j. Then wj = Sj − Sj−1 is a difference of two numbers in {0, −1}, so it lies in {−1, 0, 1}. If two consecutive actual starts differ by at least k, no admissible marked set can cross that gap, so no marked set reaches tr and wr = 0.

∎

The animation applies the recurrence to three orderings of length 10 for Example A, chosen by us so that all three outcomes appear: σ₁ has a target at every start and 21 clusters, σ₂ has six targets and 3 clusters, σ₃ has seven targets and 8 clusters. Each step adds one start, computes wj from the window of earlier starts within distance 2, and updates Sj. The last frame checks the answer by listing every admissible marked set, which the page does by brute force.

Write dn = cAn − cBn. An ordering of length k + d contributes ±wr to dk+d, with the sign set by the pattern of its last window. Let Gd be the event that targets occur at starts 0 and d and that the actual occurrences between them have successive differences less than k. By Lemma 3.1 the contribution is 0 outside Gd and at most 1 in absolute value on Gd, so dividing by the number of orderings,

The same bound holds for |cAk+d| and |cBk+d| separately. A signed sum over exponentially many marked sets has become a probability, and probabilities of long connected chains of targets are small. To make that precise the paper puts

A block of k − 1 consecutive starts uses L observations, and by the union bound it contains a target with probability at most (k − 1)p = q. Since 2(k − 1) < k! for k ≥ 3, q < 1.

Lemma 3.2 · a connected chain hits every block

If the actual target starts connect 0 to d with successive differences less than k, then every block {a, a + 1, …, a + k − 2} with 0 < a and a + k − 2 < d contains a target start.

proofWhy can a chain with short steps not jump over k − 1 consecutive starts?

Let x be the smallest start of the chain with x ≥ a; it exists because d ≥ a. Its predecessor y in the chain satisfies y < a and x − y < k, so x ≤ y + k − 1 ≤ a + k − 2. Thus x lies in the block.

∎

Lemma 3.3 · the tail is small

The two cluster series converge absolutely at 1, and

proofWhere do the factors p², L and 1/(1 − q) come from?

Fix d ≥ k, so the windows at starts 0 and d are disjoint. Between them, place blocks of L observations starting at observations k, k + L, k + 2L, …, keeping only blocks that end before observation d; there are m = ⌊(d − k)/L⌋ of them. In each block, the first k − 1 window starts have their windows inside the block. By Lemma 3.2, Gd requires a target among those starts in every block. The two end windows and the m blocks use disjoint observations, so independence gives Pr(Gd) ≤ p²qm.

Each value of m comes from exactly L values of d ≥ k, so

Equation (4) turns this into (5), and the same argument for cA and cB gives absolute convergence.

∎

The bound (5) is tiny for large k and useless for small k. Evaluating it (our arithmetic) gives 4/3 at k = 3, 1/18 at k = 4 and 1/420 at k = 5, while the first nonzero term of D is only dk+1/(k + 1)!, which is 3/24 for Example A. That is why the small cases need the sharper, computed tail bound of Section 7.

In short: on one ordering, the cluster weights obey wj = −(Sj−1 − Sℓ(j)), so the partial sums only ever copy earlier values and every total is −1, 0 or 1 (Lemma 3.1); hence |dk+d|/(k + d)! is at most the probability of a connected chain of targets, which decays geometrically (Lemmas 3.2, 3.3, Eq. 5).

5 · TWO OVERLAPPING OCCURRENCES

How many orderings carry one pattern and then another, d steps later?

With the tail under control, the head of D, the terms with d < k, decides the sign. For d < k the clusters of length k + d are simple, so the head reduces to counting orderings with two overlapping prescribed windows. For 1 ≤ d < k and U, V ∈ 𝔖k, let Nd(U, V) be the number of permutations of length k + d with pattern U at start 0 and pattern V at start d. The two windows share the k − d positions d + 1, …, k.

First, the two patterns must agree on the shared positions: st(ud+1⋯uk) = st(v₁⋯vk−d). If they do, the shared entries form a chain c₁ < ⋯ < ck−d that cuts the remaining values into k − d + 1 gaps. Let αj be the number of the first window's exclusive entries (the first d) that lie in gap j, and βj the number of the second window's exclusive entries (the last d) in gap j. These are read off from U and V alone: αj counts i ≤ d with ui between the j-th and (j + 1)-th smallest of ud+1, …, uk, and βj is defined in the same way from V. (These αj are not the avoidance counts αn; the paper reuses the letter.)

Lemma 4.1 · overlap counts

If the orders of U and V on the shared positions are incompatible, Nd(U, V) = 0. Otherwise

Moreover (αj) = (βj) if and only if {u₁, …, ud} = {vk−d+1, …, vk}.

In words: inside each gap, the entries from the left window and those from the right window can be interleaved in any way that keeps each side's own order, and different gaps do not interact.

proofWhy is the count a product of binomial coefficients?

A permutation is determined by all the pairwise comparisons among its entries. The first window fixes every comparison among its own entries, and the second window fixes every comparison among its own. The only comparisons left are between an entry exclusive to the first window and an entry exclusive to the second. If the two lie in different gaps, the shared chain already orders them. Inside gap j, the αj left entries come in an order fixed by U and the βj right entries in an order fixed by V, so a total order of the gap is a shuffle of two chains, and there are C(αj + βj, αj) shuffles. Every choice of shuffles, one per gap, gives a total order restricting to U and V. If the shared orders conflict, no total order exists.

For the last statement, encode a vector γ = (γ₀, …, γk−d) with sum d as a word of length k: γ₀ letters x, one s, γ₁ letters x, one s, and so on, ending with γk−d letters x. Let ρ(γ) be the set of positions of the letters x. Counting x's between consecutive s's recovers γ, so ρ is injective. Listing the values 1, …, k of U in increasing order and marking each as exclusive (x) or shared (s) produces exactly this word for γ = (αj), so ρ(α) = {u₁, …, ud}; likewise ρ(β) = {vk−d+1, …, vk}. Injectivity of ρ gives the claim.

∎

For d = 1 each window has a single exclusive entry, in gap u₁ − 1 for the first and vk − 1 for the second, so N₁(U, V) is 2 when u₁ = vk and 1 otherwise, provided the shared orders agree. For Example A at d = 2 (our worked case of Eq. 9), take U = 123 and V = 312. The single shared entry is the third, the largest in 123 and the largest in 312, so both exclusive pairs lie below it: α = β = (2, 0), and N₂(123, 312) = C(4, 2)·C(0, 0) = 6. Listing them confirms it: 12534, 13524, 14523, 23514, 24513, 34512.

Now the rotation enters. An ordering of length k + 1 with targets at both starts carries exactly one two-mark cluster, of weight +1, and the single-mark clusters live at length k. So

Lemma 4.2 · the first nonzero term favors the rotation

Let B = R(A). Then dk+1 ≥ 1.

proofWhy does B-then-A count twice while A-then-B counts at most once?

For (U, V) = (B, A), both shared orders are st(a₁⋯ak−1), and u₁ = ak = vk, so N₁(B, A) = 2. For (U, V) = (A, B), u₁ = a₁ and vk = ak−1, which differ because k ≥ 3, so N₁(A, B) ≤ 1.

A pattern overlaps itself in k − 1 positions only if it is monotone: compatibility of st(u₂⋯uk) with st(u₁⋯uk−1) says that ui+1 > ui exactly when ui+2 > ui+1, so all adjacent comparisons go the same way. Thus N₁(B, B) ≤ 1, with equality only for monotone B. If B = 12⋯k, then A = 23⋯k1; the last two entries of a₂⋯ak decrease while the last two of b₁⋯bk−1 increase, so N₁(A, B) = 0. The case B = k⋯21 is symmetric.

So either B is not monotone, N₁(B, B) = 0 and N₁(A, B) ≤ 1, or B is monotone, N₁(B, B) = 1 and N₁(A, B) = 0. With N₁(A, A) ≥ 0 and N₁(B, A) = 2, in both cases dk+1 ≥ 1.

∎

For Example A the paper computes N₁(A, A) = 1, N₁(B, A) = 2 and N₁(A, B) = N₁(B, B) = 0, so d₄ = 3, agreeing with uB4 − uA4 = 4 − 1 = 3. For Example B, where B = 321 is monotone, our count gives N₁(A, A) = 0, N₁(B, A) = 2, N₁(A, B) = 0 and N₁(B, B) = 1, so d₄ = 1, the value in the paper's Table 2. A monotone reply pays for overlapping itself, which is why these pairs are the closest races.

The next terms, 2 ≤ d < k, can be negative, and the paper bounds how negative.

Lemma 4.3 · the middle terms

Let B = R(A). For 2 ≤ d < k,

proofWhere do the central binomial coefficients come from?

For d < k, every start between 0 and d is within k − 1 of both ends, so every set of marks containing 0 and d is a cluster. If an ordering has r interior targets, its optional marks contribute (1 − 1)r. So an ordering contributes only if its only targets are the two ends, and then with weight +1. A negative contribution to dk+d therefore needs last pattern B, which gives (10).

For (11), put nj = αj + βj, so Σ nj = 2d. Vandermonde's identity, which counts d-element subsets of a 2d-set split into blocks of sizes nj, says

over vectors γ with 0 ≤ γj ≤ nj and Σ γj = d. Both γ = (αj) and γ = (βj) appear, and since C(nj, βj) = C(nj, αj), each term equals Nd(U, V). So Nd(U, V) ≤ C(2d, d) always, and ≤ ½C(2d, d) when (αj) ≠ (βj).

By Lemma 4.1 the vectors differ exactly when the rank sets of the exclusive entries differ. For (B, B) these are the values of B on its first d and on its last d positions, different position sets when d < k, so different value sets. For (A, B) they are the values of A on positions 1, …, d and on k − d, …, k − 1, which differ when d < k − 1. Applying the half bound to both pairs when d < k − 1, and only to (B, B) when d = k − 1, gives (11).

∎

Example A shows that (11) can be tight and that the middle terms can outweigh the first (our check). At d = 2 = k − 1, N₂(A, B) = 6 and N₂(B, B) = 3, and the bound is (3/2)·C(4, 2) = 9. Our cluster enumeration gives d₅ = −9 exactly: all nine orderings with 312 at start 2 and a target at start 0 have no target at start 1, while every ordering with 123 at start 2 and a target at start 0 does. Weighted by 1/n!, the first two terms are 3/24 − 9/120 = 0.05 > 0, so the first term still wins, but not by much.

In short: two overlapping windows determine every comparison except those inside the gaps of the shared chain, so Nd is a product of shuffle counts (Eq. 9); the rotation's overlap B-then-A counts 2 at d = 1, which makes dk+1 ≥ 1 (Lemma 4.2), and Vandermonde's identity caps the negative middle terms by central binomial coefficients (Eqs. 10, 11).

6 · EVERY LENGTH FROM EIGHT ON

How do one positive term, a few bounded terms and a small tail combine into D > 0?

Multiply D by k! and split k!D = Σd≥1 k! dk+d/(k + d)! into three pieces: the term d = 1, the terms 2 ≤ d ≤ k − 1, and the tail d ≥ k. Lemma 4.2 makes the first at least k!/(k + 1)! = 1/(k + 1). Lemma 4.3 bounds each middle term below by −C(2d, d) k!/(k + d)!, with an extra factor 3/2 at d = k − 1. Lemma 3.3 bounds the tail. With

the three lemmas give

Proposition 5.1 · the uniform estimate

For k ≥ 8 and A ∈ 𝔖k,

proofWhy do Sk and Hk together stay below 1/(k + 1)?

From (d + 1)C(2d + 2, d + 1) = 2(2d + 1)C(2d, d), consecutive terms satisfy

For d ≥ 2 this is at most 4/(k + 3), because 4(d + 1)(k + d + 1) − 2(2d + 1)(k + 3) = 4d(d − 1) + 2(k − 1) ≥ 0. So fd ≤ f₂(4/(k + 3))d−2 with f₂ = 6/((k + 1)(k + 2)). Writing Sk = Σd=2k−1 fd + ½fk−1 and summing the geometric majorant,

Both pieces decrease for k ≥ 8: the derivative of (x + 3)/((x + 2)(x − 1)) has numerator −x² − 6x − 5 < 0, and in the second the prefactor and the base decrease while the exponent increases with the base in (0, 1). Also (k + 1)Hk = 8(k² − 1)/(k! − 2(k − 1)) decreases for k ≥ 8, because the denominator at k + 1 exceeds k + 1 times the denominator at k (since 2k < 2(k + 1)(k − 1)), while the numerator grows by the factor k(k + 2)/((k − 1)(k + 1)) < k + 1. Evaluating all three at k = 8,

Combining with (12), k!D ≥ (1 − 3106970325/3245660803)/(k + 1), which is (13).

∎

We recomputed (14) in exact rational arithmetic and it holds as stated; the difference 1 − 3106970325/3245660803 is exactly 138690478/3245660803. Evaluating the right side of (12) directly, without the geometric majorant (our computation), shows why the cutoff is 8: it is −8.2, −1.48, −0.356, −0.081 and −0.0083 for k = 3 to 7, then +0.0147 at k = 8 and +0.0247 at k = 9. At k = 7 the worst-case bounds fail by 0.0083, about 7 percent of 1/(k + 1), so the small lengths need exact counts instead of bounds.

The margin itself follows from (6). For n ≥ k the first n observations contain n − k + 1 windows, so by the union bound Pr(T > n) ≥ 1 − (n − k + 1)p. Summing with M = 1/p = k!/2,

Corollary 6.3 · how big the edge is

For every k ≥ 8 and every A ∈ 𝔖k,

The constant is about 0.00534, the 0.0053/(k + 1) of the abstract. It comes from F(1)D/2 with F(1) ≥ k!/4 and (13).

In short: k!D ≥ 1/(k + 1) − Sk − Hk (Eq. 12); the middle terms shrink geometrically with ratio at most 4/(k + 3), the tail is O(k²/k!), and at k = 8 their total is 3106970325/3245660803 of 1/(k + 1) (Eq. 14), which proves D > 0 for every k ≥ 8 and an edge of at least about 0.0053/(k + 1).

7 · LENGTHS THREE TO SEVEN

How are the five remaining lengths certified exactly?

For 3 ≤ k ≤ 7 the paper replaces bounds by exact integers and rational numbers, and checks every pattern. Two reductions shrink the work. The complement Ā = (k + 1 − a₁)⋯(k + 1 − ak) turns the picture upside down; it commutes with rotation and preserves all cluster counts and first-occurrence probabilities, and no permutation of length k ≥ 2 is its own complement. So it suffices to check the k!/2 patterns that come before their complements in lexicographic order: 3, 12, 60, 360 and 2520 representatives.

For k = 6 and 7 the exact overlap counts (9) replace their upper bounds in (12):

and Lemmas 3.3, 4.2 and 4.3 give k!D ≥ J(A). For k = 3, 4 and 5, J(A) is negative for 3, 12 and 18 of the representatives respectively, so a finer certificate is used. For h ≥ 1, let Qh be the event that a target occurs at start 0 and its connected chain of actual occurrences reaches a start at least h, and let rh = Pr(Qh). By the argument of Lemma 3.2, Qh depends only on the first R = h + 2k − 2 observations.

Lemma 3.5 · a computed tail bound

For h ≥ 1 and R = h + 2k − 2,

and consequently

proofHow does rh replace one factor of p in Lemma 3.3?

For d ≥ R, the event Gd implies Qh, a target at start d, and a target among the first k − 1 starts of every block of L observations beginning at observations R, R + L, … and ending before observation d. These involve disjoint sets of observations, so Pr(Gd) ≤ rh p q⌊(d−R)/L⌋. Summing over d ≥ R gives rhpL/(1 − q), the right side of (7). Since cAk = cBk = −1, dk = 0, and (8) follows from (4) and (7).

∎

The coefficients dk+i and the probability rh come from the insertion recurrence of Section 2, started from the two orderings A and B, so that every ordering with a target at start 0 is produced exactly once. The state of an ordering records the ranks of its last k − 1 entries among all n, the distance back to its latest target start, and the last k values of a bit bi = −Si, where Si is the partial sum of Lemma 3.1 indexed by start position (constant between targets and zero at negative indices). By the proof of Lemma 3.1, a target at start i gives

and a non-target start gives bi = bi−1 and wi = 0, so each bi is 0 or 1. A final A contributes wi to dk+i and a final B contributes −wi. The starting orderings A and B have distance zero, b₀ = 1 and b−1 = ⋯ = b1−k = 0. After k − 1 starts in a row with no target, nothing later can reconnect to start 0, so such states are dropped. If Mi,g counts retained orderings with a target at start i whose preceding target is at i − g, then (Lemma 6.1)

The sum splits Qh by the first chain start i ≥ h; its predecessor is below h, so the gap g exceeds i − h, and connectivity forces g < k, hence i ≤ h + k − 2.

Proposition 6.2 · the certificates

For 3 ≤ k ≤ 7 and every A ∈ 𝔖k, D > 0. For k = 3, 4, 5 the paper evaluates k! times the right side of (8) with h = 13, 4, 1 and rh from (17), using permutations up to length 19, 13 and 13. For k = 6, 7 it evaluates J(A). The minimum certified values of k!D are

for k = 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, all strictly positive.

For 3 ≤ k ≤ 6 the smallest bound occurs when B is monotone, where dk+1 = 1; for k = 7 the monotone case is second smallest, behind A = 1526374. At k = 3 the minimum belongs to Example B (213 against 321), certified at 0.0531, against Example A's 0.3018. The whole computation over 3 + 12 + 60 + 360 + 2520 representatives took about one minute on a laptop. The paper cross-checked it three ways: the coefficients dn from the recurrence agree with direct cluster sums over all permutations through n = 8 for every pattern of length 3 and 4; Eq. (2) agrees with direct first-occurrence counts through n = 8 for the same patterns; and the product formula (9) agrees with direct counts for every pair U, V with k ≤ 5 and every 1 ≤ d < k.

The proof of Theorem 1.3 is now complete: Proposition 5.1 gives D > 0 for k ≥ 8, Proposition 6.2 for 3 ≤ k ≤ 7, Proposition 3.4 converts D > 0 into Pr(TB < TA) > Pr(TA < TB), and since a target occurs almost surely and the two patterns cannot first occur together, the two probabilities sum to one.

In short: complements halve the work; for k = 6, 7 exact overlap counts (J(A), Eq. 15) suffice, and for k = 3, 4, 5 exact cluster coefficients from an insertion recurrence carrying one bit per start (Eq. 16) plus a computed tail bound (Eqs. 7, 8, 17) certify k!D > 0 for every pattern.

8 · WHAT REMAINS OPEN

Does the rotation lead at every single time step, and how big is its edge?

The proof compares the two players only after summing over all stopping times. A stronger statement would compare them time by time. Write an = uAn and bn = uBn. The argument of Lemma 4.2 gives bk = ak = 1 and bk+1 − ak+1 = 2 + N₁(A, A) − N₁(A, B) − N₁(B, B) ∈ {1, 2, 3}. The paper computed minA(bn − an) by enumerating all permutations of length n for every 3 ≤ k < n ≤ 11, and the minimum was always positive (Table 5).

Question 7.1

Is bn > an for every k ≥ 3, every A ∈ 𝔖k and every n > k? In words: at every fixed time after the first, are there more orderings on which the rotation wins exactly then? A yes would give a second proof of Theorem 1.3.

The obvious injection fails. For A = 132 and B = 213, the ordering 1243 first meets a target at its final window, 243, which has pattern 132. Rotating its last three entries gives 1324, which ends with 213 but already begins with 132.

The second question is about size. Corollary 6.3 shows the edge is at least of order 1/k. The leading term of D suggests that order is attained: when B is monotone, dk+1 = 1 and the first term of (12) is only 1/(k + 1).

Question 7.2

Is minA∈𝔖k Pr(TR(A) < TA) − 1/2 of order 1/k as k → ∞?

In short: exhaustive enumeration up to n = 11 supports a time-by-time version of the theorem (Question 7.1), the worst-case edge may really shrink like 1/k (Question 7.2), and the optimal reply (Elizalde and Lin's Problem 6.2) is still unknown.

From the paper's Table 5, the minimum over A of bn − an is 1 at n = k + 1 for every k from 3 to 10, and for k = 3 runs 1, 2, 5, 22, 102, 587, 4120, 30624 for n = 4 to 11. The edge for k ≥ 8 is at least 69345239/(12982643212(k + 1)) ≈ 0.00534/(k + 1) (Corollary 6.3). For comparison, Elizalde and Lin's exact k = 3 probabilities give edges of 0.158, 0.039 and 0.050 above one half for the three complement classes of rotation pairs.

ASSESSMENT

What is shown, and what is claimed

Proved by hand. The reduction of the margin to F(1)D (Lemma 2.2, Proposition 3.4), the cancellation Lemma 3.1, the tail bounds (Lemmas 3.2, 3.3, 3.5), the overlap formula (Lemma 4.1), the positivity of the first term (Lemma 4.2), the middle-term bounds (Lemma 4.3) and the uniform estimate for k ≥ 8 (Proposition 5.1, Corollary 6.3). These are short and elementary, and each step can be checked with binomial coefficients, inclusion and exclusion, and a geometric series. In preparing this chapter we checked Example 1.1, Lemma 2.2 through n = 8, the values d₄ = 3 and d₄ = 1 for the two examples, the overlap counts N₂ in Example A, and the exact arithmetic of (13), (14) and Corollary 6.3; all agree with the paper.

Proved by computer. The cases 3 ≤ k ≤ 7 (Proposition 6.2) rest on exact rational computations over 2955 representatives, cross-checked against independent enumerations as described in Section 6.3. The paper states that the data and code are in a public repository; this chapter did not rerun them. The case k = 3 was already settled by Elizalde and Lin's exact formulas, which agree with the certificates.

Not claimed. The rotation is not claimed to be the best reply, and for some A it is not. The size of the edge is bounded below only; the constant 0.0053 comes from deliberately crude estimates (for instance F(1) ≥ k!/4 from the union bound), and whether the true minimum edge is of order 1/k is open (Question 7.2). The time-by-time statement bn > an is supported by enumeration through n = 11 but not proved.

Context. The paper is by a single independent researcher and appeared as an arXiv preprint; it has not yet been through peer review. The argument is self-contained and its finite computations are small, so independent verification is practical.

Why it matters. For words, the second player's advantage follows from Conway's closed formula. For permutations no such formula is known, and this paper shows that a sign question can still be settled by controlling an alternating cluster series: cancel on each ordering, bound the head with exact overlap counts, and bound the tail by a probability. That template applies to other questions about first occurrences of consecutive patterns.

FURTHER READING

Further reading

H. Roy Choudhury, The rotation strategy wins Penney's game for permutations, arXiv:2611.28063 (2026). The paper itself; numbering in this chapter follows its HTML version.

S. Elizalde and Y. Lin, Penney's game for permutations, arXiv:2404.06585, published in Discrete Mathematics & Theoretical Computer Science 28:1 (2026). The source of the game, the conjecture, the exact k = 3 probabilities used in Section 1, and Conway's formula for words.

Built from a full read of arXiv 2611.28063v1. Lemma, proposition, corollary, question, table and equation numbers match the paper; section numbers in this chapter are our own. Example B, the tables of αn, un and cn, the value d₅ = −9 and the k ≤ 7 evaluation of Eq. (12) are our computations. All three animations compute in the page: the first standardizes windows of actual numbers; the second runs the exact insertion recursion for first-occurrence probabilities; the third applies the recurrence of Lemma 3.1 and checks it against a brute-force sum over marked sets.

The Min-Cut Formulation of Ollivier-Ricci Curvature

Giorgio Micaletto · submitted Nov 24, announced Nov 25, 2026 · cs.DS · arXiv 2611.32528

Overview

The curvature of an edge in a network, a number that says whether the neighbourhoods of its two ends huddle together or splay apart, can be computed exactly with one minimum cut and without ever building a table of distances. The standard definition asks for the cheapest way to move one random-walk distribution onto another, which is a linear program whose costs are graph distances, so software either builds the distance table and calls a solver for every edge or settles for an approximation. This paper observes that for one-step walks only three distances occur, that the dual of the transport problem then has an optimal solution using only three price levels, and that writing those levels in unary turns the dual into a maximum-weight closure problem, which is a minimum cut. Adjacency lists alone decide every arc of the cut network, the network has size linear in the adjacency lists read, and the method is a median 6 times faster than the usual pipeline on 20 real networks while matching it to rounding error. A converse construction shows that no exact method can be faster than bipartite matching.

By the end you'll be able to explain
  • what Ollivier-Ricci curvature κ(i, j) = 1 − 𝒲₁(mi, mj) measures, and how to compute it by hand on a small graph;
  • the transport problem behind 𝒲₁, its dual in Eq. (1), and why a feasible dual solution certifies the answer;
  • why only the distances 1, 2 and 3 occur, decided by adjacency and common neighbours (Lemma 2);
  • why the dual has an integral optimum with three price levels, and how unary encoding turns it into a closure problem and then a minimum cut, giving 𝒲₁ = DA − F (Theorem 1, Corollary 3);
  • how to read off optimal prices and an optimal transport plan from the cut (Proposition 5), and the min-max formula of Corollary 4;
  • how relay nodes at common neighbours make the network linear in size (Proposition 6, Theorem 7), and why exact curvature is as hard as bipartite matching (Theorem 9);
  • what the experiments measure, and what they leave open.
